國朝以科目賓興天下士，每三歲一舉，禮聘儒碩以司校閱，則不異諸藩；而特出簡任，以翰林坊局詞臣二人主之，惟兩京為然。此固祖宗成法，著在令典，而公慎之意至於今日而益重。乃嘉靖丙午秋八月，寔維其期。順天府臣舉故事以請，上命左中允臣本、左贊善臣山往主試事。同考則進士臣攀龍、臣鏘、臣子充，推官臣德，知縣臣松，教
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Our dynasty selects and honors scholars throughout the realm through the examination system, holding an examination once every three years and respectfully engaging eminent Confucian scholars to oversee the assessment of papers. In this it does not differ among the provinces. Only at the two capitals, however, are two literary officials from the Hanlin Academy and the offices serving the Heir Apparent specially selected and appointed to preside. This is indeed an established practice of our imperial ancestors, recorded in the statutory codes; and the concern for impartiality and care has become still greater today.

The eighth month of autumn in the bingwu year of Jiajing [1546] was precisely the appointed time. The officials of Shuntian Prefecture invoked precedent and submitted their request. His Majesty commanded his servants Ben, Left Mentor, and Shan, Left Admonisher, to go and preside over the examination. The Associate Examiners were his servants Panlong, Qiang, and Zichong, metropolitan graduates (jinshi); De, a Prefectural Judge; Song, a District Magistrate; and an Instructor …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
授臣邦行教諭臣須樂臣履繩
臣巖皆蜚英甲科極一時之選
監試則御史臣豪臣懋提調則
府尹臣奎府丞臣瀛也而防範
綜理嚴整周密視諸曩歲有加
焉是月八日
陞辭入院臣等焚香再拜而誓曰
===
天下之事莫有大於貢士者即
如古人所稱無情如造化至公
如權衡猶懼不得眞才以塞
明詔於此而敢有一毫假公以濟其
私敢有一念自怠以奪其鑒不
惟不忠之罪莫逭而
天地鬼神共殛之矣僉曰所不與同

translation_en:
…Instructor Bangxing and Instructors Xule, Lüsheng, and Yan, all your servants, had won distinction in the higher examinations and represented the finest selection of their day. The examination monitors were Censors Hao and Mao; the Proctors were Prefect Kui and Vice Prefect Ying, all your servants. Precautions and overall administration were strict, orderly, thorough, and meticulous, surpassing those of previous years. On the eighth day of that month, we attended court to take our leave and entered the examination compound. We, your servants, burned incense, bowed twice, and swore:

“Among the affairs of the realm, none is greater than presenting worthy scholars. Even if we were, as the ancients said, as unfeeling as the workings of creation and as utterly impartial as a balance, we would still fear failing to obtain men of true talent to fulfill the illustrious edict. If in this undertaking anyone should dare, in the slightest degree, to use public duty as a pretext to advance private interests, or entertain a single thought of slackening his efforts and thereby impair his discernment, he shall not only be unable to escape punishment for disloyalty: Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits shall together strike him down.” All declared: “Should anyone fail to share in our common…

translation_en:
“…of one mind with us, may he be as this incense.” We then assembled the candidates selected by your servant Wang Da, the Education Censor, together with those selected by the six colleges and the various offices, numbering more than 3,300 in all, and examined them in three sessions. In accordance with the imperially prescribed quota, we selected 135 outstanding candidates and also transcribed twenty of their finest essays for presentation to the throne.
Your servant Ben, by virtue of the duties of his office, presumes to place this preface at the beginning of the volume. I humbly reflect that I am an insignificant scholar from the seacoast who passed the examinations while still young. Early on, I received the favor of cultivation and instruction, and was soon appointed to a historiographical post. Subsequently, I served as the second-ranking instructor at the Southern Directorate of Education and held acting charge of the seals of the Hanlin Academy at the secondary capital. During these fifteen years, the responsibilities I have unworthily held have extended no further than these two things: judging right and wrong impartially and assisting moral instruction. Whenever I examine and reproach myself, I am ashamed of my accumulating faults and neglect of duty [?]. On this occasion, I came to the imperial court for my second performance evaluation and reverently received…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
改留之
京闈校士而復蒙
任使之臣受
皇上之恩雖
天高地厚無以為喻第臣駑駘樗櫟
材不逮志愧生負結涓埃未效

translation_en:
…my reassignment to remain in the capital. For the examination of scholars at the capital’s Provincial Examination, I have again been entrusted with service. The favor Your Majesty has bestowed upon your servant cannot be likened even to the height of Heaven and the depth of Earth. Yet your servant is like a slow horse or worthless timber: my abilities fall short of my aspirations. I am ashamed that I have yet to repay your kindness, whether by bearing burdens in life or knotting grass after death [?]; I have rendered not even the slightest service. On hearing the command, I was startled and apprehensive, as though unable to remain at ease from morning to evening.

I therefore admonished myself: “There is a saying: ‘A state treasures the acquisition of worthy men; a minister shows loyalty by recommending scholars.’ How much more does this apply to the capital, the foremost seat of moral excellence and the standard for all regions! From it proceed the judgments of right and wrong throughout the realm; upon it depends the moral transformation of all under Heaven. If those selected should fail to accord with the impartial judgment of the realm—or even if their selection is impartial, but they are not men of outstanding and extraordinary talent, worthy …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
爲至寶者以觀示天下使天下
之人得以藉口曰
京師尚爾則雖就顯戮亦已晩矣
然今日冒責任之重抱氷淵之
懼者孰有過於臣哉又自解曰
我
皇上紹天闡繹
===
建極顯懿
道化周流
玄澤汪濊迄玆二十有五載乾坤
之所開陰陽之所接含生懷氣
之屬靡不淪肌浹髓喁喁嚮風
自今觀之莫高於天而景星見
而甘露降莫厚於地而醴泉出

懼者孰有過於臣哉又自解曰

punctuated: 爲至寶者，以觀示天下，使天下之人得以藉口曰：「京師尚爾！」則雖就顯戮，亦已晩矣。」然今日冒責任之重、抱氷淵之懼者，孰有過於臣哉？又自解曰：「我皇上紹天闡繹，建極顯懿，道化周流，玄澤汪濊。迄玆二十有五載，乾坤之所開、陰陽之所接，含生懷氣之屬，靡不淪肌浹髓，喁喁嚮風。自今觀之，莫高於天，而景星見，而甘露降；莫厚於地，而醴泉出，
translation_en: …to serve as supreme treasures to display before all under Heaven, giving people everywhere grounds to say, ‘Even the capital is like this!’—then, even if I were to suffer public execution, it would already be too late.” Yet today, who bears a heavier burden of responsibility, or greater fear—as though treading on thin ice or standing above a deep abyss—than your servant? I then sought to reassure myself, saying: “Our Emperor carries forward Heaven’s purposes and unfolds them, establishes the supreme standard, and manifests splendid virtue. His moral transformation circulates everywhere; his profound beneficence flows abundantly. These twenty-five years, throughout all that Heaven and Earth have opened and wherever yin and yang meet, every living creature endowed with vital breath has felt his influence penetrate flesh and marrow, eagerly turning toward it. Looking at things today, nothing is higher than Heaven, yet auspicious stars appear and sweet dew descends; nothing is more substantial than Earth, yet springs of sweet water well forth…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄

祥呈而鹿瑞遊莫無情於植物
而嘉禾生而瑞麥秀應圖合諜
者充牣郊虞皆以昭
聖德之貺徵

夫雲龍風虎聲應氣求誠有不
能自已今四海之內凡號為章

punctuated: 而黃河清。莫無知於動物，而龜祥呈，而鹿瑞遊；莫無情於植物，而嘉禾生，而瑞麥秀。應圖合諜者充牣郊虞，皆以昭聖德之貺，徵永禧之休。夫天地動植之瑞，皇上何心哉？而且表見若此。至於士之足稱國寶、以為世瑞者，皇上虛懷籲之久矣，而顧無所得哉？夫雲龍風虎，聲應氣求，誠有不能自已。今四海之內，凡號為章縫之士者，誰不振揚奮厲以出？而畿甸之間，涵濡衣被旣深且久者，
translation_en:
…and the Yellow River runs clear. None are less knowing than animals, yet auspicious tortoises appear and portentous deer roam; none are less feeling than plants, yet auspicious grain grows and propitious wheat puts forth ears. Signs corresponding to prophetic charts and tallying with records [?] fill the outskirts and hunting preserves [?], all manifesting the blessings bestowed upon sagely virtue and attesting to the good fortune of enduring felicity. As for these auspicious signs in heaven and earth, among animals and plants, what intention has His Majesty had of seeking them? Yet they have manifested themselves thus. As for scholars worthy of being called treasures of the state and auspicious signs for the age, His Majesty has long summoned them with an open mind. Could it be that he has nevertheless obtained none?
Clouds follow the dragon and winds follow the tiger; like sounds respond to one another, and kindred vital energies seek one another out. Such responses truly cannot be restrained. Now, within the Four Seas, of all those called scholars who wear the Confucian cap, who does not rouse himself and strive vigorously to come forward? And those in the metropolitan region who have been steeped in and sheltered by imperial beneficence so deeply and for so long…

translation_en: …how much more ought they to do? The Book of Odes says: “Illustrious are the many worthy men, born in this royal kingdom.” These words would find their confirmation here. Though your servant is utterly foolish and serves merely for want of someone better, might I perhaps thereby repay one ten-thousandth of the imperial bounty? Thus I exerted myself to the utmost, day and night, taking up their essays and examining them. Indeed, I found some substantial and classically disciplined, some powerful and profound yet brilliant and free-flowing, and some richly expansive and lucid. Though their expression differed from person to person, in government they took as models none other than Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao; in learning, none other than Kongzi, Mengzi, the Cheng brothers, and Zhu Xi. title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其文之本而徵孝焉於其文之
慈而徵惠焉於其文之材而徵
讓焉猗歟休哉言天下之美萃
於此矣斯其為國寶歟將不得
與天瑞地瑞動植之瑞競爽爭
奇而竝貢於
天子之廷乎臣於是有不勝其踴躍
===
===
者矣匪徒獲免於戾云爾雖然
臣之所以徵諸士子者文也亦
旣寶之矣由是而之焉敬以守
之隨其所任而不負於今日之
言利害不能奪毁譽不能亂如
此而進退如此而崇卑如此而
始如此而終抱一以見于天下
alt_text:
其文之本而徵孝焉於其文之
慈而徵惠焉於其文之材而徵
讓焉猗歟休哉言天下之美萃
於此矣斯其爲國寶歟將不得
與天瑞地瑞動植之瑞競爽爭
奇而竝貢於
天子之廷乎臣於是有不勝其踴躍
===
者矣匪徒獲免於戾云爾雖然
臣之所以徵諸士子者文也亦
旣寶之矣由是而之焉敬以守
之隨其所任而不負於今日之
言利害不能奪毀譽不能亂如
此而進退如此而崇卑如此而
始如此而終抱一以見于天下
punctuated:
其文之本而徵孝焉，於其文之慈而徵惠焉，於其文之材而徵讓焉。猗歟休哉！言天下之美萃於此矣。斯其為國寶歟？將不得與天瑞、地瑞、動植之瑞競爽爭奇，而竝貢於天子之廷乎？臣於是有不勝其踴躍者矣，匪徒獲免於戾云爾。

雖然，臣之所以徵諸士子者，文也，亦旣寶之矣。由是而之焉，敬以守之，隨其所任而不負於今日之言，利害不能奪，毁譽不能亂，如此而進退，如此而崇卑，如此而始，如此而終，抱一以見于天下
translation_en:
…from the foundations of their writing, discern their filial devotion; from its compassion, discern their beneficence; and from its talent, discern their deference. Ah, how splendid! All the excellence under Heaven may be said to converge here. Are these not treasures of the state? Could they not rival in brilliance and marvel the auspicious signs of Heaven and Earth, and those among animals and plants, and be presented together with them at the Son of Heaven’s court? At this, your servant cannot contain his elation; it is not merely a matter of having escaped blame.

Nevertheless, it is through their writing that your servant has assessed these candidates, and I have already treasured it. If they proceed along this course, preserve it with reverence, and, whatever responsibilities they assume, do not betray what they have said today; if neither advantage nor harm can deflect them, and neither disparagement nor praise can unsettle them; if they remain thus in advancement and retirement, thus in high station and low, thus at the beginning and thus at the end, holding fast to a single principle as they present themselves to the world…

左春坊左中允李本謹序。
translation_en:
…then you will indeed be treasures of the state, and the presiding examiner, too, may thereby secure an enduring name. If, however, you prove otherwise, would these rotten rats and stones of Yan not once again occasion laughter at the man of Yan [an allusion to mistaking worthless things for treasures]? You candidates, strive to live up to this! You candidates, strive to live up to this!

Preface respectfully composed by Li Ben, Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent.

書
punctuated:
第壹場

四書

天下有道，則禮樂征伐自天子出。

辟如天地之無不持載，無不覆幬；辟如四時之錯行，如日月之代明。

孔子嘗為委吏矣，曰：「會計當而已矣。」嘗為乘田矣，曰：「牛羊茁壯長而已矣。」

易

雲從龍，風從虎，聖人作而萬物覩。

天地感而萬物化生，聖人感人心而天下和平。觀其所感，而天地萬物之情可見矣。

子曰：「易其至矣乎！夫易，聖人所以崇德而廣業也。知崇禮卑，崇效天，卑法地。天地設位，而易行乎其中矣。成性存存，道義之門。」

聖人之情見乎辭。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

When the Way prevails in the world, rites, music, and punitive expeditions issue from the Son of Heaven.

It is like Heaven and Earth, which sustain and bear everything and cover and shelter everything; like the four seasons proceeding in alternation, and like the sun and moon shining in turn.

Confucius once served as a storehouse clerk. He said, “It is enough that the accounts are correct.” He once served as an officer in charge of livestock. He said, “It is enough that the cattle and sheep grow strong and healthy.”

Book of Changes (Yijing)

Clouds follow the dragon; winds follow the tiger. The sage arises, and all creatures look to him.

Heaven and Earth interact, and all things are transformed and brought into being. The sage moves human hearts, and the world enjoys peace and harmony. By observing what they move and respond to, one can discern the true dispositions of Heaven, Earth, and all things.

The Master said, “How consummate the Changes is! Through the Changes, the sage exalts his virtue and broadens his undertakings. Knowledge is lofty; ritual propriety is humble. Loftiness emulates Heaven; humility models itself on Earth. Heaven and Earth take their positions, and change operates between them. Preserving one's perfected nature continually is the gateway to the Way and righteousness.”

The dispositions of the sages are manifest in the words.

Book of Documents (Shujing)

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
帝光天之下至于海隅蒼生萬邦黎獻共
惟帝臣惟帝時舉敷納以言明庶以功
車服以庸誰敢不讓敢不敬應
臣爲上爲德爲下爲民
皇建其有極斂時五福用敷錫厥庶民惟
時厥庶民于汝極錫汝保極
簡厥修亦簡其或不修進厥良以率其或
不良
詩
===
躋彼公堂稱彼兕觥萬壽無疆
工祝致告徂賚孝孫苾芬孝祀神嗜飲食
卜爾百福如幾如式旣齊旣稷旣匡旣
敕永錫爾極時萬時億
辭之輯矣民之洽矣辭之懌矣民之莫矣
綏我眉壽介以繁祉
春秋
齊師宋師曹師城邢〔僖公元年〕
楚子伐鄭晉郤缺帥師救鄭〔宣公九年〕楚

punctuated:
帝光天之下，至于海隅蒼生，萬邦黎獻共惟帝臣，惟帝時舉。敷納以言，明庶以功，車服以庸，誰敢不讓，敢不敬應？

臣爲上爲德，爲下爲民。

皇建其有極，斂時五福，用敷錫厥庶民。惟時厥庶民于汝極，錫汝保極。

簡厥修，亦簡其或不修；進厥良，以率其或不良。

詩

躋彼公堂，稱彼兕觥，萬壽無疆！

工祝致告，徂賚孝孫。苾芬孝祀，神嗜飲食。卜爾百福，如幾如式。旣齊旣稷，旣匡旣敕，永錫爾極，時萬時億。

辭之輯矣，民之洽矣；辭之懌矣，民之莫矣。

綏我眉壽，介以繁祉。

春秋

齊師、宋師、曹師城邢。〔僖公元年〕

楚子伐鄭，晉郤缺帥師救鄭。〔宣公九年〕楚
translation_en:
The emperor’s radiance illuminated all beneath Heaven, reaching the common people at the edges of the seas. The worthy men of the myriad states were all the emperor’s servants, and these the emperor raised to office. He received them widely on the basis of their words, assessed them all through their achievements, and bestowed carriages and robes according to their service. Who dared not yield to others, or fail to respond respectfully?

A minister, in serving those above, serves virtue; in serving those below, serves the people.

The sovereign establishes the supreme standard, gathering these five blessings and distributing them widely among his common people. Then the common people turn to your standard, enabling you to preserve it.

Examine those who cultivate themselves, and also examine those who fail to do so. Advance the worthy, so as to lead those who are not worthy.

The Book of Songs

Ascend that lordly hall; raise that rhinoceros-horn cup: may you live ten thousand years, without end!

The officiating invocator delivers the announcement, conveying blessings to the filial descendant: “Fragrant are your filial offerings; the spirits relish the drink and food. They divine for you a hundred blessings, just as you hoped, just as is fitting. You have been reverent and prompt, correct and orderly. May they forever bestow upon you the utmost blessing, in tens of thousands and hundreds of millions.”

When words are harmonious, the people are united; when words are pleasing, the people are at peace.

Grant me long life, and aid me with abundant blessings.

The Spring and Autumn Annals

The armies of Qi, Song, and Cao fortified Xing. 〔First year of Duke Xi.〕

The Viscount of Chu attacked Zheng. Xi Que of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng. 〔Ninth year of Duke Xuan.〕 Chu …

吳入州來。〔成公七年〕冬，吳滅巢。〔昭公二十有四年〕
叔孫州仇帥師墮郈，季孫斯、仲孫何忌帥師墮費。十有二月，公圍成。公至自圍成。〔俱定公十有二年〕

故禮也者，義之實也。協諸義而協，則禮雖先王未之有，可以義起也。
凡音之起，由人心生也。人心之動，物使之然也。
君子之所謂義者，貴賤皆有事於天下。

translation_en:
…Prince Yingqi led an army to attack Zheng; Luan Shu of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng. 〔Sixth year of Duke Cheng.〕
Wu entered Zhoulai. 〔Seventh year of Duke Cheng.〕 In winter, Wu destroyed Chao. 〔Twenty-fourth year of Duke Zhao.〕
Shusun Zhouchou led an army to dismantle the fortifications of Hou; Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led an army to dismantle the fortifications of Fei. In the twelfth month, the duke besieged Cheng. The duke returned from besieging Cheng. 〔All in the twelfth year of Duke Ding.〕
Record of Rites
Order the official responsible for rites to examine the seasons and months, determine the days, and harmonize the pitch standards; rectify rites and music, institutions and measures, and clothing.
Thus rites are the concrete embodiment of righteousness. If a practice is tested against righteousness and accords with it, then, even if the former kings had no such rite, it may be instituted on the basis of righteousness.
All musical sounds arise from the human heart. The stirring of the human heart is brought about by external things.
What the gentleman calls righteousness is that people of both high and low status all have duties in the world.
Second Session
Discourse
The gentleman possesses the Way of the measuring square.

punctuated: 衰秦亂，取民無制，不足言矣。至漢文帝在位，再賜民田租之半，其後遂除之，而不收者十餘年。不惟不取，而且與之，何歟？洪惟我太祖高皇帝汛掃胡元，廓清函夏，登極未幾，遂下免租之詔。因時隨地，無歲不免，甚至舉天下夏稅秋糧而盡蠲免之。其間存恤老幼、哀憫惸獨、給米賜帛之類，有不可勝計者。夫文帝承高惠之後，事多仰成，稍加節約，自足於用。我聖祖當革命建極，正創制立法之始，所費視承平之日奚啻千萬，而乃蠲貸若是，何以未聞有乏財之慮乎？不知省民裕國，其道何繇？今詔令具在，御製文集皆裁自聖心，其意指所在，可得聞歟？說者謂結人心凝
translation_en:
…as the Zhou declined and the Qin brought disorder, exactions from the people knew no bounds; these need not be discussed. When Emperor Wen of the Han was on the throne, he twice remitted half the people’s land tax, and subsequently abolished it altogether, leaving it uncollected for more than ten years. He not only refrained from taking but also gave to the people. Why was this?

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao swept away the non-Chinese Yuan and cleared the Chinese realm. Shortly after ascending the throne, he issued an edict remitting the land tax. Remissions followed the circumstances of particular times and places, with none of the years passing without them. He even remitted the summer taxes and autumn grain levies throughout the realm in their entirety. His measures to support the old and young, show compassion to the solitary and bereft, and distribute rice and silk were beyond counting.

Emperor Wen succeeded Emperors Gao and Hui, inheriting established arrangements in many affairs; a little additional economy sufficed to meet his needs. Our sagely founding emperor, however, was changing the dynasty and establishing sovereign rule, at the very outset of creating institutions and laying down laws. His expenses exceeded those of peaceful times by untold multiples, yet he granted remissions and relief on this scale. Why, then, do we hear of no concern over insufficient funds? By what means did he ease the people’s burdens and enrich the state? The edicts are all still extant, and the collected imperial writings were all composed from his sagely heart. May we hear what their underlying intent was? Commentators say that winning the people’s hearts and consolidating…

天命，而培千萬年不抜之基，端在於此，豈管子所謂知與之為取者耶？我皇上臨御以來，詢求民瘼，德音屢下，叮嚀惻怛，凡所以加惠元元者，無所不至。優恤蠲免，視聖祖無間焉。比年，以京師根本重地，軫念捐瘠，每歲出錢藥施捨，累月而後止。夏秋之間，積雨為災，即詔發銀米，急為賑救。以至言官之論列、守臣之陳請，疏辭一入，俞旨即下，務使實惠及民。今仁風翔洽，德澤流濩，上繼聖祖，遠邁百王，使被災之民轉愁歎而為歌舞，固天下之所著聞也。然此亦有所本歟？諸士子生長畿甸，涵濡獨深且久，其敬鋪張揚厲之。
問：忠厚者，君子之道；廉讓者，士人之節。斯
translation_en:
…the Mandate of Heaven and establishing a foundation that will remain unshaken for countless ages depend precisely upon this. Is this what Guanzi meant by knowing that giving is a means of receiving? Since ascending the throne, our Emperor has sought to learn of the people's afflictions. His benevolent pronouncements have repeatedly been issued, earnest and compassionate; he has spared no effort to bestow kindness upon the common people. In providing compassionate relief and remitting taxes, he matches the Sagely Progenitor. In recent years, mindful that the capital is the vital foundation of the realm, he has shown concern for those wasted by hunger and abandoned to death. Each year he has provided money and medicines for distribution, continuing for months before stopping. When prolonged rains brought disaster during summer and autumn, he immediately decreed that silver and grain be released for urgent relief. Furthermore, whenever remonstrance officials submit their representations or local officials present requests, an approving decree follows as soon as the memorial arrives, with every effort made to ensure that tangible benefits reach the people. Now the influence of his benevolence spreads everywhere, and the blessings of his virtue flow far and wide. Continuing the legacy of the Sagely Progenitor and far surpassing the hundred kings, he has turned the sorrow and sighs of disaster-stricken people into song and dance. This is indeed renowned throughout the realm. Yet does this, too, have an underlying foundation? You examination candidates have grown up in the metropolitan region and have received these blessings with exceptional depth and for an exceptionally long time. Reverently expound and extol them.

punctuated:
二者雖若迂緩，然而世道之升降、風俗之美惡、天下國家之治亂，恒必由之，是不可不審也。唐虞三代之時，遐哉邈乎，不可尚已。後世乃有感時澆薄、慕尚敦篤而著《崇厚論》者，有以時多進趨、廉遜道闕而著《崇讓論》者，其辭意固各有所指也，可得而言之乎？夫視時趨向，天下之人不少。即斯二者，何以崇之？崇之之要，安所本始？豈皆隨時以相推挽歟？抑別有其道歟？究而言之，二者亦可以合一歟？方今教化隆盛，風俗醇美，視二子所遇之時，固萬萬不侔。然就二子所論之事觀之，恐亦未可謂盡無也。諸士子博觀史冊，及此必有槩于中者，又豈得無論乎？請著于篇，毋為虛讓，今之士君子固皆所樂聞也。

問：古人有言，經與史，其義一，其體二，似非
translation_en:
…Although these two virtues may seem impractical and slow to produce results, the rise and decline of the moral order, the goodness and badness of customs, and order and disorder throughout the realm invariably depend upon them. They therefore demand careful consideration. The age of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties is distant indeed, far beyond our reach. In later ages, one writer, distressed by the superficiality and meanness of his times and admiring sincerity and earnestness, composed the Discourse on Esteeming Generosity (Chong hou lun). Another, because his age abounded in competitive advancement while integrity and modest deference were lacking, composed the Discourse on Esteeming Deference (Chong rang lun). Each work’s language and meaning surely addressed particular circumstances. Can you explain these?

There are no few people in the world who take their direction from the tendencies of their times. As for these two virtues, how should they be promoted? Where does the essential basis for promoting them lie? Is it simply a matter of responding to the times by encouraging one and restraining the other, or is there a different way? Pursuing the matter to its conclusion, can the two also be united as one?

At present, moral instruction flourishes and customs are pure and fine: our age differs immeasurably from those encountered by these two writers. Yet, considering the matters they discussed, one fears that we cannot say such problems have entirely disappeared. You candidates have read widely in the historical records; on reaching these matters, you must have felt something stir within you. How, then, could you have nothing to say? Please set it down in an essay, without empty displays of modesty. The scholars and gentlemen of today would certainly all welcome hearing it.

Question: An ancient writer said that the Classics and histories are one in their meaning but two in their form. It would seem that they are not…

判然二途也夫何後世或擬經焉或擬
史焉自漢以來不可殫述姑舉顯著者
言之儒家者流若揚雄王通趙曄陸賈

一人其意皆自謂五經再生史家者流

translation_en:
…two sharply distinct paths. Why, then, did later generations produce imitations of the Classics or of the histories, in numbers too great to recount since the Han? Let us discuss only the prominent examples. Among Confucian scholars, authors such as Yang Xiong, Wang Tong, Zhao Ye, Lu Jia, Jing Fang, Sima Guang, Shu Xi, and Bai Juyi were numerous; in their own estimation, each intended his work as the Five Classics reborn. Among historians, authors such as Qiao Zhou, Gan Bao, Sun Sheng, Wu Yun, and Linghu Defen were likewise numerous; in their own estimation, each intended his work as the Three Histories appearing anew. Could there be a difference between the Classics and the histories? Or do their imitations truly stand comparison with the Classics and histories without shame? All these imitative works still survive today: can you identify and discuss them?

Some say that the Classics have no fixed rules of composition, and that what makes them unsurpassable is simply the refinement with which they express the Way. Why, then, did Yang Xiong and his fellows imitate only their rules of composition? Histories prize truthful recording, and what makes them unsurpassable is simply the aptness with which they narrate events. Why, then, did Qiao Zhou and his fellows fail to devote themselves to truthful recording? Earlier writers criticized each of these authors: wherein lay their faults?

Imitating the Classics would seem mistaken. Yet of Yang Xiong’s writings, some said that they constantly delighted in them, while others held that they would assuredly be transmitted to posterity. Of Wang Tong’s book, some said that it contained excellent maxims, while others said that it came quite close to correctness. Might it be that, although these authors imitated others, they should not hastily be belittled? Imitating the histories would seem mistaken. Yet concerning Zuo…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
氏或謂其失之誣於公羊或謂其失之
俗於穀梁或謂其才之短於遷或謂其
淺陋疎畧於固或謂其浮華剽竊無乃
雖爲人所擬而未可遽宗之乎由是觀
之經不可擬而亦或不嫌於擬史不可
擬而亦或不足於擬者其故何歟或謂
史有文淺而易模經文意深而難擬其
說然歟雄周之輩皆高才博學名重一
時固自謂命世而生者也何乃昧此而
===

士子誦讀經史之餘必嘗擬議於斯二
者矣願聞其說
問宋胡寅有言制策亦以空言取人然其
來最古得人亦多以今考之或有未然
夫所謂制策者特昉於漢以試賢良方
正直言極諫者耳遡而上之不有成周
之鄉舉里選乎虞廷之奏言試功乎惡
在其爲最古也又嘗觀漢史所載賢良

氏，或謂其失之誣；於公羊，或謂其失之俗；於穀梁，或謂其才之短；於遷，或謂其淺陋疎畧；於固，或謂其浮華剽竊。無乃雖爲人所擬，而未可遽宗之乎？由是觀之，經不可擬，而亦或不嫌於擬；史不可擬，而亦或不足於擬者，其故何歟？或謂史有文淺而易模，經文意深而難擬，其說然歟？雄、周之輩，皆高才博學，名重一時，固自謂命世而生者也。何乃昧此，而不免更相蹈襲，以來後人之指摘耶？諸士子誦讀經史之餘，必嘗擬議於斯二者矣，願聞其說。
問：宋胡寅有言：「制策亦以空言取人，然其來最古，得人亦多。」以今考之，或有未然。夫所謂制策者，特昉於漢，以試賢良方正直言極諫者耳。遡而上之，不有成周之鄉舉里選乎？虞廷之奏言試功乎？惡在其爲最古也？又嘗觀漢史所載賢良
translation_en:
…as for Zuo’s Commentary, some say its fault lies in fabrication; as for Gongyang’s Commentary, some say its fault lies in vulgarity; as for Guliang’s Commentary, some speak of its author’s limited ability; as for Sima Qian, some call his work shallow, crude, and cursory; as for Ban Gu, some call his work florid and plagiarized. Might these works, although imitated by others, nevertheless not warrant being immediately accepted as authoritative models? Viewed in this light, the Classics cannot be imitated, yet imitation is sometimes considered unobjectionable; histories cannot be imitated, yet some are themselves inadequate as models for imitation. Why is this? Some say that historical writing is straightforward and easy to copy, whereas the language and meaning of the Classics are profound and difficult to imitate. Is this explanation correct? Men such as Yang Xiong and Qiao Zhou were all highly talented and broadly learned, with great reputations in their day. They surely considered themselves born to answer the needs of their age. Why, then, were they blind to this, unable to avoid following one another’s precedents and thereby inviting criticism from later generations? In the time left over from reciting and studying the Classics and histories, you candidates must have reflected upon these two kinds of writing. We wish to hear your explanations.
Question: Hu Yin of the Song said: “Imperially prescribed policy questions likewise select men on the basis of empty words; nevertheless, this method is the most ancient in origin and has secured many worthy men.” Examined today, this may not be entirely true. What are called imperially prescribed policy questions originated only in the Han, to examine those recommended as worthy, good, upright, and capable of speaking frankly and remonstrating forthrightly. Looking further back, was there not nomination by districts and selection by villages under the Zhou? Was there not the presentation of proposals and the testing of achievements at the court of Shun? How, then, can this method be called the most ancient? Moreover, I have examined the Han histories’ records of policy responses by the worthy and good …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
策不過數篇數□□議論人品俱不免
於後世之議自此之外雖有嘉謨史固
逸其傳矣其得人又惡在其亦多也漢
旣如此自後雖皆以此爲重然品式條
貫代各不同議論取舍得失亦異可得
聞其畧歟其得人又何如也或有謂非
經國之體請與諸科並停者有謂祗足
長浮薄之風啓僥倖之路者又有謂徒
隔賢士之路者銷英雄之氣者審若是
===
則亦不足重歟豈豪傑之士有不屑於
此歟夫不仕無義苟爲不屑何以行之
抑士之所以爲學與夫所以爲人者有
不繫於此歟我
朝設科取士稽古定制至精至密寔以此爲
最重其得人之多眞有陋漢唐宋於不
居者今諸士抱負墳策侁侁然來試于
有司者凡以此耳不識平日之所學者
亦如斯而已乎請直陳所志母徒事剽

translation_en:
…policy essays amount to no more than a few pieces, a few [illegible characters; ?]; both their arguments and their authors’ character have remained subject to the criticism of later generations. Beyond these, even if there were excellent counsels, the histories have failed to transmit them. Where, then, is the evidence that this method also obtained many worthy men? Such was the case under the Han. Although subsequent dynasties all attached importance to this method, their prescribed forms and regulations differed from dynasty to dynasty, as did the arguments for adopting or rejecting it and its successes and failures. Might we hear an outline of these? And how did it fare in obtaining worthy men? Some maintained that it was inconsistent with the proper principles of governing the state and requested that it be discontinued together with the other examination categories. Some maintained that it served only to encourage a frivolous and shallow disposition and open a path to advancement through mere luck. Others maintained that it merely obstructed the path of worthy scholars or sapped the spirit of outstanding men. If this is indeed so, does it not deserve little esteem? Could there be outstanding men who disdain it? Yet to refrain from taking office is to neglect one’s duty. If they disdain this method, how are they to put that duty into practice? Or is there something in how scholars pursue learning and conduct themselves as men that does not depend upon it?

Our dynasty established examination categories to select scholars, consulting antiquity to determine its institutions with the utmost refinement and care, and has indeed accorded this method the greatest importance. In the multitude of worthy men it has obtained, it has truly made the Han, Tang, and Song appear inferior, without claiming such distinction [?]. Now you scholars, bearing the ancient books, come in throngs to be examined by the responsible officials, all for this purpose alone. I wonder whether what you have studied in your daily lives likewise amounts only to this. Please state your aspirations frankly; do not merely engage in plagiarizing…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
竊以相眩惑有司者亦能辨也
大廷之對此其階矣盍各勉之愼之
問安上治民莫善於禮移風易俗莫善於
樂自古聖人建大業得大位未有不制
禮作樂以敎化天下者也且以鄕飲酒
禮言之成周制爲此禮行於鄕校之間
以爲政敎之本在是夫鄕飲不過飲食
之節耳而孔子又曰吾觀於鄕而知王
道之易易也豈制禮作樂以敎化天下
===
者果莫有急於此禮者乎今其禮載在
儀禮見於禮記者可考也先儒謂鄕飲
有四又謂不特四者而已其行何事升
歌笙入間歌合樂各三終其詩何取自
周旣衰漢承秦亂其禮已廢至後漢西
晉唐宋諸君亦有復行之者果能合於
成周之禮否歟我
太祖高皇帝興復此禮載之官制著之
大誥而又嚴之

punctuated:
竊以相眩惑，有司者亦能辨也。大廷之對，此其階矣，盍各勉之愼之？
問：安上治民，莫善於禮；移風易俗，莫善於樂。自古聖人建大業、得大位，未有不制禮作樂以敎化天下者也。且以鄕飲酒禮言之，成周制爲此禮，行於鄕校之間，以爲政敎之本在是。夫鄕飲不過飲食之節耳，而孔子又曰：「吾觀於鄕，而知王道之易易也。」豈制禮作樂以敎化天下者，果莫有急於此禮者乎？今其禮載在《儀禮》、見於《禮記》者可考也。先儒謂鄕飲有四，又謂不特四者而已，其行何事？升歌、笙入、間歌、合樂，各三終，其詩何取？自周旣衰，漢承秦亂，其禮已廢。至後漢、西晉、唐、宋諸君，亦有復行之者，果能合於成周之禮否歟？我太祖高皇帝興復此禮，載之官制，著之《大誥》，而又嚴之
translation_en:
…plagiarizing to bewilder and deceive one another; the examining officials can discern this too. This examination is your stepping-stone to answering questions at the imperial court. Should you not each exert yourselves and proceed with care?
Question: For securing those above and governing the people, nothing excels ritual; for transforming prevailing ways and changing customs, nothing excels music. Since antiquity, whenever sages established great achievements and attained the supreme position, they invariably instituted rites and composed music to educate and transform all under Heaven. Take the district drinking ceremony, for example. The Zhou in its flourishing age instituted this rite and performed it in the district schools, considering it the foundation of government and moral instruction. Now, district drinking involves merely the prescribed forms of eating and drinking, yet Confucius said: “When I observe the district ceremony, I understand how very easy the Kingly Way is.” Among the rites and music instituted to educate and transform all under Heaven, could there truly be nothing more urgent than this rite?
Its ritual prescriptions, recorded in the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili) and found in the Record of Rites (Liji), can now be examined. Earlier Confucian scholars said that there were four forms of district drinking; others said that there were more than just these four. On what occasions were they performed? The singing upon ascending the hall, the entrance of the mouth-organ players, the alternating singing and instrumental music, and the combined music each comprised three complete performances: which poems were selected, and why?
After the Zhou declined, the Han inherited the disorder left by the Qin, and this rite had already fallen into disuse. Among the rulers of the Later Han, Western Jin, Tang, and Song, some also restored its performance. Did their ceremonies truly accord with the rites of the flourishing Zhou? Our Emperor Taizu Gao revived this rite, incorporated it into official regulations, set it forth in the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao), and further made its observance stringent…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大明律詳盡且至垂世警俗之意深矣可得
而言歟今海内毎歳再行之宜古禮可
復而風俗可同也然而戸尚罕可封之
俗士未必崇偕讓之節其故又何也伊
欲使天下之人服膺
聖訓束脩至教揖讓之治同於萬國雅頌之聲
盈於六合蔚然成周之盛復見于
今日如之何則可諸士子游於鄉校之間當
亦有年行將歌鹿鳴而賓興之也明於
===
禮樂舉而錯之而已矣請究言之以卜
他日賛理之術

俗士未必崇揖讓之節其故又何也伊
欲使天下之人胥

他日贊理之術
punctuated: 《大明律》，詳盡且至，垂世警俗之意深矣，可得而言歟？今海内毎歳再行之，宜古禮可復而風俗可同也。然而戸尚罕可封之俗，士未必崇偕讓之節，其故又何也？伊欲使天下之人服膺聖訓，束脩至教，揖讓之治同於萬國，雅頌之聲盈於六合，蔚然成周之盛復見于今日，如之何則可？諸士子游於鄉校之間，當亦有年，行將歌《鹿鳴》而賓興之也。明於禮樂，舉而錯之而已矣。請究言之，以卜他日賛理之術。
translation_en:
…in the Great Ming Code. These provisions are detailed and comprehensive; profound indeed is the intention to transmit them to later generations and admonish the people. Can you explain this? Today, this rite is performed twice each year throughout the realm. It should therefore be possible to restore the ancient rites and bring customs into conformity with them. Yet households whose virtue merits enfeoffment remain rare, and scholars do not necessarily prize mutual deference. Why is this?

If we wish to make all people under Heaven take the sagely instructions to heart and discipline their conduct according to the highest teachings, so that government through courtesy and deference prevails alike throughout the myriad states, the sounds of the Elegantiae and Hymns fill the six directions, and the flourishing splendor of the Zhou is seen again today, how can this be achieved?

You scholars must have spent years studying in the local schools. Soon, “The Deer Cry” will be sung, and you will be honored as guests and recommended for advancement. Understand rites and music, and all that remains is to put them into practice. Please discuss this fully, so that we may judge your ability to assist in governance in days to come.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
天下有道則禮樂征伐自天子出
劉斯潔
同考試官教諭陳批深得夫子語意非
苟作者宜錄之
同考試官進士藺批論語義塲中作者率
多失於冗雜可厭子能以精潔之辭發之宜錄以式
考試官左贊善吳批文有關繫結更佳
===
考試官左中允李批意味深長
聖人論至治之世而治出於一焉蓋治因於世
者也禮樂征伐一出於天子其惟有道之世乎
夫子言此殆亦有所感矣其意若謂治以一統
爲盛而勢以不移爲尊觀其所自而治可知也
彼四海永清顯耿光大烈之懿萬邦無斁襲重
熙累洽之休此非天下有道之時乎斯時也體
統正而朝廷尊教化行而風俗美天下雖大惟
知有天子之尊而已矣人心雖衆惟知有天子

聖人論至治之世，而治出於一焉。蓋治因於世者也，禮樂征伐一出於天子，其惟有道之世乎？夫子言此，殆亦有所感矣。其意若謂：治以一統爲盛，而勢以不移爲尊，觀其所自而治可知也。彼四海永清，顯耿光大烈之懿；萬邦無斁，襲重熙累洽之休，此非天下有道之時乎？斯時也，體統正而朝廷尊，教化行而風俗美。天下雖大，惟知有天子之尊而已矣；人心雖衆，惟知有天子
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“When the Way prevails throughout the realm, rites, music, and punitive expeditions proceed from the Son of Heaven.”
Liu Sijie

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: “This thoroughly grasps the meaning of the Master's words. It is no carelessly composed work and merits selection.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): “In expounding the meaning of the Analects, writers in the examination hall mostly lapse into tiresome prolixity and clutter. You have elucidated it in precise, polished language. This should be selected as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Wu, Left Mentor: “The essay's parts are connected; the conclusion is better still.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Assistant Instructor: “Its meaning and implications are profound and far-reaching.”

The Sage discusses an age of consummate government, in which government proceeds from a single source. For government depends upon the condition of the age. Rites, music, and punitive expeditions all proceeding from the Son of Heaven—surely this occurs only in an age when the Way prevails? In saying this, the Master must also have been moved by something he had witnessed. His meaning seems to be that government flourishes through unity, and authority commands reverence by remaining unshifted. By observing the source from which government proceeds, one can understand its condition.

When all within the Four Seas enjoys enduring peace, manifesting the excellence of brilliant virtue and great achievements; when the myriad states remain unwearied, inheriting the blessings of successive ages of prosperity and accumulated harmony—is this not a time when the Way prevails throughout the realm? At such a time, the hierarchical order is correct and the court is revered; moral instruction takes effect and customs are admirable. Vast though the realm is, it acknowledges only the majesty of the Son of Heaven. Numerous though the hearts of the people are, they acknowledge only the Son of Heaven's …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之法而已矣是以揖讓而天下治禮樂之謂也
而天子務焉脩五禮以防民僞而教之中同六
樂以防民情而教之和凡創制立法出乎身而
加乎民者皆聖心之自裁也大宗伯特受命以
掌之耳舎此而欲議之且不可况敢有變易者
乎則禮樂自天子出矣弧矢以威天下征伐之
謂也而天子制焉巡侯甸而四征及於弗庭正
邦國而九伐施於效逆凡克詰張皇發乎邇而
見乎遠者皆乾綱之獨斷也大司馬特受命以
===
統之耳舎此而欲請之且不可况敢有專擅者
乎則征伐自天子出矣夫如是則天下之勢定
於一而天下之治同於道聖世全盛氣象不有
以想見之哉抑論禮樂之用誠爲急也而夫子
以征伐並言何耶蓋禮樂者飾治者也征伐者

translation_en:
…his laws alone. Thus, bringing order to all under Heaven through bows and deference refers to rites and music, to which the Son of Heaven devotes himself. He cultivates the five rites to guard against deceit among the people and teach them due measure; he harmonizes the six forms of music to restrain the people's passions and teach them harmony. All institutions he creates and laws he establishes, originating with himself and applied to the people, are determined by his own sagely mind. The Minister of Rites merely receives his command to administer them. Even proposing deliberations on them apart from this authority is impermissible; how could anyone dare alter them? Thus rites and music issue from the Son of Heaven.

Inspiring awe throughout all under Heaven with bows and arrows refers to punitive expeditions, which the Son of Heaven controls. He inspects the hou and dian domains, and expeditions in the four directions reach those who fail to attend his court; he rectifies the states, and the nine forms of punitive attack are directed against those who engage in rebellion [?]. All his ordering and deploying of military power, initiated nearby and manifested afar, rests upon the sovereign's sole decision. The Minister of War merely receives his command to direct it. Even requesting such action apart from this authority is impermissible; how could anyone dare act on his own authority? Thus punitive expeditions issue from the Son of Heaven.

When this is so, authority throughout all under Heaven is settled in one ruler, and government throughout all under Heaven accords with the Way. Can we not thereby envision the flourishing grandeur of a sagely age? Yet, while the use of rites and music is indeed an urgent concern, why does the Master mention punitive expeditions alongside them? Rites and music embellish orderly government; punitive expeditions suppress disorder. The sage kings of antiquity likewise exerted themselves in these two matters as they stood facing south to rule. Through this, all under Heaven enjoyed peace. In the age of Kings Cheng and Kang, the Dukes of Zhou and Shao saw order established, achievements completed, and rites and music flourishing. Yet they still spoke earnestly of weapons and the six armies: their intention is evident. By the Spring and Autumn period, government, instruction, commands, and ordinances had long ceased to reach all under Heaven. How could…

…expect rites, music, and punitive expeditions to issue from the Son of Heaven? In these words of the Master, do we not find the aspirations of the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao? Do we not find a heart troubled for the world?

“He is like Heaven and Earth, which sustain and bear everything, shelter and cover everything; like the four seasons proceeding in alternation, and like the sun and moon shining in succession.”
Zhu Shangyi

Associate Examiner Yuan, a Professor, comments: “Without laborious explanation, you bring vividly before our eyes the sage’s grandeur, like that of Heaven and Earth. From this we can recognize your attainment in the Way.”
Associate Examiner Wang, a Prefectural Judge, comments: “The understanding is genuine and incisive, and the wording clear and apt. This is someone skilled at revealing the sage’s profound meaning.”
Associate Examiner Li, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “Since the topic touches on the workings of creation, it is inherently difficult to discuss. This essay brings out the meaning of the words ‘is like’; its language is also admirably clear and polished.”
Examiner Wu, Left Mentor, comments: “Lucid, vigorous, refined, and pure.”
Examiner Li, Left Rectifier, comments: “Concise and apt.”

In its comparisons describing sagely virtue, the Doctrine of the Mean presents something so great that nothing lies beyond it, and something that moves without ceasing. How utterly complete is the sage’s virtue! When seeking comparisons to describe it, must it not flow together with the workings of creation? Chapter Thirty of the Doctrine of the Mean elucidates the Way of Heaven through the sagehood of Confucius. At this point, its meaning is surely this: virtue reaches completeness in the sage, and sagehood reaches its utmost in Confucius. What is called Confucius’s sagehood assuredly consists in his carrying forward the traditions of his predecessors and taking their institutions as his models, thereby gathering together the accomplishments of all the sages…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之成上律下襲而體天地之撰矣抑何以擬之
哉是故自其廣大者言之業隆富有而眾善之
兼該資深溥博而萬物之皆備其譬諸天地乎
今夫至哉坤元奠麗無疆而勢著隤然之順大
哉乾元保合大和而道顯確然之健舉天下之
物無不持載覆幬者天地也而聖人之德兼體
而不遺者寔如之天地聖人一而已矣欲知聖
人舍天地將奚之耶自其不息者言之隨時從
道而酬酢以盡其神泛應曲當而推行以盡其
===
利其譬諸四時日月乎今夫一寒一暑通復無
窮而歲功成焉一往一來晝夜相禪而貞明生
焉言造化之妙極其變通流行者四時日月也
而聖人之德純亦不已者寔如之四時日月
聖人亦一而已矣欲知聖人舍四時日月將奚
取耶由是觀之則知聖人之德大而無外者神
無方也運而不息者化無體也神無方而化無
體非天下之至聖其孰能與於此噫此其所以
爲天道也雖然造化所以神萬物者誠爲之也

punctuated: 之成，上律下襲，而體天地之撰矣。抑何以擬之哉？是故自其廣大者言之，業隆富有，而眾善之兼該；資深溥博，而萬物之皆備。其譬諸天地乎？今夫至哉坤元，奠麗無疆，而勢著隤然之順；大哉乾元，保合大和，而道顯確然之健。舉天下之物，無不持載覆幬者，天地也；而聖人之德兼體而不遺者，寔如之。天地、聖人，一而已矣。欲知聖人，舍天地將奚之耶？自其不息者言之，隨時從道，而酬酢以盡其神；泛應曲當，而推行以盡其利。其譬諸四時日月乎？今夫一寒一暑，通復無窮，而歲功成焉；一往一來，晝夜相禪，而貞明生焉。言造化之妙，極其變通流行者，四時日月也；而聖人之德純亦不已者，寔如之。四時日月、聖人，亦一而已矣。欲知聖人，舍四時日月將奚取耶？由是觀之，則知聖人之德大而無外者，神無方也；運而不息者，化無體也。神無方而化無體，非天下之至聖，其孰能與於此？噫！此其所以爲天道也。雖然，造化所以神萬物者，誠爲之也。
translation_en:
…their achievements, taking his rule from above and following the patterns below, thereby embodying the workings of Heaven and Earth. Yet to what may he be compared? Thus, speaking of his vastness: his accomplishments are exalted and abundantly rich, encompassing every good; his resources are deep, ample, and broad, containing all things. May he be compared to Heaven and Earth? Now, how consummate is the primal power of Kun, Earth! Established and extending without bounds, its disposition displays effortless compliance. How great is the primal power of Qian, Heaven! Preserving and uniting supreme harmony, its Way manifests steadfast vigor. It is Heaven and Earth that support, carry, shelter, and cover everything under heaven; and the sage’s virtue, which embodies all without omission, is truly like them. Heaven and Earth and the sage are simply one. If one wishes to understand the sage, where could one turn apart from Heaven and Earth?

Speaking of his ceaseless activity: he follows the Way as circumstances change, responding to every encounter so as to give full scope to his spiritual efficacy; he responds broadly and fittingly in every particular, putting his virtue into practice so as to realize its benefits fully. May he be compared to the four seasons and the sun and moon? Now, cold and heat alternate, passing and returning without end, and the work of the year is accomplished. One departs and another arrives; day and night succeed each other, and constant illumination is produced. As for the marvels of creation and transformation, it is the four seasons and the sun and moon that carry change, adaptation, and circulation to their utmost; and the sage’s virtue, pure and likewise unceasing, is truly like them. The four seasons, the sun and moon, and the sage are also simply one. If one wishes to understand the sage, what could one take as a comparison apart from the four seasons and the sun and moon?

Viewed in this light, we know that the sage’s virtue is so great that nothing lies outside it because its spiritual efficacy has no fixed direction; it moves without ceasing because its transformations have no fixed form. With spiritual efficacy having no fixed direction and transformation no fixed form, who but the utmost sage under heaven could participate in this? Ah! This is why his virtue constitutes the Way of Heaven. Nevertheless, that by which creation and transformation work their wonders in the myriad things is sincerity.

…Such was Mengzi’s intention in instructing others. It is as though he were saying: The duty of a minister begins with attending reverently to his responsibilities; a gentleman who takes office regards occupying a position without fulfilling its duties as shameful. Those who serve because of poverty decline exalted rank and wealth and accept humble posts with meager means. Their concern is not poverty and low station, but the difficulty of adequately fulfilling their duties. I have considered Kongzi, a great sage, who at times also took office because of poverty. Thus, he once served as a granary clerk, responsible for collecting levies of grain, firewood, and fodder from the dian and shao districts [?]. His position was lowly, and some might have considered it degrading. But the sage said: “What service is not a position? What position has no duties? Having taken this position, my only fear is that I may fail to discharge its duties fully. Moreover, the shao stores provide for guests, the dian stores for travelers, and the surplus stores for gifts and grants. Although all these depend upon this office, its responsibilities are not difficult to carry out. Could it be acceptable to assess and measure these supplies unfairly?” Thus, in keeping accounts, he insisted on getting them right before he was satisfied.

He also once served as a livestock keeper, responsible for the parks and enclosures, fodder, and pasturing. The stipend was meager, and some people might have disdained it. But the sage said: “One serves in office and receives a stipend; the stipend must be matched by the service rendered. Having accepted this stipend, I reproach myself only if I fail to attend to my responsibilities. Moreover, this office supplies the great sacrifices, the reception of guests, archery ceremonies, feasts, military affairs, and funerals. Although all draw their provisions from it, its responsibilities are not difficult to fulfill. Could it be acceptable for the sacrificial animals not to reach proper maturity?” Thus, with the cattle and sheep, he insisted that they grow strong and healthy before he was satisfied.

Now Kongzi, in his sageliness, far surpassed other people. Even when taking office because of poverty, he still insisted on fulfilling his duties completely. How much more must people today do so, falling as far below the sage as they do! If they say that they serve because of poverty, then [three illegible characters] …

…[?] all have regular duties for which they receive sustenance from their superiors. These duties are readily fulfilled, and must indeed be fulfilled. [?] Can one take office without serving the Way, merely seeking a salary heedlessly? From this we can see that a ruler’s servant should seek only to devote himself wholeheartedly: whether his salary is generous or meager, there are obligations he must never treat carelessly. Are Mencius’s words binding rules only for those who take office because of poverty? As for Confucius, he certainly neither insisted upon nor ruled out any course of action. This can be understood by considering his service as Magistrate of Zhongdu, as Minister of Works and Minister of Justice, and as acting chief minister. Thus he could undertake great or small responsibilities, enter office or remain in retirement, yet never depart from the Way. This is what made him the sage who acted in accordance with the times. Mencius understood this deeply and wished to emulate him. Yet he would not grant even a single audience to the feudal lords, insisting that he must occupy the position of an honored guest and teacher in order to put his Way into practice. Here indeed lies the distinction between sage and worthy. Even so, this too accords with the times and with the Way.

The Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) draws upon the mutual responsiveness of moving things to illuminate the benefit of seeing the sage. For the sage is the hope of all the people. When he attains his position and puts the Way into practice, people benefit from seeing him. Is this not like clouds following the dragon and wind following the tiger? Expanding upon the meaning of the Commentary on the Images for the nine in the fifth place, the Wenyan says that there are encounters in the world that cannot be forestalled, and impulses in human hearts that cannot be restrained. Thus, can the benefit of seeing, spoken of in the nine in the fifth place, be understood solely through sounds and vital energies seeking their counterparts, or water and fire tending toward what accords with them?
Now, I know that the most numinous creature in the world is the dragon. At times the dragon rises; it does not summon the clouds, yet the clouds follow it of themselves. Where its numinous energy moves, they gather without anyone knowing how. I know that the fiercest creature in the world is the tiger. At times the tiger roars; it does not summon the wind, yet the wind follows it of itself. Stirred by its fierce power, the wind arises without anyone perceiving how. These are all innate capacities of things to respond, wondrous workings of Heaven’s spontaneous impulse: inevitable and irresistible. Why, then, should we doubt this responsiveness only when it comes to the sage?
The sage, truly perspicacious, ascends to become the sovereign; he possesses both the position and its requisite virtue. Receiving Heaven’s allotted succession, he establishes the supreme standard, fittingly ruling the common people and those in office alike. We shall see those who cherish the accomplishments of his transforming virtue never cease to revere and love him, and those who admire the radiance of his moral excellence look up to him and rely upon him with ever greater earnestness. Throughout the world they share the same feelings; across the myriad states they are of one mind. When the sage arises and all things behold him, how indeed does this differ from clouds and dragons, wind …

translation_en:
…the tiger—how could their following one another be any different? The line statement says: “The flying dragon is in heaven. It is beneficial to see the great man.” This, too, is simply understood by considering this principle. Yet why did the Master attend so deeply to this meaning? He rejoiced for the way of the world and for the way of ministers. For Heaven must first bring forth a sagely and enlightened ruler, and only then will there be worthy and capable ministers. Thus, when the world is at peace and its sovereign is a sage, outstanding men come of their own accord. Like clouds following the dragon and wind following the tiger, they are certain to encounter the right opportunity, and their dispositions are certain to accord. Otherwise, “Without worthy men, the sovereign cannot govern; without a sovereign, worthy men cannot receive sustenance.” The difficulty of their finding one another has been lamented since antiquity. Although these words of the Master explain the benefit of occupying the exalted position of the nine in the fifth place, they also express a hope for his own times: if, fortunately, a great man should arise, he could fulfill his wish to see him to advantage and respond to the opportunity for mutual accord. Then the flourishing age of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties could be restored. Yet in the end he grew old in his travels, saying, “No one can take me as master,” and merely lived out his life in the age of the Spring and Autumn Annals. How lamentable!
The Master said: “How supremely perfect the Changes is! The Changes is that by which the sages exalt their virtue and enlarge their undertakings. Knowledge is lofty; ritual is humble. Loftiness emulates Heaven; humility models itself on Earth. Heaven and Earth establish their positions, and change operates between them. Preserving and continually sustaining one's fully realized nature is the gateway to the Way and righteousness.”

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
乎夫其崇何似也而自與高明上覆者同一體
其知崇效天焉其卑何似也而自與博厚下載
者同一機其禮卑法地焉夫效天則德崇法地
則業廣所以然者何耶蓋天位乎上地在乎下
則陰陽動靜乘其機而神化變易隨其用是之
謂天地設位而易行乎其中矣然聖人知以成
性而純一既不已其功性以立禮而至誠又不
雜以欲則本成之性存而又存吾知由是而之
焉謂之道蓋有取之左右逢其原者矣行而宜
===
之謂之義蓋有用之終身而不能盡者矣道義
之門不由此立乎故曰成性存存道義之門信
乎猶天地設位而易行乎其中也噫聖人用易
之妙至於如此則其謂易之至也豈不信哉雖
然易之爲書當其始也隱於圖象秘於蓍龜非
聖人之神智何以闡其蘊及其終也具三才之
道體萬物之情非聖人之德行何以能時其用
大哉聖人其於易也一而已矣然則欲用之者
當何如亦惟齋戒以神明其德希聖人焉可也

當何如亦惟齋戒以神明其德希聖人焉可也
punctuated:
乎？夫其崇何似也？而自與高明上覆者同一體，其知崇效天焉。其卑何似也？而自與博厚下載者同一機，其禮卑法地焉。夫效天則德崇，法地則業廣。所以然者何耶？蓋天位乎上，地在乎下，則陰陽動靜乘其機，而神化變易隨其用，是之謂「天地設位，而易行乎其中」矣。然聖人知以成性，而純一既不已其功；性以立禮，而至誠又不雜以欲。則本成之性存而又存，吾知由是而之焉謂之道，蓋有取之左右逢其原者矣；行而宜之謂之義，蓋有用之終身而不能盡者矣。道義之門不由此立乎？故曰：「成性存存，道義之門。」信乎猶天地設位而易行乎其中也。

噫！聖人用易之妙至於如此，則其謂易之至也，豈不信哉？雖然，易之爲書，當其始也，隱於圖象，秘於蓍龜，非聖人之神智，何以闡其蘊？及其終也，具三才之道，體萬物之情，非聖人之德行，何以能時其用？大哉聖人！其於易也，一而已矣。然則欲用之者，當何如？亦惟齋戒以神明其德，希聖人焉可也。
translation_en:
…is it not? What is the sage’s loftiness like? He naturally forms one body with that which is high and luminous and covers all from above: his knowledge is lofty and emulates Heaven. What is his lowliness like? He naturally shares one animating impulse with that which is broad and substantial and bears all from below: his ritual practice is lowly and models itself on Earth. By emulating Heaven, his virtue becomes lofty; by modeling himself on Earth, his undertakings become extensive. Why is this so? Heaven occupies its place above, and Earth lies below; yin and yang, movement and stillness, follow their incipient impulses, while wondrous transformation and change accompany their operation. This is what is meant by “Heaven and Earth establish their positions, and change proceeds between them.” Yet the sage uses knowledge to perfect his nature, and his undivided purity never ceases its work; he uses his nature to establish ritual, and his utmost sincerity is unmixed with desire. Thus his originally perfected nature is preserved again and again. I understand that proceeding along this is called the Way: wherever one draws upon it, one encounters its source. Acting as is fitting is called righteousness: one may apply it throughout one’s life without exhausting it. Is not the gateway to the Way and righteousness established through this? Thus it is said: “Preserving the perfected nature continually is the gateway to the Way and righteousness.” Indeed, this resembles Heaven and Earth establishing their positions, with change proceeding between them.

Ah! Since the subtlety of the sage’s use of the Changes reaches such a degree, is it not truly justified to call the Changes the utmost? Nevertheless, when the Changes first became a book, its meaning was concealed in diagrams and images, hidden in milfoil stalks and tortoise shells. Without the sage’s wondrous wisdom, how could its inner significance have been brought to light? In its completed form, it encompasses the Way of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—and embodies the true conditions of the myriad things. Without the sage’s virtue and conduct, how could its use be made timely? Great indeed is the sage! In his relation to the Changes, there is only unity. What, then, should those who wish to use it do? They need only purify themselves through fasting and restraint, thereby making their virtue spiritually luminous and aspiring to become sages.

敷納之以觀其中之所蘊因其功也而明試之
以考其政之所成夫功既立於踐言則禮宜崇

不得已而後威之自今觀之大治之道也而禹
且不以爲然直欲明乎其德而已矣其後天下
果皆以舜之心爲心而治至無爲禹之言不誣
今千載而下猶可以想見其氣象於乎尚德之
治也如此有天下者其知所務哉
punctuated:
黎民有賢者焉，感時思奮，將有爲於治世；回心嚮道，期不負於明時，皆有帝臣之願矣。惟帝於斯時也，無賢而不舉，無舉而不用。因其言也而敷納之，以觀其中之所蘊；因其功也而明試之，以考其政之所成。夫功既立於踐言，則禮宜崇於命德，又有車服之錫，以彰厚報之典。夫善用之如此，吾知觀感之餘，激勸生焉。推遜成風，相率而勉於善也，若有所驅而不能自已矣，其誰敢有不讓者哉？奮揚之際，精白著焉，祗承休德，相率而效其能也，若有所畏而不容自已矣，其敢有不敬應者哉？由是觀之，則天下皆忠皆直，而不忠不直者，不必威而自化矣，尚何庶頑讒說之足慮耶？
抑論舜之教人，無所不極其至，必不得已而後威之。自今觀之，大治之道也，而禹且不以爲然，直欲明乎其德而已矣。其後天下果皆以舜之心爲心，而治至無爲，禹之言不誣。今千載而下，猶可以想見其氣象。於乎！尚德之治也如此，有天下者其知所務哉！
translation_en:
…among the common people there are worthy men. Inspired by the times, they think of rising to action and accomplishing something in an age of good government. Turning their hearts toward the Way, they hope not to fail this enlightened age; all wish to become the emperor’s servants. At such a time, let the emperor advance every worthy man and employ everyone he advances. On the basis of their words, let him receive and assess their proposals, to discern what lies within them; on the basis of their achievements, let him clearly test them, to examine what their administration has accomplished. Once achievement has been established through fulfilling their words, the ceremonial honors conferred in recognition of virtue should be exalted. There should also be gifts of carriages and robes, to manifest the institution of generous recompense. If he employs them so well, I know that, beyond being moved by what they observe, they will be stirred and encouraged. Deference and modesty will become customary, and they will lead one another in striving toward goodness, as though driven by something that prevents them from stopping. Who would dare fail to yield to others? As they rise to action, their purity and sincerity will become manifest. Reverently receiving his excellent virtue, they will lead one another in putting their abilities to service, as though held in awe by something that will not permit them to desist. Who would dare fail to respond respectfully? Viewed thus, all under Heaven will be loyal and upright, while those who are disloyal and crooked will reform of themselves without any need for coercion. What cause would there still be to worry about the stubborn multitude and slanderous talk?
Now, in instructing the people, Shun pursued every means to the utmost, resorting to coercion only when he had no alternative. Viewed from our own time, this was the way to perfect government. Yet even this did not satisfy Yu: he wished only that Shun make his virtue manifest. Thereafter, all under Heaven indeed took Shun’s heart as their own, and government reached the point of effortless action. Yu’s words were no falsehood. Even now, thousands of years later, we can still imagine the spirit of that age. Ah! Such is government that esteems virtue. May those who possess all under Heaven know what they must devote themselves to!

君子演皇極之義，而必著君民相與之盛焉。夫極者，達之天下者也。君錫之而民保之，觀其所與而皇極之義見矣。箕子告武王，蓋謂疇之次五，有曰「建用皇極」矣。皇極之所係大矣，而其建用之義何言乎？彼大君一身，萬化所由出也。是必經綸大經而盡其倫者，足以善天下之則；範圍物理而昭其度者，足以表萬國之儀，則極于是乎建矣。夫極之所建，福之所由集也。吾見單厚多益，而純嘏之休自昭；受于上帝，昌大無疆。
translation_en:
“The sovereign establishes his supreme standard, gathers these five blessings, and distributes them widely among his common people. Then these common people adhere to your standard and enable you to preserve it.”

Zhang Kuang 張爌

Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: “The wording is free of superficial flourishes, yet the meaning is fully expressed. Essays interpreting the classics of this quality are exceedingly rare.”

Associate Examiner Lan, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi), comments: “He expounds the meaning of the sovereign’s supreme standard, leaving none of its implications unexplored. He particularly deserves recommendation for a high ranking.”

Examiner Wu, Left Mentor, comments: “Pure and correct.”

Examiner Li, Left Rectifier, comments: “Classical and elegant.”

When the gentleman expounds the meaning of the sovereign’s supreme standard, he must make manifest the flourishing mutual relationship between ruler and people. For the standard is something extended throughout the realm. The ruler bestows it, and the people preserve it. By observing this mutual relationship, one sees the meaning of the sovereign’s supreme standard. In instructing King Wu, Jizi said of the fifth of the divisions: “Establish and employ the sovereign’s supreme standard.” Great indeed is what depends upon this standard! But how should the meaning of establishing and employing it be explained? The person of the great ruler is the source from which all transforming influences proceed. He must order the great norms and fully realize their proper relationships, thereby perfecting the rules for all under Heaven; he must encompass the principles of things and make their measures clear, thereby setting forth a model for the myriad states. Thus the supreme standard is established. Where this standard is established, blessings consequently gather. I see abundant bounty and ever greater benefits, so that the beauty of great blessings becomes manifest of itself; received from the Lord on High, they flourish and expand without limit …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□□穀之盛自用集于厥躬則五福其克備矣
然是福也非徒獨厚其身也蓋將弘保合之仁
而悉溥於民廣錫類之化而各足其分則固有
之理得而無私之福集因其福而福之是豈分
其所有哉其錫福有如此者斯民也宜若無與
於君也亦皆涵泳不忘從好于貞教之餘服膺
不倦敏德于綏猷之下蓋一德之情通而相成
之念切因其感而奮之夫豈容心也哉其保極
有如此者夫民之與君既由于君之與民然則
===
大君之建極自有不容已者矣抑洪範九疇皇
極綱之矣治天下之道建極盡之矣然極之原
雖出於天而實不外於心使不善事其心則前
之四疇不能立後之四疇不能行而欲極之建
也難矣故曰天之道太極行而萬物取足焉聖
人之道心極立而天下取足焉圖治者宜勗諸

人之道心極立而天下取足焉圖治者宜勗諸

卜爾百福如幾如式既齊既稷既匡既敕
punctuated:
□□穀之盛，自用集于厥躬，則五福其克備矣。然是福也，非徒獨厚其身也。蓋將弘保合之仁，而悉溥於民；廣錫類之化，而各足其分。則固有之理得，而無私之福集。因其福而福之，是豈分其所有哉？其錫福有如此者。斯民也，宜若無與於君也，亦皆涵泳不忘，從好于貞教之餘；服膺不倦，敏德于綏猷之下。蓋一德之情通，而相成之念切，因其感而奮之，夫豈容心也哉？其保極有如此者。夫民之與君，既由于君之與民，然則大君之建極，自有不容已者矣。抑《洪範》九疇，皇極綱之矣；治天下之道，建極盡之矣。然極之原雖出於天，而實不外於心。使不善事其心，則前之四疇不能立，後之四疇不能行，而欲極之建也難矣。故曰：「天之道，太極行而萬物取足焉；聖人之道，心極立而天下取足焉。」圖治者宜勗諸！
詩
工祝致告，徂賚孝孫。苾芬孝祀，神嗜飲食。卜爾百福，如幾如式。既齊既稷，既匡既勅。
translation_en:
…the abundance of □□ blessings [?] thereby gathers upon his person, and the five blessings can thus be complete. Yet these blessings do not merely enrich him alone. He will extend the benevolence that preserves harmony and spread it universally among the people; he will broaden the transforming influence that bestows blessings upon others, so that each receives their due. Thus inherent principle is realized, and blessings free of selfish partiality gather. To bless the people in accordance with their own capacity for blessing—how could this merely mean dividing up what he himself possesses? Such is his bestowal of blessings.
The people might seem to have no part to play toward their ruler. Yet all immerse themselves in his influence without forgetting it, following what is good under the enduring influence of his upright instruction; they hold it to their hearts without tiring, diligently cultivating virtue under his tranquil guidance. Their feelings communicate through a shared virtue, and their desire to bring one another to fulfillment is earnest. Stirred by his influence, they rouse themselves: how could this involve any calculated intent? Such is their preservation of the supreme standard. Since what the people give their ruler arises from what the ruler gives the people, establishing that standard is something the great ruler cannot cease to do.
Moreover, the sovereign standard governs the nine categories of the Great Plan, and establishing that standard encompasses the entire way of governing the world. Although the standard originates in Heaven, it is in truth inseparable from the heart. If one fails to cultivate one’s heart properly, the preceding four categories cannot be established, and the following four cannot be put into practice; establishing the standard will then be difficult indeed. Thus it is said: “In Heaven’s Way, the Supreme Ultimate operates, and all things obtain their sufficiency from it; in the sage’s Way, the supreme standard of the heart is established, and all under Heaven obtain their sufficiency from it.” Those who seek good government should exert themselves in this!
Book of Odes
The officiating invocator delivers the announcement,
Bringing gifts to the filial descendant.
Fragrant is the filial offering;
The spirits relish the food and drink.
He foretells for you a hundred blessings,
As you hoped, according to the prescribed pattern.
You have been reverent and prompt,
Upright and diligent.…

…admonished; may you forever be granted the utmost blessing, in tens of thousands and hundreds of millions.
Ao Quan.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Professor: The topic is inherently dignified, but writers constrain themselves to conventional correspondences: their conception lacks breadth, and their language is glib and shallow. This composition explains it directly through the blessing pronounced at the Lesser Offering (Shaolao). Its language is economical, yet its meaning is complete. This captures the point.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Judge: The central conception is exceptional; this is no carelessly composed work.
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): The explanation of “expectation” and “rule” is effective. The sense of “田奉祭” [?] also suggests someone skilled at interpreting the Book of Odes.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Left Mentor: The language is natural throughout, and the meaning emerges clearly of itself.
Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion: The tone is harmonious and the language dignified.
The poet recounts the blessing in full in order to praise the dukes and ministers for serving the spirits and receiving blessings. To sacrifice and unfailingly receive blessings is something only the worthy can accomplish. By examining the words of the blessing, we can understand how the dukes and ministers commune with the spirits. The poet’s meaning in “Thick Tribulus” (Chu ci) is as though he were saying: In the sacrifice our dukes and ministers conduct today, they follow ritual without error, bringing their reverence to perfection. Could the spirits come without any intention? At this moment, within the ancestral temple, someone skilled in the duties of the invocator conveys the spirits’ intentions in words, approaching the filial descendant to deliver their message. What does he announce? It is that, in your sacrifice, you prepare wine and food for the offerings, yet it is your luminous virtue that supplies the fragrance; you purify oxen and sheep to furnish the bamboo offering vessels [?], and your wholehearted sincerity reaches its utmost. The food and drink are fragrant and pure: with what shall you be rewarded? Surely…

text:
將俾爾單厚而百福之是介乎意之所欲保之
右之受祿于天眉壽萬年福之來也秩秩而無
疆有不如期者耶制之所定引之翼之宜稼于
田歲取十千積之多也陳陳而相因有不如法
者耶豈惟此哉猶以爾之祭也盡其愨而愨焉
旣齊旣稷而無所於怠盡其敬而敬焉旣匡旣
敕而罔有弗欽禮容則莊敬矣又何予之其將
俾爾戩穀永盛衆善之極乎一日二日事幾有
萬以時措之無不宜也祿之受于天者其亦於

盛政修有以致之不然豈溢美乎故先儒謂此

…will they cause you to enjoy abundant bounty and aid you with a hundred blessings? In accordance with your heart’s desires, they will preserve and protect you: you will receive Heaven’s bounty and live to venerable old age, for ten thousand years. Blessings will come in orderly succession, without limit. Could any fail to meet your expectations? In accordance with the established ordinances, they will guide and assist you: your crops will flourish in the fields, and each year you will reap ten thousand measures. Your stores will accumulate, old grain piled upon old. Could any of this fail to follow the prescribed pattern? Nor is this all! In your sacrifice, you have also shown the utmost sincerity, being reverent and prompt, without any negligence; you have shown the utmost respect, being correct and circumspect, with nothing lacking in reverence. Your ritual bearing is thus solemn and respectful. What further reward will they give you? Will they cause your blessings to flourish forever, bringing every good thing to its utmost fulfillment? In a single day or two, the incipient affairs to be dealt with number ten thousand; by handling them at the proper time, you leave nothing improperly managed. Will the bounty you receive from Heaven not likewise endure for ten thousand years? Affairs great and small are beyond counting; by issuing measures at the proper time, you ensure that none fails to bring benefit. Will the crops flourishing in your fields not likewise yield countless myriads of measures?
Ah! The dukes and ministers devote themselves to agriculture and offer sacrifices to express their filial piety. The blessings bestowed upon them by the spirits seem thus to answer each undertaking with a corresponding reward. Can the workings of the unseen and visible worlds, and the principle of their sympathetic communion, be denied?

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
病者非天之絕人也人自絕于天耳則夫安民
以回天者豈可以他求哉亦在於吾人耳誠能
無易由言於凡發之爲詞命而播之於中外者
本大猷以爲經匪言則勿言焉愼爾出話於凡
渙之爲號令而敷之於遐邇者則先王以爲訓
非法則弗道焉揆諸天理而無所於逆慈祥豈
弟之意藹如也其辭不亦和乎協乎人情而無
所於乖忠厚慘怛之誠盎如也其辭不亦悅乎
夫此亦自謹其言耳若無與於民也然民至愚
===
而聽則聰善言之所加莫不奔走以相告而曰
盍歸來乎民雖異而心則同仁聲之所達莫不
傾耳而承聽而曰其生我乎呻吟愁苦者謳歌
而歡悅向之所謂勞止者由是而汔康也寧有
携貳者耶流離渙散者還定而安集昔之所謂
卒痒者於此其少瘳矣寧有失所者耶吁言之
謹於我者甚微而效之得於民者甚速如此得
民斯得天而方難方蹶者可回矣憲憲泄泄其
可乎哉於此可以見天人之理焉可以見上下

translation_en:
…and the people suffer, it is not Heaven that cuts humanity off; people cut themselves off from Heaven. How, then, could the means of bringing peace to the people and thereby turning Heaven back in our favor be sought elsewhere? They lie in us alone. If we can truly refrain from speaking lightly, then in all pronouncements issued and circulated within the court and beyond, we will take the great Way as our guiding principle and leave unsaid whatever ought not to be said. If we are cautious in uttering words, then in all commands promulgated and disseminated far and near, we will take the former kings as our model and utter nothing contrary to their standards. Measured against Heaven’s principles, our words will oppose them in nothing; kindness and gracious ease will pervade their intent. Will such words not be harmonious? In accord with human feelings and at variance with them in nothing, they will overflow with the sincerity of generosity and heartfelt compassion. Will such words not be pleasing?

This is merely to be cautious in one’s own speech, seemingly without any connection to the people. Yet though the people may be most simple, their hearing is discerning. Wherever good words reach, all will hurry to tell one another, saying, “Why should we not return?” Though people differ, their hearts are alike. Wherever the voice of benevolence reaches, all will incline their ears and listen, saying, “Will he not give us life?” Those who groaned in sorrow and distress will sing in joy. Those previously described as “toiling” will thereby attain some ease. Could any remain estranged or divided in allegiance? Those displaced and scattered will return, settle, and gather in peace. The condition formerly described as “suffering everywhere” will now be somewhat relieved. Could any remain without a place to belong?

Ah! Being cautious in our own words is so small a thing, yet its effects among the people come so swiftly! Win the people and one wins Heaven; the situation in which calamity and upheaval are upon us can then be reversed. How could self-satisfaction and indolence be permissible? Here one may perceive the principles linking Heaven and humanity; here one may perceive how those above and those below…

text:
兵于鄭其惡大矣苟不即晉救之善□□見
其然哉昔者楚莊在位圖伯中國因鄭之服于
晉也將兵以伐之而經于此稱爵焉君子以為
非與之者何蓋亂賊之黨雖夫人得以舉義而
華夷之辨則裔不可以謀夏也歸生既斃鄭則
何罪而莊乃以重兵臨之由是晉也念我懿親
遣郤缺以往救焉柳棼之役楚焰息而鄭有賴
矣晉之善寧容揜乎故經于伐鄭之下特書晉

===
為國君自將陵蔑中華書其重者耳貶之之意
不於是而見邪既而楚共嗣位侵軼諸姬因鄭
之盟于晉也命將以伐之而經于此直書焉君
子以為深惡之者何蓋反正之善固悔悟之方
新而有君之喪則仁人之所憫也成公初立鄭
則可矜而共乃以背巳仇之由是晉也恤我同
盟遣欒書以往救焉桑隧之遇楚氛遏而鄭克
紓矣晉之善不亦彰乎故經于伐鄭之下特書

爲國君自將凌蔑中華書其重者耳良之之意
不於是而見邪既而楚共嗣位侵軼諸姬因鄭
之盟于晉也命將以伐之而經于此直書焉君
子以爲深惡之者何蓋反正之善固悔悟之方
新而有君之喪則仁人之所憫也成公初立鄭
則可矜而共乃以背已仇之由是晉也恤我同
盟遣欒書以往救焉桑隧之遇楚氛遏而鄭克
紓矣晉之善不亦彰乎故經于伐鄭之下特書
晉欒書救鄭亦予晉也予晉則楚之直書乃知
punctuated:
兵于鄭，其惡大矣！苟不即晉救之善□□見其然哉？昔者楚莊在位，圖伯中國，因鄭之服于晉也，將兵以伐之，而經于此稱爵焉。君子以為非與之者，何？蓋亂賊之黨，雖夫人得以舉義，而華夷之辨，則裔不可以謀夏也。歸生既斃，鄭則何罪？而莊乃以重兵臨之。由是晉也念我懿親，遣郤缺以往救焉。柳棼之役，楚焰息而鄭有賴矣。晉之善，寧容揜乎？故經于伐鄭之下，特書「晉郤缺救鄭」，蓋予晉也。予晉，則楚之書爵，乃知其為國君自將，陵蔑中華，書其重者耳。貶之之意，不於是而見邪？

既而楚共嗣位，侵軼諸姬，因鄭之盟于晉也，命將以伐之，而經于此直書焉。君子以為深惡之者，何？蓋反正之善，固悔悟之方新，而有君之喪，則仁人之所憫也。成公初立，鄭則可矜，而共乃以背巳仇之。由是晉也恤我同盟，遣欒書以往救焉。桑隧之遇，楚氛遏而鄭克紓矣。晉之善，不亦彰乎？故經于伐鄭之下，特書「晉欒書救鄭」，亦予晉也。予晉，則楚之直書，乃知

…troops against Zheng: its wickedness was indeed great! If this were not revealed through the goodness of Jin’s rescue, [two illegible characters] how could it be seen as such [?]? Formerly, when King Zhuang of Chu occupied the throne, he sought hegemony over the Central States. Because Zheng had submitted to Jin, he led troops to attack it, and here the Classic names him by his noble rank. Why do learned gentlemen consider this no expression of approval? Against a faction of rebels and malefactors, anyone may indeed take up arms in righteousness; but in the distinction between the Chinese states and the foreign peoples, those on the periphery may not plot against the Chinese states. Guisheng was already dead: what crime, then, had Zheng committed? Yet King Zhuang descended upon it with a great army. Thereupon Jin, mindful that Zheng was its close kinsman, dispatched Xi Que to rescue it. In the campaign at Liufen [?], Chu’s blaze was extinguished, and Zheng found support. Could Jin’s goodness be allowed to remain obscured? Thus, beneath the attack on Zheng, the Classic expressly records: “Xi Que of Jin rescued Zheng.” This approves of Jin. From this approval of Jin, we understand that Chu’s ruler is recorded by rank because, as ruler of a state, he personally commanded the troops and trampled upon the Chinese states: the text simply records the graver aspect of his offense. Is its intent to censure him not thereby made evident?

Later, King Gong of Chu succeeded to the throne and encroached upon the states of the Ji lineage. Because Zheng had entered into a covenant with Jin, he ordered a general to attack it, and here the Classic records the matter directly. Why do learned gentlemen consider this an expression of profound abhorrence? The goodness of returning to the right path marked Zheng’s newly awakened repentance; moreover, its mourning for its ruler was something a humane person would pity. Duke Cheng had only just assumed the throne, so Zheng deserved compassion. Yet King Gong treated it as an enemy for turning its back on him. Thereupon Jin, concerned for its covenant partner, dispatched Luan Shu to rescue it. In the encounter at Sangsui, Chu’s threatening force was checked, and Zheng gained relief. Was Jin’s goodness not also manifest? Thus, beneath the attack on Zheng, the Classic expressly records: “Luan Shu of Jin rescued Zheng.” This too approves of Jin. From this approval of Jin, we understand that the direct recording of Chu’s action…

其爲利人之難恣行私憤不待貶者耳惡之之
意又不於是而見邪故觀此則聖人攘夷安夏
之意可識矣雖然晉楚之所視以爲盛衰者顧

…that Chu was taking advantage of another state's distress and freely venting its private resentment: no additional disparagement was needed. Is the intention to condemn it not also apparent here? From this we can discern the Sage's intention to repel the barbarians and secure the Xia states. Nevertheless, what Jin and Chu regarded as the measure of their strength or decline was merely whether Zheng submitted to or resisted them. As leader of the covenant, had Duke Jing cultivated his virtuous government in his dealings with Zheng and assisted its defense, Zheng would surely never have turned south toward Chu. How, then, could Chu's designs upon the north have arisen? His plans did not follow this course; he merely contended over allegiance and defection. No wonder warfare was incessant! Alas! This is why the gentleman condemns Duke Jing of Jin for lacking a strategy to repel the barbarians and secure the Xia states, and regrets that Duke Dao came so late.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
國者有四鄰焉以藩外也故封境之寧不寧于
寧之日以其守在四鄰也州來非楚之鄰乎制
之自我而敵毋敢乘焉將謂共必有見于此矣
孰意其吳得以入之耶夫吳之所能入由楚先
事之防疎而有間可乘耳不然近在邊陲之側
固宜得而制之彼豈敢以嘗試之謀徑造其地
而不顧哉噫四鄰之害楚以爲憂止于鄰而已
吾聞撤籬以禦寇其誰能遏之此謀臣所以料
其爲疲楚之端也傳曰書吳入州來著陵楚之
===
漸非與有四境焉以衛內也故國都之安不安
于安之時以其守在四境也巢非楚之境乎保
之自我而敵勿敢窺焉將謂平必不昧于此矣
孰意其吳得以滅之耶夫吳之所能滅由楚預
備之政弛而有隙可窺耳不然密邇疆場之間
固宜得而保之彼豈敢以再逞之欲遂奪其邑
而不忌哉噫四境之亡楚以爲患及于境而已
吾聞開門以延盜其誰能禦之此識者所以知
其爲亡郢之始也傳曰書吳滅巢著入郢之漸

漸非與有四境焉以衛内也故國都之安不安
于安之時以其守在四境也巢非楚之境乎保
之自我而敵勿敢窺焉將謂乎必不昧于此矣
孰意其吳得以滅之耶夫吳之所能滅由楚預
備之政弛而有隙可窺耳不然密邇疆埸之間
固宜得而保之彼豈敢以再逞之欲遂奪其邑
而不忌哉噫四境之亡楚以爲患及于境而已
吾聞開門以延盜其誰能禦之此識者所以知
其爲亡郢之始也傳曰書吳滅巢著入郢之漸
punctuated:
國者，有四鄰焉，以藩外也。故封境之寧，不寧于寧之日，以其守在四鄰也。州來非楚之鄰乎？制之自我，而敵毋敢乘焉，將謂共必有見于此矣，孰意其吳得以入之耶？夫吳之所能入，由楚先事之防疎，而有間可乘耳。不然，近在邊陲之側，固宜得而制之，彼豈敢以嘗試之謀，徑造其地而不顧哉？噫！四鄰之害，楚以爲憂止于鄰而已。吾聞撤籬以禦寇，其誰能遏之？此謀臣所以料其爲疲楚之端也。傳曰：「書吳入州來，著陵楚之漸。」非與？
有四境焉，以衛內也。故國都之安，不安于安之時，以其守在四境也。巢非楚之境乎？保之自我，而敵勿敢窺焉，將謂平必不昧于此矣，孰意其吳得以滅之耶？夫吳之所能滅，由楚預備之政弛，而有隙可窺耳。不然，密邇疆場之間，固宜得而保之，彼豈敢以再逞之欲，遂奪其邑而不忌哉？噫！四境之亡，楚以爲患及于境而已。吾聞開門以延盜，其誰能禦之？此識者所以知其爲亡郢之始也。傳曰：「書吳滅巢，著入郢之漸。」
translation_en:
…the state: there are its neighbors on all four sides, serving as an outer screen. Thus, the tranquility of its frontiers is not secured merely in days of tranquility, for their defense lies with those neighboring states. Was Zhoulai not a neighbor of Chu? Control over it rested with Chu itself, so that an enemy should not have dared exploit an opening there. One would have thought that King Gong must have understood this. Who could have imagined that Wu would manage to enter it? Wu was able to enter only because Chu’s advance precautions were lax, leaving an opening to exploit. Otherwise, situated so close to Chu’s frontier, Zhoulai surely ought to have been kept under control. How would Wu have dared march straight into its territory without hesitation, merely to put Chu to the test? Alas! When its neighbors suffered harm, Chu thought the grounds for concern extended only to those neighbors. Yet I have heard it said: if one tears down the fence to ward off raiders, who can stop them? This is why a counselor foresaw that this would mark the beginning of Chu’s exhaustion. The Commentary says: “Recording Wu’s entry into Zhoulai reveals the gradual encroachment upon Chu.” Is this not so?
There are also the territories on all four borders, serving to protect the interior. Thus, the security of the capital is not secured merely in times of security, for its defense lies in those border territories. Was Chao not part of Chu’s borderlands? Its protection rested with Chu itself, so that an enemy should not have dared covet it. One would have thought that King Ping could not have been blind to this. Who could have imagined that Wu would manage to destroy it? Wu was able to destroy it only because Chu’s measures for preparedness had grown lax, leaving a vulnerability to probe. Otherwise, situated so close along the frontier, Chao surely ought to have been protected. How would Wu have dared seize its town without restraint, seeking once again to have its way? Alas! When its border territories were lost, Chu thought the calamity affected only those territories. Yet I have heard it said: if one opens the gate to invite robbers in, who can resist them? This is why those with discernment knew that this marked the beginning of the loss of Ying. The Commentary says: “Recording Wu’s destruction of Chao reveals the gradual advance toward entering Ying.” …
