translation_en:
…Is that not so? Here we see that Chu allowed Wu’s gradual encroachment to develop earlier as though it were no cause for concern, while the harm it suffered afterward was beyond description. Should not those who possess states therefore take care to secure their frontiers, so as not to bring upon themselves the disaster of peril and destruction? Yet there is a further point: governing a state rests fundamentally upon obtaining worthy men. If a state lacks such men, with whom can its ruler share the work of government? In Chu at that time, Wuchen and Wu Yun both served Wu, while those with whom the ruler deliberated morning and evening were merely the wine-loving Zifan and Wuji, who entrenched himself in the ruler’s favor. Jealous of the worthy and obstructing the capable, they together threw the state into disorder. With its vital organs diseased and its eyes and ears obstructed, could it possibly escape danger? Thus, the nine guiding principles give high priority to honoring the worthy, and the four requirements place removing slanderers first. This, too, is something a ruler ought to understand.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
觀先王巡守命禮官之事見大一統之治焉蓋
天下一統則政不容以或異也先王巡守所以
命之禮官者不有在於此哉記王制者之意若
曰昔先王之巡守旣舉祀典覲諸侯矣觀民風
察民志矣而有所謂命典禮者焉其命維何
蓋以四時日月皆天之所以示乎人者也固嘗
曆象授時而頒之天下矣今茲所歷之地庸詎
知其無或差乎咨汝典禮盍精察於斯盍詳審
於斯於凡時之節氣早晚也月之弦望晦朔也
===

In considering how the former kings, on their inspection tours, issued commands to the ritual officials, we see government founded on grand unification. For when All-under-Heaven is united, no divergence in governance can be permitted. Was this not the purpose of the commands that the former kings gave the ritual officials on their inspection tours? The intention of the author of the “Royal Regulations” (Wang zhi) may be expressed thus: When the former kings made their inspection tours, they had already performed the prescribed sacrifices and received the feudal lords in audience; they had observed the people’s customs and examined their sentiments. There was also what is called issuing commands to those in charge of ritual. What were these commands?
The four seasons, the days, and the months are all means by which Heaven gives instruction to humankind. The kings had already calculated and observed the celestial phenomena, determined the seasons, and promulgated the calendar throughout All-under-Heaven. Yet how could they know that the places through which they now traveled had no discrepancies? “Hear this, you who administer ritual! Should you not examine these matters closely and scrutinize them thoroughly? As to the early or late arrival of the seasonal solar terms, the quarters and full moons, the last and first days of the lunar months, and the sequence of days designated by jia, yi, and the other cyclical signs, ensure that each accords with its proper timing.” Thus, through astronomical calculation, calendrical methods might accord with Heaven; through harmonization and correction, government might observe the proper seasons. What was used in the many states would be just what was used at the royal court. Would not the calendar thereby be unified?
As for pitch standards, rites and music, institutional regulations, and dress, these are all means by which superiors give instruction to inferiors. The kings had already examined antiquity, established regulations, and disseminated them in all directions. Yet how could they know that the states they now visited had no divergences? “Since you are in charge of ritual, you should now bring these matters into conformity and correct them. As to the pitch pipes used to detect the seasonal qi, the rites and music employed, the regulations governing palaces, chambers, carriages, and banners, and the dress distinguishing the honored from the humble and superiors from inferiors, ensure that all are correct and without □ [?].” Thus, above, there might be the Way as the guiding standard, so that states would not differ in their governance; below, there might be adherence to established rules, so that …

translation_en:
…households do not differ in their customs. What is practiced among the various states is just what is practiced within the royal domain. Would not the people then commit few errors? Ah! When the Way of Heaven is verified above, the intention to revere Heaven and diligently care for the people becomes manifest; when royal institutions are made uniform below, the Way of establishing and preserving the supreme standard becomes evident. Such was the former king’s government during his eastern tour. Extended and put into practice, all these measures followed their original principles: surely this was how he magnified the rule of comprehensive unity! Nevertheless, these were the institutions of the house of Yu. The Xia ruling house followed them, and under the Zhou they became still more complete. When the Zhou declined, the institutions of the former kings came close to being abolished. Earlier scholars held that the chapter “Royal Regulations” was composed during the transition from Qin to Han; perhaps its author, too, perceived this state of affairs! Should someone arise later to renew these institutions, the canons of Yu remain available.
“Every arising of musical sound is born of the human heart. When the human heart is stirred, external things cause it to be so.”
Wang Liangce
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Magistrate: The topic is based on the very first principle set forth at the opening of the “Record of Music.” It traces back the source from which musical sound arises and the cause by which the heart is stirred, taking these as the foundation of music. Writers commonly explain musical sound through such descriptions as ‘expansive and relaxed’ and ‘coarse and fierce’ in the subsequent text, and explain the heart through joy, anger, and the like. Even accomplished writers draw upon these passages, but this is not the original intention of the author of the Record. This composition is rich and comprehensive in meaning, and its wording is precise and apt. It surely reflects sincere and substantial learning.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Left Assistant Mentor: The wording is precise and apt.
Comment by Examiner Li, Left Assistant Instructor: Measured and unhurried, pure and elegant.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
記者原音生于人心之感物所以著樂之本也
夫物感于中而音發於外人心之不能已者也
樂之本其在兹乎記者首揭之以示人其意深
矣若曰生民之道樂焉大夫樂何爲者也天下
之理感應而已矣觀其所感而樂可知矣是故
樂必有音也音之起果何所自耶蓋人也者萬
物之靈而心也者萬事之本音在外若無與於
心也然虛靈之體固涵聲氣之元神明之舍實
具至和之妙故夫相生相成音固若是乎其不
===
窮矣究而言之其皆本於此乎相和相應音固
若是乎其不一矣遡而論之其皆原於斯乎苟
非心焉則音或幾乎息矣是音固生於人心也
心之動又孰使之然耶蓋寂然不動者心之體
感而遂通者心之用靜以上固不容說也惟夫
事變於前則天機不容以自秘物交于外則性
術不容以終藏是惟無感感之即應其來也無
窮而其應也不測全體呈露抑之而不能止也
是惟無觸觸之即覺其至也無常而其知也不

punctuated:
記者原音生于人心之感物，所以著樂之本也。

夫物感于中而音發於外，人心之不能已者也。樂之本，其在兹乎？記者首揭之以示人，其意深矣。若曰：生民之道，樂焉大。夫樂何爲者也？天下之理，感應而已矣。觀其所感，而樂可知矣。是故樂必有音也，音之起果何所自耶？蓋人也者，萬物之靈；而心也者，萬事之本。音在外，若無與於心也；然虛靈之體，固涵聲氣之元；神明之舍，實具至和之妙。故夫相生相成，音固若是乎其不窮矣；究而言之，其皆本於此乎？相和相應，音固若是乎其不一矣；遡而論之，其皆原於斯乎？苟非心焉，則音或幾乎息矣。是音固生於人心也。

心之動，又孰使之然耶？蓋寂然不動者，心之體；感而遂通者，心之用。靜以上，固不容說也。惟夫事變於前，則天機不容以自秘；物交于外，則性術不容以終藏。是惟無感，感之即應，其來也無窮，而其應也不測，全體呈露，抑之而不能止也。是惟無觸，觸之即覺，其至也無常，而其知也不
translation_en:
The author of the Record traces the birth of musical tones to the human heart’s being moved by things, thereby making clear the foundation of music.

Things stir the heart within, and tones issue forth without: this is something the human heart cannot help doing. Does not the foundation of music lie here? The author sets this out at the very beginning to instruct others; his intention is profound. It is as though he were saying: in the way of human life, music holds a great place. What, then, does music do? The principle governing all under Heaven is simply stimulus and response. Observe what moves people, and music can be understood. Thus music necessarily has tones. But where, in fact, do tones originate? Human beings are the most spiritually perceptive of the myriad creatures, and the heart is the foundation of all affairs. Tones exist outwardly and seem to have nothing to do with the heart. Yet the heart’s empty and numinous substance inherently contains the source of sound and vital energy; as the dwelling of spiritual intelligence, it truly possesses the subtle workings of perfect harmony. Thus tones generate and complete one another, inexhaustibly. If we investigate the matter, do they not all have their foundation here? Tones harmonize with and respond to one another, in all their variety. If we trace them back, do they not all originate here? Were it not for the heart, tones would perhaps all but cease. Thus tones assuredly arise from the human heart.

What, in turn, causes the heart to move? Stillness without movement is the heart’s substance; responding to a stimulus and thereby attaining comprehensive awareness is its function. As for what precedes this stillness, it cannot properly be spoken of. But when events change before us, the spontaneous workings of Heaven cannot remain concealed; when things engage us from without, the workings of our nature [?] cannot remain hidden forever. Only in the absence of a stimulus is there no response; once stimulated, the heart responds immediately. What comes to it is inexhaustible, and its responses are unfathomable. Its entire substance stands revealed: even if one tries to suppress it, it cannot be stopped. Only in the absence of contact is there no awareness; once touched, the heart is immediately aware. What reaches it follows no fixed pattern, and its knowing does not…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
時妙用顯行遏之而不可禦也使非物焉則固
未發之中耳是則物動乎心則音有所本矣心
生乎音則樂有所飾矣動其本治其節其斯以
爲樂乎抑心之感物而成音固也然物感無窮
人情無節道心人心之感德音溺音之所由分
是不可不愼也夫惟君子反情以和志比類以
成行則德音發而正樂興可以感人心而天下
和平矣故曰先王愼所以感之者不知出此而
徒較之金石絫之秬黍抑末矣此語樂者又不
===

…at no fixed time; its wondrous functioning becomes manifest, and attempts to check it cannot restrain it. Were there no external things, there would simply be the equilibrium of feelings not yet aroused. Thus, when things stir the heart, sound has its source; when the heart arises from sound [?], music has that which gives it embellishment. To activate its source and regulate its measures—is this perhaps how music is made? That the heart responds to things and produces sound is certainly so. Yet the stimuli of things are inexhaustible, and human feelings know no bounds. Responses arising from the moral mind and from the human mind are what distinguish virtuous sounds from debasing sounds. One must therefore exercise care.
Only when the gentleman turns back upon his feelings to harmonize his intentions, and follows what is fitting to form his conduct, do virtuous sounds issue forth and correct music flourish. These can move people's hearts, bringing peace and harmony to all under Heaven. Hence the saying: “The former kings were careful about that by which they moved people's hearts.” To fail to proceed from this, merely comparing pitches on metal and stone instruments and piling up grains of black millet to establish measures, is surely to attend to the periphery! This, too, is something those who discuss music must understand.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
切就傳措詞又雜而無叙此篇只就本傳敷演成文意
義精切是能發曾子之蘊者錄之
考試官左贊善吳批是題人皆知之但多勦
說可厭此作只本傳註或問融會成篇而意見超卓
自不可及宜錄以式
考試官左中允李批議論精確而步驟悠揚
其必醞藉之深者矣
論曰君子之於天下使人各得其所者非人人
爲之所也亦惟因其心之所同者而推之耳天
===
下至大也人至衆也使人人而爲之所而後天
下之人始各得其所焉則其勢固有所不能且
無益於天下君子不爲也是必有要道焉何也
蓋天下之所不同者人也而所同者心也吾惟
因其心之所同者而體諸身而推之人所以處
之者無不當則人之心亦我之心彼我之間分

The discourse reads: In dealing with all under Heaven, the noble man enables everyone to find their proper place. He does not do so by arranging a place for each person individually; he simply takes what their hearts share and extends it to others. All under Heaven is exceedingly vast, and its people exceedingly numerous. If everyone could find their proper place only after a place had been arranged for each individually, this would necessarily exceed what circumstances permit and would moreover bring no benefit to all under Heaven. The noble man does not act thus. There must therefore be an essential way. What is it? What differs throughout the world is the people; what they share is the heart. I need only take what their hearts share, embody it in myself, and extend it to others, so that every way I deal with them is fitting. Others’ hearts are thus also my own heart. Between others and myself, each person’s due portion and aspirations are satisfied. Extend this throughout all under Heaven, and surely no one will fail to find their proper place. title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
論之夫所謂矩者何物也所以爲方之器也吾
嘗觀夫梓匠輪輿欲成器於天下而使長短小
大無不如其意者是故賴有此耳天下大器也
以君子而平天下大事也顧亦賴於此乎吁非
然也吾人之心固有天理當然之則是乃所以
爲矩即孔子所謂從心所欲不踰者是也是矩
也人皆有之惟聖人全體渾然故隨其心之所
欲而自無所踰也衆人有之而不知知之而不
能自遂此天下之所以有不平也有之而能知
===
知之而不自有其有而復推之人使天下無不
平者君子耳君子何能若是乎亦曰物格知至
有以通天下之志而知千萬人之心即一人之
心意誠心正有以勝一己之私而能以一人之
心爲千萬人之心如此而已矣何以知千萬人
之心即一人之心也蓋天下之理感之而不應
倡之而不和則未可必其同也今也老吾老非
欲使民之孝也而民自興於孝長吾長非欲使
民之弟也而民自興於弟恤吾孤非欲使民之

translation_en:
…discuss this further. What is this thing called a carpenter’s square? It is an instrument for making things square. I have observed carpenters, joiners, wheelwrights, and carriage makers: when they wish to fashion objects in the world, making every length and size accord with their intentions, it is upon this that they rely. All under Heaven is a great vessel; for the gentleman to bring peace to all under Heaven is a great undertaking. Yet does this too depend upon such an instrument? Ah, it is not so! Our hearts inherently possess the normative standard of heavenly principle. This is what serves as the square: it is precisely what Confucius meant by following his heart’s desires without overstepping the bounds. Everyone possesses this square. Only in the sage is its entirety perfectly integrated; thus he follows whatever his heart desires and naturally never oversteps. Ordinary people possess it but do not recognize it, or recognize it but cannot fully realize it themselves. This is why there is discord under Heaven. It is the gentleman alone who possesses it and recognizes it, and, recognizing it, does not keep what he possesses to himself, but extends it to others, bringing peace everywhere under Heaven. How can the gentleman achieve this? Simply thus: with things investigated and knowledge fully attained, he can comprehend the aspirations of all under Heaven and know that the hearts of millions are the same as the heart of one person; with intentions sincere and the heart rectified, he can overcome his own selfishness and make one person’s heart the heart of millions. That is all.
How do we know that the hearts of millions are the same as the heart of one person? In the workings of the world, if something is stirred but does not respond, or called to but does not answer in harmony, we cannot be certain of their underlying sameness. Yet when I honor my aged kin, I do not intend thereby to make the people filial, but the people naturally rise to filial devotion. When I respect my elders, I do not intend thereby to make the people deferential to their elders, but the people naturally rise to such deference. When I care for my orphans, I do not intend thereby to make the people…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□倍也而民自爾其不倍由此觀之是惟無感
感之斯應是惟無倡倡之斯和蓋真有捷於影
響者矣非心之本同能若是乎心之所同者若
是使吾失其所以處之之道則彼雖欲同於我
而不可得於是始紛然而異於天下陵逼侵越
無所底極其何以平君子者既知其同則固有
所不忍恝然於中而使其異之若是也於是乎
有處之之道焉是道也非有所付畀增益於彼
我之間也無亦曰因其所同以一人之心爲千
===
萬之心耳是故好惡者其端也用人理財者其
要也公私得失之幾則在於吾心而已矣故觀
其所惡於上下左右前後之間而皆勿之施焉
而天地萬物之情見矣絜矩之義著矣夫爲天
下國家而所以處心制事者一出於此則天地
之間將無一物不得其所而凡天下之欲爲孝
弟不倍者皆得以自盡其心而無不均之歎天
下其有不平者乎故能存此心而不失則可以
爲民之父母也可以得衆得國得天命也可以

…[not?] turn their backs on others, yet the people naturally refrain from doing so. Viewed in this light, it is only a matter of whether anyone moves them: once moved, they respond; whether anyone leads them: once led, they join in harmony. Indeed, their response is swifter than a shadow or an echo. Could this happen if their hearts were not fundamentally alike? Such is what hearts have in common. If I lose the proper way of dealing with them, then even though they wish to be of one mind with me, they cannot. Only then do differences proliferate throughout the world, with oppression, coercion, encroachment, and transgression knowing no limit. How could the world be brought to peace? Since the gentleman understands this common ground, he cannot bear to remain indifferent in his heart and allow such differences to arise. Thus there is a proper way of dealing with them. This way involves no bestowal or addition between others and oneself. It consists simply in following what their hearts have in common and making the heart of one person the heart of the multitude.
Thus likes and dislikes are its starting point; employing people and managing wealth are its essentials. The pivotal distinction between public concern and private interest, success and failure, lies solely in my own heart. Accordingly, consider what one dislikes in dealings with those above and below, to the left and right, ahead and behind, and never inflict any of it upon others. Then the true dispositions of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things become manifest, and the meaning of measuring by the square becomes clear. If, in governing the world, the state, and the family, one's disposition of mind and handling of affairs proceed entirely from this, then nothing between Heaven and Earth will fail to find its proper place. All under Heaven who wish to practice filial devotion, respect for elders, and fidelity will be able fully to realize what is in their hearts, with no lament over unequal treatment. Could anything under Heaven then remain unsettled? title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人有土有財用也又推之如楚書之寶善也
舅犯之仁親也秦誓之休休有容也仁人之能
愛惡人也生財有大道而以財發身也孟獻子
之不畜聚斂臣也其或反是則爲天下僇矣則
失衆失國失天命矣則爭民施奪而民散而悖
出矣又推之如秦誓之媚疾也見賢不能舉舉
而不能先見不善不能退退而不能遠也極之
而拂人之性菑必逮身也務財用而菑害並至
也吁一矩也能絜之與不能絜之其效之相懸
===
有如此亦可畏已然其得失之故豈有他哉亦
在於吾心而已矣故曰君子有大道必忠信以
得之驕泰以失之言得失之繫乎其心者也故
能忠信以爲心則公公則物我貫通上下融徹
反是而驕泰則私私則物我相侵彼此交病蓋
至此而天理存亡之幾决矣天理存亡之幾决
則天命人心之去留得失判矣愚以是而知絜
矩者平天下之要道而忠信者又絜矩之本也
又由是而知絜矩者恕之事然必本之於忠而

If one acts contrary to these principles, one will be disgraced throughout the world, lose the multitude, lose the state, and lose Heaven’s Mandate. One will contend with the people for gain and practice expropriation: the people will scatter, and wealth will depart by wrongful means. Extend this further: there is the favoritism and jealousy [?] described in the Oath of Qin; seeing worthy men but being unable to promote them, or promoting them but being unable to give them precedence; seeing the unworthy but being unable to dismiss them, or dismissing them but being unable to keep them at a distance. Carried to the extreme, this runs counter to human nature, and calamity will surely reach oneself; pursuing wealth and resources brings calamity and injury together.

Alas! It is the same measuring square, yet the consequences of being able or unable to apply it differ so greatly. This is indeed cause for fear! But could the reason for such gain and loss lie anywhere else? It lies only in our own hearts. Thus it is said: “The gentleman has a great way: he must gain it through loyalty and trustworthiness, and lose it through arrogance and extravagance.” This means that gain and loss depend upon the heart. If one makes loyalty and trustworthiness the basis of one’s heart, one is impartial. With impartiality, oneself and others are joined in mutual understanding, and those above and below communicate without obstruction. Conversely, arrogance and extravagance lead to selfishness. With selfishness, oneself and others encroach upon one another, and each side causes the other distress. At this point, the decisive issue of whether Heaven’s principle survives or perishes is settled. Once that is settled, it is determined whether Heaven’s Mandate and the people’s allegiance remain or depart, are gained or lost.

text:

分願不相侵越不相陵逼上下四旁均齊方正

之謂聖人之事也故曰天地無心而成化聖人
有心而無爲君子者能常存此心而不失則公
公則久久則安安則天天則神而至公至神之

化不異於聖人而與天合一矣故曰此平天下
之要道也

translation_en:
…only then can it be attained. Thus wholehearted sincerity and sympathetic consideration are not two separate things. Through this, each person attains what befits his station and fulfills his aspirations, without encroaching upon or oppressing the other. Above and below and on all four sides, all is evenly aligned and properly ordered, and the world is at peace. The sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity all followed this Way to bring about the flourishing of harmony and supreme concord. Yet that which served them as a measuring square was integrally present within: quiescent and unmoving, it responded to stimulation and thereby penetrated all things, answering every circumstance appropriately in all its particulars, without needing to extend it through deliberate comparison. It was like the transforming work of Heaven and Earth, which simply endows the myriad things without labor. This is what is meant by the work of the sage. Thus it is said: “Heaven and Earth accomplish transformation without conscious intention; the sage has conscious intention yet acts without contrivance.” If the gentleman can always preserve this mind without losing it, he becomes impartial. Impartiality leads to constancy; constancy to ease; ease to accord with Heaven; and accord with Heaven to spiritual efficacy. His utterly impartial and spiritually efficacious transforming influence then becomes indistinguishable from that of the sage, and he unites with Heaven as one. Thus it is said: “This is the essential Way to bring peace to the world.”

永樂二十一年某月某日，臣某等恭覩壽星見，謹表賀者。伏以道隆宸極，聖王綏永命之圖；瑞應星躔，昭代荷祈天之祜。基鴻休于億載，獻上壽于千齡。慶洽臣民，懽騰寰宇。臣某等忻忭忻忭，頓首頓首，上言：竊惟上及太清，下及太寧，景福懋隆于紫禁；天不愛道，地不愛寶，休祥協應于清時。粤攷壽星，允為聖瑞。圖存元命，薦君壽以無疆；志載西京，表時安而永泰。應在春秋之候，出自丙丁之隅。彩耀丹霄，迥麗圓車之運；精凝玄昊，獨依合璧之光。有道
translation_en:
Examiner Li, Left Admonisher, comments: “Ornamentation, classical refinement, and elegance are all fully present.”
On a certain day of a certain month in the twenty-first year of Yongle, we, your servants, having reverently witnessed the appearance of the Star of Longevity, respectfully submit this memorial of congratulation.
We humbly consider that, as the Way flourishes at the imperial pole, the sage king secures the design of an enduring mandate; as auspicious signs appear along the stars’ courses, this illustrious age receives the blessings sought from Heaven. Vast beneficence is founded for a hundred million years; we offer wishes for supreme longevity through a thousand years. Rejoicing embraces officials and people, and jubilation fills the realm. We, your servants, exult and rejoice, exult and rejoice; we knock our heads upon the ground, knock our heads upon the ground, and submit these words:
We humbly reflect that, reaching upward to the highest heavens and downward to the realm of supreme peace, great blessings flourish abundantly within the Purple Forbidden Precinct. Heaven does not withhold its Way, nor does earth withhold its treasures: auspicious signs respond in harmony to this age of good government. Examining the Star of Longevity, we find it truly an auspicious sign of sage rule. The charts of Yuanming [?] preserve it, commending boundless longevity to the ruler; the treatises of the Western Capital record it, indicating peace in the age and lasting tranquillity. It manifests in the seasons of spring and autumn, emerging from the quarter of bing and ding, in the south. Its colors shine in the crimson skies, splendid far above amid the revolving celestial chariot [?]; its essence gathers in the dark heavens, attending uniquely upon the radiance of the joined jade discs of sun and moon. When the Way prevails …

鳳鑾肇回于伊水祗承
上帝集大命于
聖躬昭纘丕基覲耿光于

punctuated:
方明，非時不見。彼誇聞東井，漢基五載以開天；暨傳美西奎，宋治百年而麗日。歷稽往事，卓有明徵。豈若映彼三台，莫辨皤如之象；嚮茲五福，用垂耄矣之名。振古稀聞，迄今始有。
茲蓋伏遇皇帝陛下，睿德日新，神謨天啟。仙源毓秀，龍標早協于瑤山；璿極降芳，鳳響是回于伊水。祗承上帝，集大命于聖躬；昭纘丕基，覲耿光于皇考。闢堯封而跨南北，奠周鼎以限華夷。萬里風清，塵斷玉關之路；百蠻霧淨，威踰銅柱之鄉。道徹三光。
translation_en:
…only then does it shine forth; outside its proper season it does not appear. They boasted of its being reported in the Eastern Well constellation, when the Han foundation, five years established, opened a new heaven; and they transmitted praise of its appearance in the Western Legs constellation, when a century of Song rule shone like the sun. Examining past events in succession, we find outstanding and clear attestations. Yet how could these compare with its shining upon the Three Platforms, though its white-haired form cannot be discerned, and its turning toward these Five Blessings to bestow the name of venerable longevity? Rarely heard of since antiquity, such a thing has appeared only now.
This, we humbly submit, is because we have encountered Your Majesty the Emperor, whose sagely virtue is renewed daily and whose divine counsels are revealed by Heaven. Your immortal lineage nurtured excellence: your dragon-like bearing accorded early with Yaoshan. The jeweled celestial pole sent down its splendor: the phoenix’s notes echoed over the Yi River. Reverently receiving the Lord on High, you gathered the great Mandate upon your sacred person; illustriously continuing the mighty foundation, you beheld the brilliant glory of your imperial father. You extended Yao’s domain to span north and south, and firmly established Zhou’s tripods to mark the bounds between the Chinese realm and the foreign peoples. Across ten thousand li the winds are clear, and dust has ceased along the road to the Jade Gate; among the hundred foreign peoples the mist has cleared, and your might reaches beyond the land of the bronze pillars. Your Way penetrates the Three Luminaries—the sun, moon, and stars.…

punctuated: 誠通四序。皇天眷德，畀壽域以弘開；上帝何言？露珠躔而作麗。祥耀燁于弧外，散色澄霞；顥氣肅于商中，垂芒助月。南山俯映，流光遥掩於白榆；北闕前瞻，絢采適騰於黃道。二十年之內，疊見此祥；五百載以來，欣逢茲盛。臣等叨際煕朝，躬瞻玄象。帝圖永固，載歌天保之章；聖業彌昌，敢效華封之祝。伏願聿脩至德，克配兩儀；茂享遐齡，允過五帝。玉樞旋轉，亘萬古以常新；金粟焜煌，麗千星而久照。臣等無任瞻天仰聖、踴躍屏營之至，謹奉表稱
translation_en:
…Your sincerity penetrates the four seasons. August Heaven cherishes Your virtue, granting that the realm of longevity may spread far and wide. What words does the Lord on High speak? He reveals the pearl-like star in its course, displaying its beauty. Its auspicious radiance blazes beyond the Bow constellation, diffusing colors through the clear sunset clouds; its luminous influence is solemn amid autumn, shedding rays to aid the moon. It shines down upon the Southern Mountain, its streaming light far outshining the white elms of heaven—the stars. Looking ahead from the northern palace towers, we see its brilliant colors now rising along the ecliptic. Within twenty years this auspicious sign has appeared repeatedly; across five hundred years, we rejoice to encounter such splendor. We, Your servants, have undeservedly been privileged to live in this flourishing reign and personally behold this celestial manifestation.

May the imperial dominion remain secure forever: we sing anew the ode “Heaven Protects You.” May Your sagely enterprise flourish ever more: we venture to emulate the blessings offered by the border warden of Hua. We humbly wish that You may continue cultivating consummate virtue, fully matching Heaven and Earth; and abundantly enjoy a long life, truly surpassing the Five Emperors. May the jade pivot revolve, ever renewed through countless ages; may the golden grain shine brilliantly, gleaming among a thousand stars and casting its light enduringly. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your sagely person, we, Your servants, cannot contain our utmost joy and reverent awe. We respectfully submit this memorial to express…

賀以聞。

第參塲，策五道。

第一問。

同考試官教諭陳批：我聖祖以仁創業，我皇上以仁中興，俱見于優免之詔。我朝億萬年之基，端在於斯。子獨能鋪張揚厲之無遺，眞可謂識時務、達國體者矣。末復歸重我皇上敬一之心，尤見知本之學。噫！若子者，豈非所謂天下士乎？擢冠多士，允協輿論。

同考試官進士藺批：我聖祖劉斯潔皇上仁心仁政，誠祈天永命之本。子能揚厲之無遺，必其涵濡聖化之深者，録之。
translation_en:
…to convey our congratulations to Your Majesty.

Third Session: Five Policy Questions.

First Question.

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: Our sagely founder established the dynasty through benevolence, and our reigning emperor has brought about its resurgence through benevolence. Both are manifest in the edict granting preferential exemptions. Here indeed lies the foundation of our dynasty’s endurance for countless ages. You alone have been able to expound and extol this fully, leaving nothing out. You may truly be called one who understands the affairs of the age and comprehends the principles of government. At the end, you again place the emphasis on our emperor’s resolve to revere the One, showing especially your learning that grasps the root. Ah! Is not someone like you what is called an outstanding scholar of the realm? Promoting you to first place among the candidates accords fully with general opinion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Our sagely founder [the text here reads 劉斯潔, possibly the name Liu Sijie; its connection is unclear], our emperor—their benevolent hearts and benevolent government [?] are truly the foundation for praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate. You have been able to extol this fully, leaving nothing out; surely you are one deeply steeped in the civilizing influence of the sage ruler. Accept this essay.

借君以爲心而邦本以固惟其安也則君
punctuated:
考試官左贊善吳批：我皇上好生之德，同符皇祖，遠邁百王。子能鋪張揚厲之，末復歸重於聖心之精一、聖政之純懿，可謂知所本矣。宜錄以傳。

考試官左中允李批：我聖祖、皇上仁德侔造化，詔令懸日月。子能次頌而對揚之，是誠沐浴膏澤而歌詠太平者乎！錄之。

聖人有與民爲一之心，而後有仁覆天下之政。夫至貴者君也，至賤者民也。以分言，則其勢誠相懸；然君者民之父母也，民者君之赤子也。以情言，則其事誠相屬。故《易》著乾下坤上之謂泰，損上益下之謂益；《書》稱：「衆非元后何戴？后非衆罔與守邦。」蓋言民雖極賤，而存上交之理則安矣；君雖極貴，而盡合下之義則仁矣。惟其仁也，則民借君以爲心，而邦本以固；惟其安也，則君
translation_en:
Examiner Wu, Left Admonisher, comments: Our Emperor’s virtue of cherishing life accords with that of his imperial ancestor and far surpasses that of the hundred kings. You have expounded and extolled it fully, concluding by placing primary emphasis on the refined singleness of the imperial mind and the unalloyed excellence of imperial government. You may indeed be said to understand their foundation. This should be recorded and transmitted.

Examiner Li, Left Assistant Mentor, comments: The benevolent virtue of our sagely founder and our Emperor matches the creative workings of Heaven and Earth; their edicts shine aloft like the sun and moon. You have set forth their praises in order and fittingly extolled them in your response. Are you not truly one who, bathed in their bountiful favor, sings of an age of great peace? Record this.

Only when the sage possesses a heart that is one with the people does he establish a government whose benevolence shelters all under Heaven. The ruler occupies the most exalted position, and the people the lowliest. In terms of rank, their positions are indeed far apart. Yet the ruler is the father and mother of the people, and the people are the ruler’s infant children. In terms of affection, their concerns are indeed bound together. Thus the Book of Changes explains that Qian below and Kun above constitute Peace, and that diminishing what is above to augment what is below constitutes Increase. The Book of Documents says: “Without the sovereign, whom would the multitude uphold? Without the multitude, the sovereign would have none with whom to preserve the state.” This means that although the people occupy the lowliest position, they will be at peace if the principle of intercourse with those above is maintained; although the ruler occupies the most exalted position, he will be benevolent if he fully discharges his duty to unite with those below. Through his benevolence, the people take the ruler as their heart, and the foundation of the state is thereby secured; through their being at peace, the ruler…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
得民以為用而天命常留是以聖人惟仁
之務而使我之心惻惻然日浹於民而不
可已惟安之圖而使民之心顒顒然日注
於我而不可解君無所為心心乎民而已
矣民亦無所為心心乎君而已矣故其起
福也求之心而天下之福以起其除禍也
求之心而天下之禍以除凡生於其心者
皆民之至願而發於其政者皆民之膏澤
夫是之謂與民一心而仁覆天下矣雖有
===
凶荒水旱之災尚何足為
聖世之慮也乎知此則執事所謂周禮散財
薄征振窮恤貧施惠之政漢文帝減租稅
之意我
太祖高皇帝暨我
皇上蠲免優恤之恩至深且渥者皆可得而仰
窺其萬一矣請敬陳之自庶土交正而作
貢三壤咸則而成賦國家之取民也久矣
夏后氏五十而貢殷人七十而助周人百

得民以為用，而天命常留。是以聖人惟仁之務，而使我之心惻惻然日浹於民而不可已；惟安之圖，而使民之心顒顒然日注於我而不可解。君無所為心，心乎民而已矣；民亦無所為心，心乎君而已矣。故其起福也，求之心，而天下之福以起；其除禍也，求之心，而天下之禍以除。凡生於其心者，皆民之至願；而發於其政者，皆民之膏澤。夫是之謂與民一心，而仁覆天下矣。雖有凶荒水旱之災，尚何足為聖世之慮也乎？知此，則執事所謂《周禮》散財、薄征、振窮、恤貧、施惠之政，漢文帝減租稅之意，我太祖高皇帝暨我皇上蠲免優恤之恩，至深且渥者，皆可得而仰窺其萬一矣。請敬陳之。
自庶土交正而作貢，三壤咸則而成賦，國家之取民也久矣。夏后氏五十而貢，殷人七十而助，周人百
translation_en:
…gains the people’s service, and Heaven’s Mandate endures. Thus the sage devotes himself solely to benevolence, allowing his compassionate heart to reach the people day after day without ceasing. He seeks solely their peace, so that their hearts turn toward him day after day in reverent expectation, with a bond that cannot be loosened. The ruler has no concern except for the people; the people likewise have no concern except for their ruler. Thus, when he brings forth blessings, he seeks their source in his heart, and blessings arise throughout the realm; when he eliminates calamities, he seeks the means in his heart, and calamities throughout the realm are removed. Everything conceived in his heart answers the people’s deepest wishes, and everything expressed in his government brings them nourishing benefits. This is what it means to be of one heart with the people and to extend benevolence over all under Heaven. Even should there be famine, flood, or drought, how could these give cause for anxiety in a sage’s age?
Once this is understood, one may reverently glimpse something of all those measures you have mentioned: the policies in the Rites of Zhou of distributing wealth, lightening levies, relieving the distressed, aiding the poor, and bestowing benefits; Emperor Wen of the Han’s intention in reducing land taxes; and the exceedingly profound and abundant grace of our Emperor Taizu Gao and our present Emperor in granting remissions and generous relief. Allow me respectfully to set this forth.
Ever since the various lands were duly classified and tribute established, and the three grades of soil were taken as standards for assessing taxes, the state has collected resources from the people. This practice is of long standing. title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
畝而徹三代聖王豈以不賦爲仁哉蓋惟
天惠民惟辟奉天則愛民者固人君之道
而民生有欲無主乃亂則事君者亦小民
之義仁主於施而取之以制不害其爲仁
義存於供而適或以災不失其爲義聖人
者虛其心以應天下之變隨其時以安天
下之民故其爲政也藏富於民不足則取
有餘則與固有取之而民悅則取之者矣
有與之而民悅則與之者矣觀之周官可
===
知也太宰以九賦斂財賄此取民之常耳
方其無事之時豐稔之歲爲之民者秉義
竭忠輸納于上乃分之宜也亦何過哉不
幸而有凶荒之災疾疫之厄由是而不已
焉不幾於病民乎故大司徒以保息六養
萬民而三曰振窮四曰恤貧焉以荒政十
有二養萬民而一曰散財二曰薄征焉又
有司救以天患民病而以王命施惠焉由
大司徒者而言之則歲之凶荒有賴由司

translation_en:
…mu under the che system of taxation. Did the sage kings of the Three Dynasties consider refraining from taxation to be benevolence? Heaven bestows kindness upon the people, and the sovereign serves Heaven; thus loving the people is certainly the way of a ruler. Yet people are born with desires, and without a ruler there is disorder; thus serving the ruler is also the duty of the common people. Benevolence chiefly consists in giving, but taking according to established regulations does not impair its benevolence. Duty lies in supplying what is owed, but if disaster happens to intervene, this does not mean that duty has been forsaken. The sage empties his mind to respond to changes throughout the realm and adapts to circumstances to bring peace to its people. Thus, in governing, he stores wealth among the people: when resources are insufficient, he takes; when there is a surplus, he gives. There are indeed occasions when taking pleases the people, and then he takes; there are occasions when giving pleases the people, and then he gives. This can be understood by examining the Offices of Zhou.

The Grand Steward collects wealth and goods through the nine levies. This is simply the regular means of taking from the people. In peaceful times and years of abundant harvests, the people uphold their duty, exhaust their loyalty, and deliver their payments to those above. This is proper to their station—what fault is there in it? But if, unfortunately, famine strikes or epidemic disease brings distress, would continuing such exactions without respite not come close to afflicting the people? Thus the Minister of Education sustains all the people through six measures for their protection and well-being, the third being relief for those in dire need and the fourth assistance to the poor. He also sustains all the people through twelve famine-relief measures, the first being the distribution of wealth and the second the reduction of levies. There is also the Relief Officer, who, when natural calamities occur and the people suffer, bestows aid by command of the king. Through the Minister of Education, there is support to rely upon in years of famine; through the Relief Officer…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
救者而言之則時之災祲無虞聖人恤民
之心莫有詳於周官者矣自周之衰魯公
履畝而稅穀逮秦之亂秦君舍地而稅人
皆道乖於中正而毒盈於暴橫尚何望其
有周官司徒司救之事哉至漢之文帝躬
脩玄默力行節儉雖承高惠之後而秦項
之彫弊未甦也雖當承平之日而侯王之
强大已甚也於是憫然念外人之有非惻
然哀窮民之無賴乃重本而抑末先人而
===
後已旣納晁錯之言賜民田租之半又思
勸農之道悉除民田之租其後遂除之而
不收至十餘年而不止不曰惟正之供不
爲過也而顧減之不曰軍國之需不可缺
也而顧蠲之聖人恤民之心莫有切於文
帝者矣執事所謂不惟不取而且與之者
豈不以周官漢文良有見於此哉洪惟我
聖祖以神聖之資當貞元之會應天順人變夷
用夏洗滌開闢所未有之腥膻恢復帝王

…As for the Relief Official (sijiu), there was no cause for anxiety over the calamities and baleful influences that arose from time to time. Nowhere is the sages’ concern for the people set forth more fully than in the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan). When Zhou declined, the lord of Lu assessed grain taxes by the acreage cultivated; when Qin brought disorder, its ruler abandoned assessment by land and taxed people instead. Both departed from the correct and balanced way, and their oppressive violence inflicted suffering to the utmost. How could one still hope to find among them the practices of the Minister of Education (situ) and the Relief Official described in the Offices of Zhou?

When Emperor Wen of Han came to rule, he personally cultivated profound quietude and earnestly practiced frugality. Although he succeeded Emperors Gao and Hui, the devastation wrought by Qin and Xiang Yu had not yet been repaired. Although his was a time of peace, the power of the marquises and kings had already become excessive. Thus, with compassion he considered the wrongs affecting people outside the court [?], and with sorrow pitied the poor who had nothing to depend upon. He therefore honored the fundamental occupation of agriculture and restrained secondary pursuits, putting others before himself. Having accepted Chao Cuo’s advice, he remitted half the people’s land tax. Then, considering how to encourage agriculture, he abolished their land tax entirely. Thereafter he continued to waive it without collecting it, maintaining this for more than ten years. He did not say that collecting the regular, legitimate dues was no excess; instead, he reduced them. He did not say that the requirements of the army and state could not go unmet; instead, he remitted the tax. No one embodied the sages’ concern for the people more earnestly than Emperor Wen. When you speak of ‘not merely refraining from taking, but also giving,’ is it not because the Offices of Zhou and Emperor Wen of Han truly understood this principle?

We reverently reflect that our Sagely Progenitor, endowed with divine sagacity, came at the turning point from an ending to a new beginning. Responding to Heaven and complying with the people, he transformed barbarian ways and adopted those of Chinese civilization. title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
所自有之土宇拯生民於塗炭躋斯世於
唐虞其德侔天地恩齊造化固有終身言
之而不能盡者矣若執事所舉蠲貸之事
乃自古帝王得民心之本而未有如
聖祖之優渥者也蓋
聖祖之心惟恐天下有一民之不被其澤一時
之不安其生夙興昧旦若有望而未至宏
規遠圖如有追而莫及一則曰中原之民
久困兵殘於是乎有山東北平等八郡稅

是乎有應天太平鎮江寧國稅糧之免焉

科徵轉運未免勞民於是乎有江西兩浙

punctuated: 所自有之土宇，拯生民於塗炭，躋斯世於唐虞，其德侔天地，恩齊造化，固有終身言之而不能盡者矣。若執事所舉蠲貸之事，乃自古帝王得民心之本，而未有如聖祖之優渥者也。蓋聖祖之心，惟恐天下有一民之不被其澤、一時之不安其生。夙興昧旦，若有望而未至；宏規遠圖，如有追而莫及。一則曰：「中原之民，久困兵殘。」於是乎有山東、北平等八郡稅糧之免焉。一則曰：「創業之初，軍國取辦。」於是乎有應天、太平、鎮江、寧國稅糧之免焉。一則曰：「肇興丕基，京師羽翼。」於是乎有應天等郡、廣德等州稅糧之再免焉。一則曰：「供給有先後，豐歉有不同。」於是乎有應天至無爲州等七郡、徽州至廬州等九郡、河南、山東、北平等諸處稅糧之免焉。一則曰：「科徵轉運，未免勞民。」於是乎有江西、兩浙秋糧之免焉。一則曰：「雖當蠲免，未報前勞。」
translation_en:
…the territories that rightfully belonged to the emperors and kings, rescued the people from utter misery, and raised this age to the level of the reigns of Yao and Shun. His virtue matched Heaven and Earth, and his beneficence equaled the transforming power of creation. Indeed, one could speak of these throughout a lifetime without exhausting them. As for the remissions and loans that you, sir, have cited, these have been the foundation upon which emperors and kings won the people’s hearts since antiquity; yet none were ever as generous as those of our Sagely Progenitor. For the Sagely Progenitor feared only that a single person under Heaven might fail to receive his bounty, or that for a single moment someone might lack security in their livelihood. He rose early, before daybreak, as though looking toward a goal he had yet to reach; he devised grand plans for the distant future, as though pursuing something he could never catch.

On one occasion he said: “The people of the Central Plain have long suffered the ravages of war.” Thus grain taxes were remitted for eight prefectures in Shandong, Beiping, and elsewhere. On another he said: “At the founding of the dynasty, the needs of the army and state were met from their resources.” Thus grain taxes were remitted for Yingtian, Taiping, Zhenjiang, and Ningguo. On another he said: “When our great foundation was first established, they served as the wings of the capital.” Thus grain taxes were again remitted for Yingtian and other prefectures, and Guangde and other subprefectures. On another he said: “Some supplied provisions earlier and others later; some have had plentiful harvests and others poor ones.” Thus grain taxes were remitted for the seven prefectures from Yingtian through Wuwei Subprefecture, the nine prefectures from Huizhou through Luzhou, and various places in Henan, Shandong, Beiping, and elsewhere. On another he said: “Tax levies and transport inevitably impose toil upon the people.” Thus the autumn grain tax was remitted for Jiangxi and the Two Zhe regions. On another he said: “Although remissions have been granted, their earlier toil has yet to be recompensed.” …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
於是乎有應天等五府秋糧之免焉一則
曰土木之工復興愈勞繁重於是乎有河
南等省揚州等府秋糧之免焉一則曰外
有轉運艱辛内有秦晋二府宫殿之役於
是乎有山西陜右二省稅糧之免焉一則
曰六州四縣之民久勞於前於是乎有姑
孰金陵京口等州縣秋糧之免焉一則曰
有司差役不均有傷和氣致令民艱於樹
藝於是乎有北平稅糧之免焉一則曰荷
===
上天眷佑君主華夷倉廩盈府庫充皆民
之所供今民力未甦於是乎有凡天下稅
糧悉蠲免焉以至民之孤獨殘疾不能自
生者又立為養濟院月給之米歲給之布
不論豐歉存恤為常此執事所謂具在
御製文集皆裁自
聖心者也雖周官之法漢文之政又安能若是
之懇切而詳盡也哉然周官行於三代之
盛世而漢文仰於高惠之垂成故凶荒之

之懇切而詳盡也哉然周官行於三代之
盛世而漢文仰於高惠之垂成故凶荒之
punctuated: 於是乎有應天等五府秋糧之免焉。一則曰：「土木之工復興，愈勞繁重。」於是乎有河南等省、揚州等府秋糧之免焉。一則曰：「外有轉運艱辛，内有秦晋二府宫殿之役。」於是乎有山西、陜右二省稅糧之免焉。一則曰：「六州四縣之民久勞於前。」於是乎有姑孰、金陵、京口等州縣秋糧之免焉。一則曰：「有司差役不均，有傷和氣，致令民艱於樹藝。」於是乎有北平稅糧之免焉。一則曰：「荷上天眷佑，君主華夷，倉廩盈，府庫充，皆民之所供。今民力未甦。」於是乎有凡天下稅糧悉蠲免焉。以至民之孤獨殘疾不能自生者，又立為養濟院，月給之米，歲給之布，不論豐歉，存恤為常。此執事所謂具在《御製文集》，皆裁自聖心者也。雖周官之法、漢文之政，又安能若是之懇切而詳盡也哉？然周官行於三代之盛世，而漢文仰於高惠之垂成，故凶荒之
translation_en:
…Thereupon the autumn grain tax was remitted for Yingtian and four other prefectures. Another pronouncement said: “Construction work has begun again, making the burden of labor still heavier.” Thereupon the autumn grain tax was remitted for Henan and other provinces, and Yangzhou and other prefectures. Another said: “Outside there are the hardships of transport; within there is the labor of building palaces for the two princely establishments of Qin and Jin.” Thereupon the grain tax was remitted for the two provinces of Shanxi and Shanyou. Another said: “The people of the six subprefectures and four counties have long borne the burden of earlier labors.” Thereupon the autumn grain tax was remitted for Gushu, Jinling, Jingkou, and other subprefectures and counties. Another said: “The responsible officials have apportioned labor service unevenly, impairing harmonious influences and making it difficult for the people to cultivate their crops.” Thereupon the grain tax was remitted for Beiping. Another said: “Favored by Heaven’s watchful protection, I rule over Chinese and non-Chinese alike. The granaries are full and the treasuries well supplied, all through what the people provide. Yet the people’s strength has not recovered.” Thereupon the grain tax was entirely remitted throughout the realm.

Furthermore, almshouses were established for those among the people who were orphaned, bereft of family, or disabled and unable to support themselves. They were given grain each month and cloth each year. Whether harvests were abundant or poor, their care and relief remained a regular provision. These are what you, sir, have described as fully recorded in the Collected Imperial Writings, all decided by the sagely imperial mind itself. How could even the institutions of the Offices of Zhou or the government of Emperor Wen of Han have been so solicitous and thorough? Yet the institutions of the Offices of Zhou operated in the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties, while Emperor Wen of Han relied upon the nearly completed achievements bequeathed by Emperors Gao and Hui. Thus, as for the calamities of famine…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天災或不能無而秦項之餘虐似未盡去
其視我
聖祖革命之初生民之塗炭方拯犬羊之遺風
未殄此何時也而征討吳漢削平隴蜀驅
逐胡元招取歐廣兵興之費莫甚於此其
他若建宮殿立城池分藩府設官署置壇
壝脩學校事事而須爲之備一一而創爲
之始誠有如執事所謂視承平之日奚翅
千萬者尚有餘貲以資國用而免租之
詔無歲無之此豈有奇異之術哉蓋以
聖祖敦朴以爲先而革勝國之侈靡節儉以爲
用而舉天下之要務觀其毀陳氏之鏤金
牀碎元氏之水晶漏則凡天下之事有一
毫之無益有一時之可緩者皆不得以傷
其財而費其用故省民之政不勞而舉而
裕國之道不求而得其意指之所在恤民
之外無餘事蠲貸之
詔無虛時矣吾知民者天之所生者也食者

===

用而舉天下之要務觀其毀陳氏之鏤金

毫之無益有一時之可緩者皆不得以傷
其財而費其用故省民之政不勞而舉而
裕國之道不求而得其意指之所在恤民
之外無餘事蠲貸之
詔無虛時矣吾知民者天之所生者也食者
punctuated: 天災或不能無，而秦項之餘虐似未盡去。其視我聖祖革命之初，生民之塗炭方拯，犬羊之遺風未殄，此何時也？而征討吳漢，削平隴蜀，驅逐胡元，招取歐廣，兵興之費莫甚於此。其他若建宮殿，立城池，分藩府，設官署，置壇壝，脩學校，事事而須爲之備，一一而創爲之始，誠有如執事所謂視承平之日奚翅千萬者。尚有餘貲以資國用，而免租之詔無歲無之，此豈有奇異之術哉？蓋以聖祖敦朴以爲先，而革勝國之侈靡；節儉以爲用，而舉天下之要務。觀其毀陳氏之鏤金牀，碎元氏之水晶漏，則凡天下之事，有一毫之無益、有一時之可緩者，皆不得以傷其財而費其用。故省民之政不勞而舉，而裕國之道不求而得。其意指之所在，恤民之外無餘事，蠲貸之詔無虛時矣。吾知民者，天之所生者也；食者，
translation_en:
…natural disasters might not have been entirely absent, and the lingering cruelties of Qin and Xiang Yu seem not yet to have been wholly eradicated. Compare this with the beginning of our Sagely Ancestor’s change of dynasty: the people were only just being rescued from misery, and the lingering ways of dogs and sheep had not yet been extinguished. What a time this was! Yet he campaigned against Wu and Han, subdued Long and Shu, drove out the alien Yuan, and secured the submission of Ou and Guang [?]. Never were the expenses of raising armies greater than these. Other undertakings included building palaces, erecting city walls and moats, establishing princely establishments in their separate domains, setting up government offices, constructing sacrificial altars and their enclosures, and repairing schools. Everything required provision; each undertaking had to be initiated anew. It was indeed as you have said: compared with days of settled peace, the demands were greater by far more than a thousand or ten thousand times. Yet there were still surplus resources to support state expenditure, and not a year passed without an edict remitting the land tax. Could there have been some extraordinary technique behind this?

It was because the Sagely Ancestor gave priority to plainness and simplicity, abolishing the extravagance of the preceding dynasty, and made frugality his practice while carrying out the essential business of the realm. Consider his destruction of the Chen ruler’s bed adorned with carved gold and his smashing of the Yuan rulers’ crystal clepsydra. In all the affairs of the realm, anything that was even slightly unbeneficial, or that could be deferred for a time, was never permitted to deplete his resources or consume his funds. Thus policies that lightened the people’s burdens were implemented without difficulty, and the means of enriching the state were attained without being sought. His intention admitted no concern beyond caring for the people, and edicts granting remissions and relief followed without interruption. I know that the people are those whom Heaven brings into being; as for food …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
民之所天者也天人之勢雖若遼邈而休
咎之徵如符節之合君民之分雖若隔絕
而交感之理如影響之隨民心所欲天必
從之民心所感天必同之未有民懷而天
不親者也未有天親民懷而不享無疆之
休者也則其
皇圖之鞏固胤祚之蕃衍蓋將與天地相為終
始又何疑哉而姬曆之八百炎祚之四百
又不足言矣丘氏所謂結人心凝天命而
===
培千萬年不拔之基端在於此者要之自
其理而觀之而已矣管子所謂知與之為
取者亦惟自其理而論之而已矣惟我
皇上嗣登大寶首頒
明詔蠲積歲之逋減田租之半天下之人巳
皆知
皇上之心即
聖祖之心矣既而寬恤之
詔或行於災異或行於

休者也則其

始又何疑哉而姬曆之八百炎祚之四百
又不足言矣丘氏所謂結人心凝天命而

punctuated:
民之所天者也。天人之勢雖若遼邈，而休咎之徵如符節之合；君民之分雖若隔絕，而交感之理如影響之隨。民心所欲，天必從之；民心所感，天必同之。未有民懷而天不親者也，未有天親民懷而不享無疆之休者也。則其皇圖之鞏固、胤祚之蕃衍，蓋將與天地相為終始，又何疑哉？而姬曆之八百、炎祚之四百，又不足言矣。丘氏所謂結人心、凝天命，而培千萬年不拔之基，端在於此者，要之，自其理而觀之而已矣。管子所謂知與之為取者，亦惟自其理而論之而已矣。
惟我皇上嗣登大寶，首頒明詔，蠲積歲之逋，減田租之半。天下之人巳皆知皇上之心即聖祖之心矣。既而寬恤之詔，或行於災異，或行於
translation_en:
…is what the people regard as Heaven. Though Heaven and humanity may seem far removed from one another, the signs of good and ill fortune fit together like the matching halves of a tally. Though ruler and people may seem separated by their stations, their mutual responsiveness operates like a following shadow or answering echo. What the people desire, Heaven will surely follow; what moves the people’s hearts will surely move Heaven likewise. Never have the people cherished a ruler without Heaven favoring him; never has a ruler favored by Heaven and cherished by the people failed to enjoy boundless blessings. The solidity of his imperial dominion and the flourishing of his descendants and dynastic fortune will surely endure alongside Heaven and Earth. What doubt can there be? Even the eight hundred years of the Ji house of Zhou and the four hundred years of the Han’s fiery mandate would scarcely merit mention. Master Qiu’s statement that winning the people’s hearts, securing Heaven’s mandate, and establishing a foundation unshakable for countless ages depend precisely upon this is, ultimately, simply an observation grounded in this principle. The Guanzi’s statement about understanding that giving is a means of taking likewise merely discusses the matter in light of this principle.
When our Emperor succeeded to the imperial throne, he first issued an illustrious edict remitting arrears accumulated over many years and reducing the land tax by half. All the people under Heaven already knew that His Majesty’s heart was one with that of the sagely founder. Thereafter, edicts granting relief were issued sometimes on the occasion of disasters and anomalies, sometimes on the occasion of …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
徽號或行於禮成或行於
建儲誠有如執事所謂
德音屢下叮嚀惻怛凡所以加惠元元爲
國家深長之計者無所不至優恤蠲貸視
聖祖無間焉者然
皇上之心又不但已也於
京師則有錢藥之施至於累月焉是未災而
存恤者也銀米之給遍於市廛焉是遇災
而加恤者也然
===
皇上之心又不但已也近而
畿甸遠而諸省一聞言官之論列亟爲
俞允每行有司之賑發務期實惠今天地之
間跂行喙息含生有識被潤澤而鼓舞感
恩德而歌頌者二十五年于茲矣雖堯仁如
天舜德好生禹之拯溺湯之來蘇文之如
傷武之大賚何以加哉固宜上繼
聖祖而遠邁百王也然執事又謂其必有所本
者愚以爲二帝三王之治本於道二帝三

punctuated: 徽號，或行於禮成，或行於建儲，誠有如執事所謂「德音屢下，叮嚀惻怛」。凡所以加惠元元、爲國家深長之計者，無所不至。優恤蠲貸，視聖祖無間焉者。然皇上之心又不但已也。於京師則有錢藥之施，至於累月焉，是未災而存恤者也；銀米之給，遍於市廛焉，是遇災而加恤者也。然皇上之心又不但已也。近而畿甸，遠而諸省，一聞言官之論列，亟爲俞允；每行有司之賑發，務期實惠。今天地之間，跂行喙息、含生有識，被潤澤而鼓舞、感恩德而歌頌者，二十五年于茲矣。雖堯仁如天、舜德好生、禹之拯溺、湯之來蘇、文之如傷、武之大賚，何以加哉？固宜上繼聖祖而遠邁百王也。然執事又謂其必有所本者，愚以爲二帝三王之治本於道，二帝三
translation_en: …on the conferral of an honorific title, or upon the completion of ceremonies, or upon the designation of an heir apparent—truly, as you have said, “Benevolent pronouncements have repeatedly been issued, earnest and compassionate.” Nothing has been left undone that might benefit the common people and provide for the state’s enduring welfare. In generous relief, remission of dues, and aid, His Majesty is no different from the Sagely Founder. Yet His Majesty’s concern does not stop there. In the capital, money and medicines have been distributed for months on end: this is care and relief before disaster strikes. Silver and grain have been supplied throughout the marketplaces: this is additional relief when disaster occurs. Yet His Majesty’s concern does not stop there. In the nearby metropolitan domain and the distant provinces alike, as soon as he hears the representations of remonstrance officials, he promptly grants approval; whenever the responsible authorities distribute relief, he insists that it bring tangible benefit. For twenty-five years now, all beneath Heaven and Earth that move on their feet and breathe through their mouths, all that possess life and awareness, have received his bounty and rejoiced, felt gratitude for his gracious virtue and sung his praises. Even Yao’s benevolence, vast as Heaven; Shun’s life-loving virtue; Yu’s rescue of those drowning; Tang’s coming to restore life to the people; King Wen’s care for them as though they were injured; and King Wu’s great bestowal of gifts—how could these surpass it? He assuredly deserves to carry on the legacy of the Sagely Founder and far outstrip the hundred kings. Yet you also say that this must have a foundation. In my humble view, the government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings was rooted in the Way; the Two Emperors and Three…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
王之道本於心精一執中堯舜禹相傳之
心法也建中建極商湯周武相傳之心法
也我
皇上聖由於天縱而學本於日新
敬一之箴五箴之註頒示海內家傳人誦皆
得以仰窺
聖心之精一眞有以紹二帝三王之心法而
聖政之純懿自足以爲祈天永命之根本矣愚
生也畿甸之間沐浴膏澤而歌咏太平蓋
===
亦有年敢以此對雖然古人有言終身戴
天而不知天之高也終身履地而不知地
之厚也
聖德之高厚又豈愚之所能頌其萬一哉執事
幸進而教之

事故忠厚者自崇讓未有崇讓而不本於忠厚者

王之道本於心。精一執中，堯舜禹相傳之心法也；建中建極，商湯周武相傳之心法也。我皇上聖由於天縱，而學本於日新。敬一之箴、五箴之註，頒示海內，家傳人誦，皆得以仰窺聖心之精一，眞有以紹二帝三王之心法，而聖政之純懿，自足以爲祈天永命之根本矣。愚生也，畿甸之間沐浴膏澤，而歌咏太平，蓋亦有年，敢以此對。雖然，古人有言：「終身戴天，而不知天之高也；終身履地，而不知地之厚也。」聖德之高厚，又豈愚之所能頌其萬一哉？執事幸進而教之。

第二問
祝尚義

同考試官教授袁批：忠厚廉讓，自非兩事，故忠厚者自崇讓，未有崇讓而不本於忠厚者。
translation_en:
…Kings was rooted in the mind. Refinement and singleness of mind, and holding fast to the Mean: this was the teaching of the mind transmitted from Yao to Shun to Yu. Establishing the Mean and establishing the supreme standard: this was the teaching of the mind transmitted by Tang of Shang and Wu of Zhou. Our Emperor’s sageliness is Heaven-endowed, while his learning rests on daily renewal. His Admonition on Reverent Unity and his annotations on the Five Admonitions have been promulgated throughout the realm, passed down in every household and recited by all. Everyone can thereby glimpse, with reverence, the refinement and singleness of his sagely mind. He truly carries forward the teaching of the mind of the Two Emperors and Three Kings; the purity and excellence of his sagely government are themselves sufficient foundations for praying to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. I, an unworthy scholar, have for years basked in his beneficence in the capital region and sung the praises of peace. I venture to offer this reply. Nevertheless, the ancients said: “All their lives people bear Heaven above them, yet do not know its height; all their lives they tread the earth, yet do not know its depth.” How could someone as unworthy as I praise even one ten-thousandth of the height and depth of His Majesty’s sagely virtue? May you, honored examiners, favor me with further instruction.

Second Question
Zhu Shangyi

Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Professor: Loyalty and generosity, and integrity and deference, are certainly not two separate matters. Thus, those who are loyal and generous naturally esteem deference; no one esteems deference without being rooted in loyalty and generosity.

今日崇厚崇讓之故尤為有見佳士佳士
同考試官推官王批崇厚崇讓二論方今

…You are able to articulate this, and moreover bring out the reasons for promoting generosity and deference today: this is especially perceptive. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Prefectural Judge: The two discussions on promoting generosity and deference concern urgent tasks in moral influence and transformation today. You expound them earnestly and thoroughly; in particular, you trace the crucial mechanism to the maintenance of governing discipline. Truly, you understand these matters! How admirable! How admirable!

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Only when governing discipline sustains things above can customs guide people below. This is precisely where the crucial mechanism lies. Your ability to articulate this gives evidence of your learning in statecraft.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Left Mentor: Surely there is something to be said about the present spirit of loyalty, generosity, integrity, and deference throughout the realm? Taking up the two discussions, you repeatedly set out your points, fully and carefully covering their subtleties. Ah! You yourself may truly be called generous and deferential. Reading this gives one much cause for deep reflection.

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Rectifier: To turn away from meanness and return to generosity, to prize deference and refrain from contention—this is the practice of the Great Way. The two discussions were written with an earnest intention to remedy the ills of the age. Your exposition is detailed and clear, and at the end you further locate the means of transformation in those above. Are you not someone who thoroughly understands the essentials of government!

There is a crucial means of directing the inclinations of all under Heaven; everything depends on how it is wielded. What an age esteems and what the multitude pursues are like water flowing downward. Without something to embank and restrain them, where would they finally stop? As for where this crucial means resides, there is indeed something brought to bear upon …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
朝廷行於天下貫乎人心關乎氣運而非有
品式條目之可指形迹象類之可求聲音
笑貌之可爲者是豈可以不謹哉司馬光
曰上行下效謂之風薰蒸漸漬謂之化淪
胥委靡謂之流衆心安定謂之俗及乎風
化已失流俗已成則雖辨智弗能諭也强
毅不能制也重賞不能勸也嚴刑不能正
也自非聖人得位而臨之莫之能變也朱
子曰四海之廣兆民之衆人各有意欲行
===
其私善爲治者乃能總攝而整齊之使之
各循其理者則以先有紀綱以持之於上
而後有風俗以驅之於下然紀綱之所以
振則以宰執秉持而不敢失臺諫補察而
無所私人主又以大公至正之心恭已於
上而照臨之則不待黜陟刑賞而禮義之
風廉耻之俗自不變矣噫此皆機之說也
而所以操之者本始具在其要固無踰於
此矣執事以忠厚廉讓望天下乃援朱穆

punctuated: 朝廷，行於天下，貫乎人心，關乎氣運，而非有品式條目之可指、形迹象類之可求、聲音笑貌之可爲者，是豈可以不謹哉？司馬光曰：「上行下效謂之風，薰蒸漸漬謂之化，淪胥委靡謂之流，衆心安定謂之俗。及乎風化已失，流俗已成，則雖辨智弗能諭也，强毅不能制也，重賞不能勸也，嚴刑不能正也。自非聖人得位而臨之，莫之能變也。」朱子曰：「四海之廣，兆民之衆，人各有意，欲行其私。善爲治者，乃能總攝而整齊之，使之各循其理者，則以先有紀綱以持之於上，而後有風俗以驅之於下。然紀綱之所以振，則以宰執秉持而不敢失，臺諫補察而無所私，人主又以大公至正之心恭已於上而照臨之，則不待黜陟刑賞，而禮義之風、廉耻之俗自不變矣。」噫！此皆機之說也，而所以操之者，本始具在，其要固無踰於此矣。執事以忠厚廉讓望天下，乃援朱穆
translation_en: …operates at court, takes effect throughout the realm, permeates people’s hearts, and bears upon the course of the age. Yet it offers no prescribed forms or detailed rules that one can point to, no outward traces or comparable manifestations that one can seek, and nothing that can be achieved through tone of voice or smiling demeanor. How could one fail to exercise care over it? Sima Guang said: “When those above act and those below imitate them, this is called moral influence. When that influence gradually permeates and imbues people, this is called transformation. When people sink together into slackness, this is called a prevailing trend. When the hearts of the multitude settle into an established pattern, this is called custom. Once moral influence and transformation have failed, and prevailing customs have become established, even eloquence and wisdom cannot persuade people, strength and resolution cannot restrain them, lavish rewards cannot encourage them, and severe punishments cannot correct them. Unless a sage gains the throne and presides over them, no one can change them.” Master Zhu said: “Across the vast expanse within the Four Seas, among the multitude of the people, each person has intentions of his own and wishes to pursue his private interests. Those skilled in governing can bring them all under direction and into order, causing each to follow the proper principles. They accomplish this by first establishing the governing framework to uphold them from above, and then customs to guide them from below. This framework is sustained because the chief councillors uphold it without daring to let it lapse, while the censors and remonstrance officials remedy deficiencies and scrutinize affairs without partiality. The ruler, moreover, with a heart of utmost impartiality and rectitude, conducts himself reverently above and watches over all. Then, without waiting for demotions and promotions, punishments and rewards, the influence of ritual propriety and righteousness, and the customs of integrity and a sense of shame, will of themselves remain unchanged.” Ah! These are all explanations of the pivotal means of influence. The foundations for exercising it are fully set forth here; its essentials surely extend no further than this. You, honored examiners, expect loyalty, generosity, integrity, and deference from the realm, and thus have cited Zhu Mu…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
劉寔二子之論下詢承學愚嘗讀史至此
誠亦有所槩於中者雖未敢妄有所論然
亦嘗聞之矣天下將治則人必尚行也天
下將亂則人必尚言也尚行則篤實之風
行焉尚言則詭詐之風行焉天下將治則
人必尚義也天下將亂則人必尚利也尚
義則謙讓之風行焉尚利則攘奪之風行
焉而執事所謂世道之升降風俗之美惡
天下國家之治亂恒必由之者是已顧可
===
以為迂緩也哉唐虞三代之時無容論矣
請就明問而敬陳之昔者朱穆當東漢之
末感時澆薄慕尚敦篤於是有崇厚論之
著今觀其辭大抵反覆於古今時俗之厚
薄故首之以仲尼之歎中引老氏之經馬
援戒其兄子之言與夫邴張之行韓翟之
操末復論厚薄不同之極致其用意亦厚
矣而其言之近理者如曰天不崇大則覆
幬不廣地不深厚則載物不博人不敦龐

劉寔二子之論，下詢承學。愚嘗讀史至此，誠亦有所槩於中者。雖未敢妄有所論，然亦嘗聞之矣：天下將治，則人必尚行也；天下將亂，則人必尚言也。尚行則篤實之風行焉，尚言則詭詐之風行焉。天下將治，則人必尚義也；天下將亂，則人必尚利也。尚義則謙讓之風行焉，尚利則攘奪之風行焉。而執事所謂世道之升降、風俗之美惡、天下國家之治亂，恒必由之者，是已。顧可以為迂緩也哉？
唐虞三代之時，無容論矣。請就明問而敬陳之。昔者朱穆當東漢之末，感時澆薄，慕尚敦篤，於是有《崇厚論》之著。今觀其辭，大抵反覆於古今時俗之厚薄，故首之以仲尼之歎，中引老氏之經、馬援戒其兄子之言，與夫邴張之行、韓翟之操，末復論厚薄不同之極致。其用意亦厚矣。而其言之近理者，如曰：「天不崇大，則覆幬不廣；地不深厚，則載物不博；人不敦龐
translation_en:
…and Liu Shi, citing the discourses of these two men to consult us students. Whenever I have read this passage in the histories, I too have felt deeply stirred within. Though I have not ventured to offer rash judgments, I have heard this: when the realm is approaching good order, people invariably esteem deeds; when it is approaching disorder, they invariably esteem words. Esteeming deeds spreads a spirit of sincerity and substance; esteeming words spreads a spirit of deceit. When the realm is approaching good order, people invariably esteem righteousness; when it is approaching disorder, they invariably esteem profit. Esteeming righteousness spreads a spirit of humility and deference; esteeming profit spreads a spirit of seizure and plunder. These are precisely the things upon which, as you say, the rise and decline of the moral order, the goodness and badness of customs, and the order and disorder of the realm and state invariably depend. Can these matters really be dismissed as impractical and slow to take effect?
There is no need to discuss the age of Tang and Yu or the Three Dynasties. Allow me respectfully to address your illuminating question. In the closing years of the Eastern Han, Zhu Mu was moved by the shallowness of his times and admired sincerity and steadfastness; thus he wrote the Discourse on Esteeming Generosity (Chonghou lun). Examining its language now, we find that it repeatedly considers the generosity and meanness of customs, ancient and modern. It therefore begins with a lament of Zhongni (Confucius), then cites the classic of Laozi, Ma Yuan’s admonition to his elder brother’s sons, the conduct of Bing and Zhang, and the integrity of Han and Zhai. Finally, it returns to the divergent ultimate consequences of generosity and meanness. Its intent, too, is generous indeed. Among its statements that accord with principle is this: “If Heaven were not lofty and great, its sheltering canopy would not extend far; if Earth were not deep and substantial, it would not bear things so widely; if people were not sincere and generous…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
則道數不遠者是已劉寔當晉室之初以
世多進趨廉遜道闕於是有崇讓論之作
今觀其辭大抵懇切於推讓爭競之本末
故首之以堯舜之揖遜與孔子禮讓爲國
之言中言漢魏以來官人之失讓道不興
之弊至引春秋范宣子之讓且深屬望於
當時焉其用心亦勤矣而其言之尤切者
如曰推讓之道興則賢能之人日見推舉
爭競之心生則賢能之人日見謗毀者是
===
已此二子之論之大略也蓋皆爲矯時之
作故其辭意各有所主初若不相通者然

…then one’s moral attainments will not extend far”: this is an example. At the beginning of the Jin dynasty, Liu Shi, finding that many people sought advancement and that integrity and modest deference were lacking, composed his Discourse on Esteeming Deference (Chongrang lun). Reading it now, we find that it chiefly addresses, with earnest concern, the roots and consequences of yielding precedence and competing for advantage. It therefore opens with Yao and Shun’s courteous yielding of the throne and Confucius’s words on governing a state through ritual propriety and deference. It then discusses failures in appointing officials since the Han and Wei dynasties and the harm caused by the failure of deference to flourish. It goes so far as to cite Fan Xuanzi’s deference in the Spring and Autumn period, placing profound hopes in the people of its own time. His concern was indeed painstaking. Among his especially pertinent statements is this: “When the practice of yielding precedence flourishes, worthy and capable men are increasingly recommended for office; when the desire to compete arises, worthy and capable men are increasingly slandered.”
Such is the broad outline of these two men’s discourses. Both were written to correct the failings of their times, so each has its own focus in wording and intent, and at first they seem unrelated. Yet if we consider the two together, their underlying principles have never differed, and in practice they continually depend upon one another. Why is this? Generosity of character is the foundation of deference, and deference is its realization. Looking at the world, have we ever seen frivolous and shallow people who do not compete for advantage? Those who compete are generally frivolous and shallow. Conversely, have we ever seen people who yield precedence yet lack loyalty and generosity of character? Can it be that our own times contain nothing resembling what these words describe? These are all matters that I, in my ignorance, dare not claim to know.
What I do know is that the prevailing habits of frivolity and rivalry have their origins. Can there be any other way to reverse them and restore loyalty, generosity, integrity, and deference? 昭彞倫之懿而萬世之典常攸係焉者也
史也者紀言動之迹明治亂之端嚴邪正
之辨而萬世之是非攸寓焉者也道非文
不載而經之所尚不專以其文事非體不
立而史之所難不專以其體道在斯爲經
視其文則經而究其道則拂非經也事在
斯爲史觀其體則史而論其事則繆非史

===

文之似而已夫人而能之也奚俟於聖人
如使史不在事則其爲史者祗取其體之

不載而經之所尚不專以其文事非體不
立而史之所難不專以其體道在斯爲經
視其文則經而究其道則拂非經也事在
斯爲史觀其體則史而論其事則繆非史
也是故古之君子立言脩辭凡以明道屬
===
事而已矣所以明道屬事者皆惟其自得
而已矣苟有得乎吾心而言也則辭不索
而獲理不求而遇吐之則爲經書之則爲
史又何必蘄蘄然若影之守形擬其模擬
也哉如使經不以道則其爲經者祇取其
文之似而已夫人而能之也奚俟於聖人
如使史不在事則其爲史者祇取其體之
似而已夫人而能之也奚俟乎良史是□
不能免執事之疑而起議者之紛紛也□
punctuated: 如史。故經也者，發天下之蘊，談性命之妙，昭彞倫之懿，而萬世之典常攸係焉者也。史也者，紀言動之迹，明治亂之端，嚴邪正之辨，而萬世之是非攸寓焉者也。道非文不載，而經之所尚不專以其文；事非體不立，而史之所難不專以其體。道在斯爲經，視其文則經，而究其道則拂，非經也；事在斯爲史，觀其體則史，而論其事則繆，非史也。是故古之君子立言脩辭，凡以明道屬事而已矣。所以明道屬事者，皆惟其自得而已矣。苟有得乎吾心而言也，則辭不索而獲，理不求而遇，吐之則爲經，書之則爲史，又何必蘄蘄然，若影之守形，極其模擬也哉？如使經不以道，則其爲經者祗取其文之似而已，夫人而能之也，奚俟於聖人？如使史不在事，則其爲史者祗取其體之似而已，夫人而能之也，奚俟乎良史？是固不能免執事之疑，而起議者之紛紛也。□□
translation_en: …so well as histories. Thus, the classics disclose the hidden profundities of all under Heaven, discuss the subtleties of human nature and destiny, and illuminate the excellence of the enduring human relationships; upon them depend the constant norms of all ages. Histories record the traces of words and deeds, clarify the origins of order and disorder, and distinguish rigorously between the perverse and the upright; in them reside the judgments of right and wrong for all ages. The Way cannot be conveyed without writing, yet what is prized in the classics does not lie solely in their writing. Events cannot be set forth without an organizing form, yet the difficulty of writing history does not lie solely in its form. The presence of the Way makes a work a classic: if its writing appears to be that of a classic, but examination reveals that its principles run counter to the Way, it is no classic. The presence of actual events makes a work a history: if its form appears to be that of a history, but consideration reveals that its account of events is erroneous, it is no history. Therefore, when the gentlemen of antiquity set forth their words and refined their language, their sole purpose was to illuminate the Way and relate events. What enabled them to illuminate the Way and relate events was simply their own independent understanding. If I speak from an understanding attained in my own mind, then words come without searching, and principles are encountered without seeking. Spoken, they become classics; written down, they become histories. Why, then, strive so insistently to imitate to the utmost, like a shadow clinging to a form? If classics were not grounded in the Way, then making a classic would require only a resemblance in writing. Anyone could do this; why wait for a sage? If histories did not depend upon events, then making a history would require only a resemblance in form. Anyone could do this; why wait for an able historian? This indeed cannot escape your doubts, honored sir, and provokes a welter of debate among critics. [Two illegible characters] …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以爲百姓之羣居苦紛雜之莫顯君子之
處世疾名德之不章惟英才特達則炳耀
垂文騰其姓氏懸諸日月自古所務焉今
亦何怪其紛紜於作述之多而競能於經
史之籍也哉言經者道法勝而已矣言史
者事辭勝而已矣史足以證經之褒貶經
足以酌史之輕重如蘇氏所謂其義一其
體二體不相沿而用實相資以此而脩已
而治人而立言而屬事而信今而傳後方
===
將誦服之不暇矣而況敢置譏評於其間
哉夫何儒家者流知經之可尚而不知發
其蘊者聖無聖之德而任聖之事則其罪
也僣史家者流知史之可傳而不知擅其
美者才無史之才而任史之責則其失也
淺古之人不知已之非聖擬經而作者如
執事所謂揚雄之徒是也古之人不知已
之非才擬史而作者如執事所謂譙周之
輩是也今以其擬經者言之若揚雄者以

哉夫何儒家者流知經之可尚而不知發

也僭史家者流知史之可傳而不知擅其

淺古之人不知巳之非聖擬經而作者如

之非才擬史而作者如執事所謂譙周之
輩是也今以其擬經者言之若揚雄者以
punctuated:
以爲百姓之羣居，苦紛雜之莫顯；君子之處世，疾名德之不章。惟英才特達，則炳耀垂文，騰其姓氏，懸諸日月，自古所務焉。今亦何怪其紛紜於作述之多，而競能於經史之籍也哉？言經者，道法勝而已矣；言史者，事辭勝而已矣。史足以證經之褒貶，經足以酌史之輕重。如蘇氏所謂，其義一，其體二，體不相沿，而用實相資。以此而脩已，而治人，而立言，而屬事，而信今，而傳後，方將誦服之不暇矣，而況敢置譏評於其間哉！

夫何儒家者流，知經之可尚，而不知發其蘊者聖；無聖之德，而任聖之事，則其罪也僣。史家者流，知史之可傳，而不知擅其美者才；無史之才，而任史之責，則其失也淺。古之人不知已之非聖，擬經而作者，如執事所謂揚雄之徒是也。古之人不知已之非才，擬史而作者，如執事所謂譙周之輩是也。今以其擬經者言之，若揚雄者以
translation_en:
…hold that ordinary people living among the multitude suffer from remaining undistinguished amid its confusion, while gentlemen living in the world lament that their reputations and virtue remain unrecognized. Only those of exceptional talent and outstanding attainment shine brilliantly and leave writings to posterity, raising their names aloft to hang beside the sun and moon. This has been an aspiration since antiquity. Why, then, should we now marvel that they vie in producing so many writings and compete in ability in works of classics and history? In discussing the classics, what matters is excellence in the Way and its standards; in discussing history, excellence in events recorded and language. History can substantiate the praise and blame expressed in the classics; the classics can weigh the relative importance of historical matters. As Master Su said, their underlying meaning is one, but their forms are two: their forms do not follow one another, yet in use they indeed support each other. Using them to cultivate oneself, govern others, establish enduring teachings, arrange accounts of events, win credence in the present, and transmit knowledge to posterity, one would scarcely have time enough to recite and put them into practice. How, then, would one dare interpose criticism of them?

Why is it, then, that Confucian scholars know that the classics deserve esteem but do not know that it takes a sage to reveal their depths? To lack a sage’s virtue yet undertake a sage’s work is to commit the offense of presumption. Historians know that histories deserve transmission but do not know that it takes talent to achieve excellence in them. To lack a historian’s talent yet assume a historian’s responsibilities is to fall into shallowness. Among the ancients, those who failed to recognize that they were not sages and composed imitations of the classics were men such as Yang Xiong, whom you mention. Those who failed to recognize that they lacked the requisite talent and composed imitations of histories were men such as Qiao Zhou, whom you mention. Now, to speak of those who imitated the classics, a man such as Yang Xiong believed that…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
為經莫大於易則作太玄以準之易有彖
而玄則有首易之爻有辭而玄之贊有測
分為三卷焉以為傳莫大於論語則作法
言以擬之曰學行吾子脩身問道問神問
明寡見五百先知重黎淵騫君子孝至凡
十三卷焉昔人譏其如吳楚僭王不亦宜
乎若王通者則見夫子之述六經而遂有
王氏六經之作見夫子之有論語而遂有
文中子中說之名既續詩矣而又續書既
===
元經矣而又易讚既禮論矣而又樂論以
董常比顏子以公卿大夫比顏曾門第昔
人譏其為六經奴婢不亦宜乎以至京房
之卦氣司馬光之潛虛皆擬易而作者也
趙曄之吳越春秋陸賈之楚漢春秋皆擬
春秋而作者也束皙之補亡以擬詩而作
者也白居易之湯征以擬書而作者也雖
模擬之志甚勤而僭竊謬妄之罪莫逃曾
是而可以為五經再生耶以擬史者言之

元經矣而又易讚既禮論矣而又樂論以
董常比顏子以公卿大夫比顏曾門弟昔
人譏其爲六經奴婢不亦宜乎以至京房
之卦氣司馬光之潛虛皆擬易而作者也
趙曄之吳越春秋陸賈之楚漢春秋皆擬
春秋而作者也束晳之補亡以擬詩而作
者也白居易之湯征以擬書而作者也雖
模擬之志甚勤而僭竊謬妄之罪莫逃曾
是而可以爲五經再生耶以擬史者言之
punctuated: 為經莫大於《易》，則作《太玄》以準之。《易》有彖，而《玄》則有首；《易》之爻有辭，而《玄》之贊有測，分為三卷焉。以為傳莫大於《論語》，則作《法言》以擬之，曰學行、吾子、脩身、問道、問神、問明、寡見、五百、先知、重黎、淵騫、君子、孝至，凡十三卷焉。昔人譏其如吳楚僭王，不亦宜乎？若王通者，則見夫子之述六經，而遂有王氏六經之作；見夫子之有《論語》，而遂有《文中子中說》之名。既續詩矣，而又續書；既《元經》矣，而又《易讚》；既《禮論》矣，而又《樂論》。以董常比顏子，以公卿大夫比顏曾門第。昔人譏其為六經奴婢，不亦宜乎？以至京房之卦氣、司馬光之《潛虛》，皆擬《易》而作者也；趙曄之《吳越春秋》、陸賈之《楚漢春秋》，皆擬《春秋》而作者也；束皙之《補亡》，以擬《詩》而作者也；白居易之《湯征》，以擬《書》而作者也。雖模擬之志甚勤，而僭竊謬妄之罪莫逃，曾是而可以為五經再生耶？以擬史者言之，
translation_en:
…believed that no classic surpassed the Changes, and so composed the Supreme Mystery (Taixuan) to match it. The Changes has judgments on its hexagrams, while the Mystery has heads; the lines of the Changes have statements, while the appraisals of the Mystery have explanations. It is divided into three scrolls. Believing that no transmitted teaching surpassed the Analects, he composed Model Sayings (Fayan) in imitation of it. Its chapters are “Learning and Conduct,” “My Master,” “Cultivating the Self,” “Asking about the Way,” “Asking about the Spiritual,” “Asking about Understanding,” “Limited Vision,” “Five Hundred,” “Foreknowledge,” “Chong and Li,” “Yuan and Qian,” “The Gentleman,” and “The Height of Filial Piety”—thirteen scrolls in all. Earlier writers mocked him as resembling Wu and Chu in their usurpation of the royal title. Was this not fitting?

As for Wang Tong, he saw that the Master had transmitted the Six Classics and consequently produced the Six Classics of the Wang Family; he saw that the Master had the Analects and consequently brought forth a work entitled Master Wenzhong’s Discussions of the Mean (Wenzhongzi Zhongshuo). Having continued the Odes, he also continued the Documents; having written the Primal Classic (Yuanjing), he also wrote Praises of the Changes; having written a Discourse on Rites, he also wrote a Discourse on Music. He compared Dong Chang to Master Yan, and dukes, ministers, and grand masters to the households of Yan and Zeng [?]. Earlier writers mocked him as a slave of the Six Classics. Was this not fitting?

Further examples include Jing Fang’s theory of hexagram qi and Sima Guang’s Hidden Void (Qianxu), both composed in imitation of the Changes. Zhao Ye’s Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue and Lu Jia’s Spring and Autumn Annals of Chu and Han were both composed in imitation of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Shu Xi’s Supplementing the Lost Poems was composed in imitation of the Odes; Bai Juyi’s Tang’s Campaign was composed in imitation of the Documents. Though their zeal for imitation was most diligent, they cannot escape the guilt of presumptuous appropriation, error, and falsehood. Can such works possibly be regarded as the Five Classics reborn? As for those who imitated histories…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
昔者列國命官卿與大夫爲别至於國史
卿亦呼爲大夫而譙周古史效之則書李
斯以大夫列國相稱每書他邦以顯號至
於魯國直云我而已而干寶晉紀效之則
云天子爲我皇帝左傳邢遷如歸衛國忘
亡言上下安堵不失舊物也而干寶晉紀
云吳國旣滅江外忘亡豈江外被典午之
善政同歸命之滅亡乎春秋書元年春王
正月言年則魯君之年月則周王之月也
===
而孫盛魏晉二陽秋每書年首必曰某年
春帝正月豈年旣編帝紀而月又列帝名
乎公羊先引經語而繼以釋辭屢云何以
書至吳均齊春秋每書灾異而亦曰何以
書則乖叙事之理矣漢書首書人名而傳
内有呼字者文從簡省至令狐德棻周書
首云伊婁穆字奴干而續云太祖字之曰
奴干則犯重複之文矣雖模擬之法不爽
而貌同心異之誚不免曾是而可以爲三

善政同歸命之滅亡乎春秋書元年春王

而孫盛魏晉二陽秋每書年首必曰某年
春帝正月豈年旣編帝紀而月又列帝名
乎公羊先引經語而繼以釋辭屢云何以

書則乖叙事之理矣漢書首書人名而傳

首云伊婁穆字奴干而續云太祖字之曰
奴干則犯重複之文矣雖模擬之法不爽
而貌同心異之誚不免曾是而可以爲三
punctuated: 昔者列國命官，卿與大夫爲别。至於國史，卿亦呼爲大夫，而譙周《古史》效之，則書李斯以大夫。列國相稱，每書他邦以顯號，至於魯國，直云我而已。而干寶《晉紀》效之，則云天子爲我皇帝。《左傳》「邢遷如歸，衛國忘亡」，言上下安堵，不失舊物也。而干寶《晉紀》云「吳國旣滅，江外忘亡」，豈江外被典午之善政，同歸命之滅亡乎？《春秋》書「元年春王正月」，言年則魯君之年，月則周王之月也。而孫盛《魏》《晉》二《陽秋》，每書年首，必曰「某年春帝正月」，豈年旣編帝紀，而月又列帝名乎？《公羊》先引經語，而繼以釋辭，屢云「何以書」。至吳均《齊春秋》，每書灾異，而亦曰「何以書」，則乖叙事之理矣。《漢書》首書人名，而傳内有呼字者，文從簡省。至令狐德棻《周書》，首云「伊婁穆字奴干」，而續云「太祖字之曰奴干」，則犯重複之文矣。雖模擬之法不爽，而貌同心異之誚不免。曾是而可以爲三
translation_en:
In antiquity, when the various states appointed officials, ministers and grand masters were distinct ranks. In their state histories, however, ministers were also called grand masters. Qiao Zhou imitated this in his Ancient History, consequently describing Li Si as a grand master. When the states referred to one another, they always designated other states by their proper names; Lu, however, was simply called “our state.” Gan Bao imitated this in his Annals of Jin, consequently referring to the Son of Heaven as “our emperor.” The Zuo Commentary says, “Xing’s relocation was like returning home; Wei forgot its destruction.” This means that high and low alike lived securely, without losing what they had formerly possessed. Yet Gan Bao’s Annals of Jin says, “Once the state of Wu had been destroyed, the lands beyond the Yangzi forgot their destruction.” Could the lands beyond the Yangzi, enjoying the good government of the Sima house—here called Dianwu—be equated with the downfall of the Lord Who Returns to Allegiance, Sun Hao [?]?

The Spring and Autumn Annals records, “First year, spring, the king’s first month.” The year is the year of the ruler of Lu; the month is the month prescribed by the king of Zhou. Yet Sun Sheng’s two works, the Annals of Wei and the Annals of Jin, invariably begin each year with “Such-and-such year, spring, the emperor’s first month.” When the year is already recorded in the emperor’s annals, why attach the emperor’s designation to the month as well? The Gongyang Commentary first quotes the classic and then supplies explanatory remarks, repeatedly asking, “Why is this recorded?” But Wu Jun’s Spring and Autumn Annals of Qi likewise asks “Why is this recorded?” whenever it records a disaster or anomaly. This violates the principles of historical narration.

The History of Han gives a person’s personal name at the outset and sometimes uses his courtesy name within the biography, keeping the wording concise. But Linghu Defen’s History of Zhou first says, “Yilou Mu’s courtesy name was Nugan,” and then continues, “Taizu gave him the courtesy name Nugan.” This commits the fault of repetition. Although their methods of imitation may be exact, they cannot escape the criticism that their outward forms agree while their underlying intentions differ. Could such works possibly constitute a reappearance of the Three …

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
史重出耶聖經之立言也無意於爲文而
道以文顯夫是之謂天下之至文良史之
屬事也無意於撰體而義以體明夫是之
謂大體要之道之精者爲經而文不與焉
天下未嘗無經而文以載道者爲難義之
精者爲史而體不與焉天下未嘗無史而
體以達義者爲難若圖畫之寫眞鎔鑄之
象物以此而似彼執影以合形謂之似則
可也謂之是則未也若是而以爲得也蒼
===
梧人娶妻而美以讓其兄者可以爲讓道
也乎隣女見西子之顰而美以效其顰者
可以爲善學也乎昔人云仲尼祖述堯舜
憲章文武亦未必居九五之位處南面之
尊而後謂之連類也知此則揚雄之徒擬

translation_en: …could these be considered the Three Histories appearing anew? When the sages’ classics set forth their words, they have no deliberate intent to produce literary ornament, yet the Way is made manifest through their writing: this is what is called the finest writing under Heaven. When a good historian arranges events, he has no deliberate intent to devise a formal structure, yet their significance is clarified through that structure: this is what is called a grand organizing form. In sum, the essence of the Way makes a classic; literary ornament has no part in determining this. The world has never lacked classics, but writing that carries the Way is difficult to achieve. The essence of meaning makes a history; formal structure has no part in determining this. The world has never lacked histories, but a structure that conveys meaning is difficult to achieve. Painting a likeness or casting an object’s image makes one thing resemble another: it grasps the shadow to match the form. One may call it similar, but one cannot yet call it the thing itself. If such resemblance counts as success, can the man of Cangwu who married a beautiful wife and yielded her to his elder brother be said to embody the way of deference? Can the neighboring woman who saw beauty in Xizi’s frown and imitated it be said to have learned well? An earlier writer said, “Zhongni transmitted the traditions of Yao and Shun and took Wen and Wu as his models.” Surely he did not have to occupy the sovereign’s place—the ninth in the fifth position—or assume the dignity of facing south before he could be counted in their company. Once this is understood, those like Yang Xiong who imitate the classics have much to be ashamed of before the classics; those like Qiao Zhou who imitate histories have much to be ashamed of before the histories. Nevertheless, to fault imitations of the classics is not to say that they stand opposed to the Way as ice does to burning charcoal, but that, measured against the sages, they fall short. Thus Zhang Heng was deeply devoted to the Classic of the Supreme Mystery, and Huan Tan even thought it certain to be transmitted to posterity. This…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
蓋好而不見其惡焉者也程子許文中子
極有格言而朱子亦謂其頗近於正此蓋
惡而知其美焉者也豈以其擬者盡爲得
哉史學之難非謂其於義若經傳之精也
而視諸史則優矣故范寗謂左氏之失誣
穀梁之失短公羊之失俗蓋以通方之理
望之也蘇子由譏遷之淺陋疎畧鄭漁仲
譏固之浮華剽竊以瑜瑕不掩論之也豈
以其作者即爲失哉史不可擬而謂其不
===
必擬則可經不可擬而謂其不嫌於擬則
不可何也蓋史之述唯才者能之苟有才
也體自我出矣是故不必於擬經之作唯
聖者能之苟非聖也道自我晦矣是故不
易於擬劉知幾謂史才文淺而易模蓋有
見於體之似者而言也經文意深而難擬
蓋有見於道之背者而言也夫雄譙之輩
誠有如執事所謂高才博學名重一時自
謂命世而生者豈其昧於此以犯天下□
