謂命世而生者豈其昧於此以犯天下□
punctuated: 蓋好而不見其惡焉者也。程子許文中子極有格言，而朱子亦謂其頗近於正，此蓋惡而知其美焉者也。豈以其擬者盡爲得哉？史學之難，非謂其於義若經傳之精也，而視諸史則優矣。故范寗謂左氏之失誣，穀梁之失短，公羊之失俗，蓋以通方之理望之也。蘇子由譏遷之淺陋疎畧，鄭漁仲譏固之浮華剽竊，以瑜瑕不掩論之也。豈以其作者即爲失哉？史不可擬，而謂其不必擬則可；經不可擬，而謂其不嫌於擬則不可。何也？蓋史之述，唯才者能之。苟有才也，體自我出矣，是故不必於擬。經之作，唯聖者能之。苟非聖也，道自我晦矣，是故不易於擬。劉知幾謂史才文淺而易模，蓋有見於體之似者而言也；經文意深而難擬，蓋有見於道之背者而言也。夫雄、譙之輩，誠有如執事所謂高才博學，名重一時，自謂命世而生者，豈其昧於此，以犯天下□
translation_en:
…This is surely a case of liking something without seeing its faults. Master Cheng acknowledged that Wenzhongzi had some truly excellent maxims, and Master Zhu likewise said that his teachings came quite close to what was correct. This is surely a case of disliking something while recognizing its merits. Could they have regarded everything he produced in imitation as sound?

As for the difficulty of historical scholarship, this does not mean that its treatment of principles matches the refinement of the classics and their commentaries; yet, when compared with the histories, it is superior [?]. Thus Fan Ning said that the fault of the Zuo Commentary was misrepresentation, that of the Guliang Commentary, inadequacy, and that of the Gongyang Commentary, vulgarity. He was judging them against principles of comprehensive understanding. Su Ziyou criticized Sima Qian for shallowness and sketchiness, while Zheng Yuzhong criticized Ban Gu for floridity and plagiarism. They judged them without allowing either merits or faults to obscure the other. Could they have regarded the very act of composing these works as a fault?

One may say that histories cannot be imitated if one means that there is no need to imitate them. But classics cannot be imitated, and to say that there is no objection to imitating them is unacceptable. Why? Only those with talent can compose historical narratives. If one has talent, the form will emerge from oneself; hence there is no need for imitation. Only sages can compose classics. If one is not a sage, the Way will be obscured through one's own intervention; hence imitation is no easy matter. Liu Zhiji said that historical writing is shallow in its literary expression and easy to copy [?]; surely he spoke with an eye to similarities of form. His statement that the language of the classics is profound in meaning and difficult to imitate surely concerned departures from the Way.

Now, men such as Yang Xiong and Qiao Zhou were indeed, as you say, highly talented and widely learned, renowned in their day, and considered themselves born to answer the needs of their age. Could they have been ignorant of this, thereby incurring the world's [illegible character]…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
世之議哉然好龍之喻世每同於葉公而
楮葉之巧俗或取於宋人則其經與史固
未必經史若而與經史並存於不朽者多
矣愚故曰立言明道惟其自得而已矣如
其因人而成欺人而傳者何足道哉愚非
惡夫經史也惡夫似經史而非者也不知
執事以為何如
第四問
江圻
===
同考試官進士畢批制策之來尚矣子能博
於研究而條舉不遺且卓有定趨其志可知
大廷之對端有望於子矣
考試官左贊善吳批以策學發問殊無難答但欲
觀士子趨向何如耳此篇首言為學終言立志其識趣過人遠
甚噫一第豈足以溷子耶敬羨敬羨
考試官左中允李批自古賢科制舉欲聞大道之
要以待非常之才不特為其决科榮身而已此篇議論竑博而
志復奇偉足以占他日不負所學矣

punctuated:
世之議哉？然好龍之喻，世每同於葉公；而楮葉之巧，俗或取於宋人。則其經與史，固未必經史若，而與經史並存於不朽者多矣。愚故曰：立言明道，惟其自得而已矣。如其因人而成、欺人而傳者，何足道哉？愚非惡夫經史也，惡夫似經史而非者也。不知執事以為何如？
第四問
江圻
同考試官進士畢批：制策之來尚矣。子能博於研究，而條舉不遺，且卓有定趨，其志可知。大廷之對，端有望於子矣。
考試官左贊善吳批：以策學發問，殊無難答，但欲觀士子趨向何如耳。此篇首言為學，終言立志，其識趣過人遠甚。噫！一第豈足以溷子耶？敬羨，敬羨！
考試官左中允李批：自古賢科制舉，欲聞大道之要，以待非常之才，不特為其决科榮身而已。此篇議論竑博，而志復奇偉，足以占他日不負所學矣。
translation_en:
…the world's criticism? Yet, as the parable of loving dragons illustrates, people commonly resemble Lord Ye; and vulgar taste sometimes prizes the ingenuity of the man of Song who fashioned a paper-mulberry leaf. Thus their classics and histories may not necessarily resemble the Classics and Histories [?], yet many attain immortality alongside them. Hence I humbly say: in establishing teachings and elucidating the Way, all depends on one's own understanding. As for works produced by relying on others and transmitted by deceiving others, how are they worth discussing? I do not dislike classics and histories; I dislike works that resemble classics and histories but are not such. I wonder what you think of this.
Fourth Question
Jiang Qi
Comment by Associate Examiner Bi, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi): Imperial policy questions have a long history. Your research is broad, and you enumerate the points without omission. Moreover, your direction is notably clear and settled, revealing your aspirations. We may indeed look forward to your response before the imperial court.
Comment by Examiner Wu, Left Admonisher: A question about the study of policy essays presents little difficulty in answering; its purpose is simply to observe the direction in which candidates incline. This essay begins by discussing learning and ends by discussing the establishment of resolve. Its discernment and aspirations far surpass those of others. Ah! How could merely passing an examination suffice to entangle you? My respect and admiration! My respect and admiration!
Comment by Examiner Li, Left Mentor: Since antiquity, special examinations for worthy men, instituted by imperial decree, have sought to hear the essentials of the Great Way and to provide for men of extraordinary talent. Their purpose has not merely been to enable men to pass examinations and bring honor upon themselves. This essay's arguments are extensive and wide-ranging, and its aspirations are exceptional and lofty. It gives ample grounds to predict that in the years ahead you will live up to your learning.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
士何為而學乎曰求諸內而已矣不求諸
內而求諸外者非學也求諸本而已矣不
求諸本而求諸末者非學也何謂外孜孜
於功利者是已何謂末規規於文詞者是
已故學而能知內外本末之分則必反之
於身以求所謂仁義禮智之性君臣父子
夫婦長幼朋友之倫講明乎古先聖賢之
道視天下事無一而非吾之所當為亦無
一而非吾之所當學吾惟俛焉於此而已
===
矣人之知不知世之用不用於我何與焉
是雖富貴貧賤死生禍福日交乎前且有
不暇顧者夫豈以一科第動其心哉雖或
為之亦自有道又豈其所能累哉嗚呼此
固士之所以為士與夫所以為學者也愚
雖未能有行焉乃所願則在是矣執事以
古今策學試諸生無亦姑就其所嘗習而
不傲以所難知且勉之以直陳所志戒之
以毋事剽竊則固拳拳接引後學之盛心

以母事剽竊則固拳拳接引後學之盛心
punctuated:
士何為而學乎？曰：「求諸內而已矣。不求諸內而求諸外者，非學也。求諸本而已矣。不求諸本而求諸末者，非學也。」何謂外？孜孜於功利者是已。何謂末？規規於文詞者是已。故學而能知內外本末之分，則必反之於身，以求所謂仁義禮智之性、君臣父子夫婦長幼朋友之倫，講明乎古先聖賢之道。視天下事，無一而非吾之所當為，亦無一而非吾之所當學。吾惟俛焉於此而已矣。人之知不知，世之用不用，於我何與焉？是雖富貴貧賤、死生禍福日交乎前，且有不暇顧者，夫豈以一科第動其心哉？雖或為之，亦自有道，又豈其所能累哉？嗚呼！此固士之所以為士，與夫所以為學者也。愚雖未能有行焉，乃所願則在是矣。

執事以古今策學試諸生，無亦姑就其所嘗習，而不傲以所難知，且勉之以直陳所志，戒之以毋事剽竊，則固拳拳接引後學之盛心
translation_en:
For what purpose does a scholar study? The answer is: “Simply to seek within himself. To seek outside rather than within is not learning. Simply to seek the root. To seek the branches rather than the root is not learning.” What is meant by the external? Diligent pursuit of success and profit. What is meant by the branches? Narrow preoccupation with literary expression. Thus, if in learning one can distinguish the internal from the external and the root from the branches, one will surely turn back to oneself, seeking the nature endowed with benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom, and the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, and friend and friend, while investigating and clarifying the Way of the ancient sages and worthies. Looking upon the affairs of the world, there is not one that I ought not to undertake, nor one that I ought not to study. I simply apply myself diligently to these things. Whether others recognize me, and whether the world employs me—what have these to do with me? Even if wealth and honor, poverty and low station, life and death, calamity and good fortune pass before such a person daily, he may have no leisure to heed them. How could success in a single examination move his heart? Even if he pursues it, he has a proper way of doing so; how could it encumber him? Alas! This is indeed what makes a scholar a scholar, and what constitutes his pursuit of learning. Though I, in my ignorance, have not yet been able to put this into practice, it is nevertheless what I aspire to.

You, honored examiners, test the students through policy questions on learning in ancient and present times. Might your intention be simply to draw upon what they have already studied, without intimidating them with what is difficult to know [?]? Moreover, you encourage them to state their aspirations frankly and admonish them not to plagiarize. This surely expresses your generous and earnest desire to welcome and guide younger students…

也夫套括之習愚亦惡之况敢效之以相
眩惑乎雖然妄肆胷臆亦不敢也請以平
日所聞於父師及涉獵於史冊者陳之于
先可乎慨自虞廷奏言試功之世遠成周
鄉舉里選之法廢是故上之所以待士者
日薄而士之所以自待者日輕此教化之
所以益微而人才之所以益衰幸而有漢
文帝者當嬴秦坑焚之後繼高祖掃除之
餘專務休息以德化民乃詔有司舉賢良
===
方正能直言極諫者親策之而親覽之後
之所謂制策者實昉於此原帝本意咨訪
懇惻眞有古帝王舍已從人好問好察之
風况詔諸侯王公卿郡守舉之於先是猶
有鄉舉里選之遺意致堂胡氏以為其來
最古是矣而以為空言其可乎哉柰何當
時所對者百餘人有鼂錯者固裒然高第
者也觀其所對如五帝神聖之說三王臣
主俱賢之說與夫五霸不及其臣之說大

鄉舉里選之法廢是故上之所以待士者
日薄而士之所以自待者日輕此教化之
所以益微而人才之所以益衰幸而有漢
文帝者當嬴秦坑焚之後繼高祖掃除之
餘專務休息以德化民乃詔有司舉賢良

有鄉舉里選之遺意致堂胡氏以爲其來

translation_en:
…indeed. I too detest the habit of relying on stock formulas; how could I dare imitate it to dazzle and mislead you? Even so, I would not dare give reckless rein to my own notions either. May I first set forth what I have ordinarily heard from my father and teachers and gleaned from historical writings?

Alas, the age when men presented their proposals and had their accomplishments tested at the court of Shun is long past, and the institutions of local recommendation and selection under the Zhou have fallen into disuse. Consequently, those above treat scholars with ever less consideration, while scholars hold themselves to ever lower standards. This is why moral instruction has grown increasingly feeble and talented men increasingly scarce. Fortunately, Emperor Wen of Han arose after the burying of scholars and burning of books under the Ying house of Qin, and following Emperor Gaozu’s clearing away of disorder. He devoted himself to allowing the people rest and recovery and transformed them through virtue. He therefore commanded the responsible officials to recommend worthy, upright men capable of speaking frankly and remonstrating without reserve. He personally posed policy questions to them and personally read their responses. What later ages called imperially commissioned policy examinations actually began here.

If we examine the emperor’s original intent, his inquiries were earnest and heartfelt. He truly possessed the spirit of the ancient sage emperors and kings, who set aside their own views to follow others and delighted in asking questions and examining matters closely. Moreover, he ordered the feudatory kings, dukes and ministers, and commandery governors to recommend candidates beforehand. This still preserved something of the intention behind local recommendation and selection. Hu Zhitang was right to regard its origins as most ancient; but could it be right to dismiss it as empty words?

Yet, among the more than one hundred men who submitted responses at the time, there was Chao Cuo, who certainly stood out among the highest ranked. title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
槩多導諛納諂之詞而畧無所建明噫錯
之對如此則其他可知已此則賢良負文
帝帝何負賢良哉武帝踵行之矣前後所
對亦以百數有董仲舒者固度越諸子者
也觀其所對如天心仁愛人君之說彊勉
學問之說正心以正朝廷之說大抵皆醇
正近理之言而非諸儒所可及噫舒之對
如此柰何帝覽而異焉乃再策之復策之
而遂有江都之命此則帝之不用舒而舒
===
之不能諫也至於曲學阿世如公孫弘雖
太常奏第居下帝則親擢為第一待詔金
馬封侯平津終其身而不衰焉噫二帝所
得之人如此則其後又何議哉是故杜欽
谷永則阿王氏論益卑矣杜鄴指陳外戚
譏切丁傅稍不負方正之名耳此皆漢史
所載後世得而論焉者也餘如王吉貢禹
之正大朱雲何武之剛方雖有嘉論史逸
其傳後世莫知矣夫制策始於漢也雖云

translation_en:
…were mostly words that encouraged flattery and offered adulation, with scarcely any constructive proposals. Alas! If Chao Cuo’s answers were like this, one can infer what the others were like. It was the men recommended as worthy and good who failed Emperor Wen; how did the emperor fail them? Emperor Wu continued this practice, and those who answered his questions over successive occasions likewise numbered in the hundreds. Among them was Dong Zhongshu, who certainly surpassed the others. Consider his answers: his explanation that Heaven’s heart cherishes the ruler with benevolence, his exhortation to diligent learning, and his teaching that the ruler should rectify his own heart in order to rectify the court. These were, for the most part, sound and upright statements consonant with principle, beyond the reach of the other scholars. Alas! With answers such as these, why was it that the emperor, having read them and recognized their exceptional merit, questioned him a second time and yet again, only to appoint him to Jiangdu? Here the emperor failed to employ Zhongshu, while Zhongshu failed to remonstrate.
As for those who distorted learning to curry favor with the age, such as Gongsun Hong, although the Chamberlain for Ceremonials ranked him low in the results submitted to the throne, the emperor personally raised him to first place. He was appointed to await imperial commands at the Golden Horse Gate and enfeoffed as Marquis of Pingjin; imperial favor toward him never waned throughout his life. Alas! If such were the men obtained by these two emperors, what more is there to say about those who came afterward? Thus Du Qin and Gu Yong ingratiated themselves with the Wang clan, and their arguments were baser still. Du Ye explicitly criticized the imperial affinal relatives, sharply censuring the Ding and Fu families, and so did somewhat live up to the designation “upright and principled.” These are all cases recorded in the histories of the Han that later generations can assess. As for others—the upright and broad-minded Wang Ji and Gong Yu, or the firm and principled Zhu Yun and He Wu—even if they offered admirable arguments, the histories failed to transmit them, and later generations have no knowledge of them.
Imperial policy questions originated under the Han. Although it is said…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
得人於玆爲盛然已不免於議如此自時
厥後固皆以此爲重然勢分隔而情意日
疎等威嚴而震怖易起甚者惡聞而諱聽
逐末而棄本詞尚浮華人務奔競噫弊也
久矣漢之初意可復見乎以唐言之則全
付之有司矣故牛僧孺輩條對甚直無所
畏避則有司坐其累劉蕡指陳時事言詞
激切則隨例而見斥取舎如此又其科目
猥多詩賦雜試故當時楊綰條奏謂非經
===
國之體請與諸科竝停賈至以爲正論且
有祇足長浮薄之風啓僥倖之路之議則
其所得之人又何暇數哉五季分離雖皆
未廢然益無足觀者以宋言之其議論則
愈多矣故欲先試論策者歐陽修等之議
也欲以德行爲先者司馬光之議也至於
分路取人之說則歐陽司馬又各不同乃
若王安石之三經不過一家之私說欲以
是而一道德興學校以復古見之偏矣善

punctuated:
得人於玆爲盛，然已不免於議如此。自時厥後，固皆以此爲重，然勢分隔而情意日疎，等威嚴而震怖易起。甚者惡聞而諱聽，逐末而棄本，詞尚浮華，人務奔競。噫！弊也久矣！漢之初意可復見乎？
以唐言之，則全付之有司矣。故牛僧孺輩條對甚直，無所畏避，則有司坐其累；劉蕡指陳時事，言詞激切，則隨例而見斥。取舎如此，又其科目猥多，詩賦雜試，故當時楊綰條奏謂非經國之體，請與諸科竝停。賈至以爲正論，且有「祇足長浮薄之風，啓僥倖之路」之議，則其所得之人又何暇數哉？五季分離，雖皆未廢，然益無足觀者。
以宋言之，其議論則愈多矣。故欲先試論策者，歐陽修等之議也；欲以德行爲先者，司馬光之議也。至於分路取人之說，則歐陽、司馬又各不同。乃若王安石之三經，不過一家之私說，欲以是而一道德、興學校，以復古，見之偏矣。善
translation_en:
… the recruitment of worthy men flourished most at this time, yet it was already open to criticism of this kind. Thereafter, successive ages indeed all attached great importance to this examination. Yet differences in power and station created barriers, and mutual understanding grew more distant by the day; the strict hierarchy of rank readily inspired fear. At worst, rulers disliked hearing advice and shunned listening, pursued secondary matters and abandoned fundamentals, while literary expression prized empty ornament and candidates devoted themselves to competing for advancement. Alas! These abuses have persisted for so long! Can the original intention of the Han ever be seen again?
In the Tang, the matter was entrusted entirely to the responsible officials. Thus, when Niu Sengru and others answered the questions with great frankness, avoiding nothing out of fear, the responsible officials were punished on their account. When Liu Fen pointed out current problems in vehement language, he was rejected in the routine course of selection. Such were their choices and rejections. Moreover, examination categories proliferated excessively, and poetry and rhapsodies were included among the tests. Yang Wan therefore submitted a detailed memorial arguing that this was no proper way to govern the state, and requesting that this examination be suspended together with the other categories. Jia Zhi regarded this as a sound argument, and further argued that the system “merely encourages a frivolous ethos and opens a path to advancement by luck.” What occasion, then, is there to enumerate the men it recruited? During the fragmentation of the Five Dynasties, none abolished it, yet there was even less worthy of attention.
In the Song, discussions of the matter became still more numerous. The proposal to test discourses and policy essays first was advanced by Ouyang Xiu and others; the proposal to give priority to virtuous conduct was Sima Guang’s. As for recruiting candidates separately by circuit, Ouyang and Sima differed in their views. Wang Anshi’s interpretations of the Three Classics were merely the private doctrines of a single school. To seek through these to unify moral teachings and promote schools, thereby restoring antiquity, was a narrow view indeed. How well …

text:
乎蘇軾有言此數者皆知其一未知其二
者也至若王旦謂條貫之嚴徒隔天下賢
士之路朱熹謂科目之設徒銷天下英雄
之氣者亦皆言其法之敝耳求其確實可
採行者其惟朱熹之私議乎論其得人則
大儒如程顥如張載如朱熹亦皆胥此焉
出豪傑之士豈有不屑者哉若夫士之所
以為學與所以為人則誠有不繫於此者
故如仲舒之下帷發憤潛心大業其為學
===
何如也進退容止非禮不行其為人何如
也雖災異之說不無可議然其大者則得
矣獨惜夫生於絕學之後而未能窺大道
之全耳吁仲舒如是則夫大儒如程朱輩
可知已此宋史所以有道學傳也然則科
舉之學不足為乎噫何言之易哉程子曰
人若不習舉業而望及第却是責天理而
不修人事又曰科舉不患妨功惟患奪志
朱子曰舉業亦不害為學前輩何嘗不應

translation_en:
…How apt was Su Shi’s remark: “These several proposals all show knowledge of one side, but not of the other.” As for Wang Dan’s assertion that stringent regulations merely block the path of worthy scholars throughout the realm, and Zhu Xi’s assertion that the establishment of examination categories merely saps the spirit of the realm’s outstanding men, these too speak only of the abuses of the system. If we seek something sound and practicable, might it be Zhu Xi’s personal proposals alone? As to the men the system recruited, great Confucian scholars such as Cheng Hao, Zhang Zai, and Zhu Xi all emerged through it. How could outstanding men have disdained it? Yet how a scholar pursues learning and conducts himself does indeed involve matters independent of it.

Consider, then, Zhongshu: he lowered his curtains, applied himself with determination, and devoted his mind to the great undertaking of learning. What was his pursuit of learning like? In his movements and bearing, he did nothing contrary to ritual propriety. What was his personal conduct like? Although his explanations of calamities and anomalies are not beyond criticism, he grasped what was essential. One can only regret that, born after the transmission of learning had been broken, he could not perceive the Great Way in its entirety. Ah! If Zhongshu was like this, we can understand what the great Confucian scholars, such as Cheng and Zhu, were like. This is why the History of the Song contains “Biographies of Scholars of the Learning of the Way.”

Does it follow, then, that study for the civil-service examinations is unworthy of pursuit? Alas! How lightly such words are spoken! Master Cheng said: “If a man does not practice examination composition but hopes to pass, he is demanding something of Heaven’s principle while failing to attend to human duties.” He also said: “The concern with the examinations is not that they impede one’s efforts, but that they divert one’s resolve.” Master Zhu said: “Examination composition does not harm the pursuit of learning either. title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
舉又曰非是科舉累人自是人累科舉由
是觀之是豈可以為不足為哉但其於內
外本末輕重先後之間則不可以不辨而
其要又在於立志耳志不先定而汩溺於
此則得失之念未免橫於胷中僥倖冒為
奔逐無已雖或偶捷一第其驕淫縱恣將
無所不至苟焉不得則怨天尤人悲愁放
曠將無所不為此則名教中之罪人又何
可謂之士哉愚生也鄙雖曰學未聞道然
===
此志則亦未肯若是乎其卑也况當
聖明之世道學大明之日又豈敢甘為自暴自
棄者哉第今日之所以抱牒而來者以此
執事之所問者以此故不敢不以所誦習
者為對而區區之志尚未敢遽陳也倘執
事進而教之使得以畢所志焉固所願也
他日得與
大廷之對尚當以董子為法以公孫弘為戒
庶幾如昔人所謂上不負

此則得失之念未免横於胷中僥倖冒爲
奔逐無已雖或偶捷一第其驕淫縱恣將
無所不至苟爲不得則怨天尤人悲愁放
曠將無所不爲此則名教中之罪人又何
可謂之士哉愚生也鄙雖曰學未聞道然
===
此志則亦未肯若是乎其卑也況當
聖明之世道學大明之日又豈敢甘爲自暴自
棄者哉第今日之所以抱牒而來者以此
執事之所問者以此故不敢不以所誦習
者爲對而區區之志尚未敢遽陳也倘執
事進而敎之使得以畢所志焉固所願也
他日得與
大廷之對尚當以董子爲法以公孫弘爲戒
庶幾如昔人所謂上不負
punctuated: 舉。」又曰：「非是科舉累人，自是人累科舉。」由是觀之，是豈可以為不足為哉？但其於內外本末輕重先後之間，則不可以不辨，而其要又在於立志耳。志不先定，而汩溺於此，則得失之念未免橫於胷中，僥倖冒為，奔逐無已。雖或偶捷一第，其驕淫縱恣將無所不至；苟焉不得，則怨天尤人，悲愁放曠，將無所不為。此則名教中之罪人，又何可謂之士哉？愚生也鄙，雖曰學未聞道，然此志則亦未肯若是乎其卑也。况當聖明之世，道學大明之日，又豈敢甘為自暴自棄者哉？第今日之所以抱牒而來者以此，執事之所問者以此，故不敢不以所誦習者為對，而區區之志尚未敢遽陳也。倘執事進而教之，使得以畢所志焉，固所願也。他日得與大廷之對，尚當以董子為法，以公孫弘為戒，庶幾如昔人所謂上不負
translation_en:
…sit the examinations.” He also said: “It is not the examinations that burden people; people themselves burden the examinations.” Viewed in this light, how could one regard examination study as unworthy of pursuit? Yet one must distinguish between the inner and the outer, the root and the branches, the weightier and the lighter, and what comes first and what comes afterward. The essential point, moreover, lies in setting one’s resolve. If one does not first establish that resolve but becomes submerged in this pursuit, thoughts of success and failure will inevitably fill one’s breast. One will recklessly seek success through luck and chase after it without end. Even if one happens to pass an examination, one’s arrogance, excess, and self-indulgence will know no bounds. If one fails, one will blame Heaven and resent others, sink into sorrow, and cast off restraint, stopping at nothing. Such a person is an offender against the moral teachings. How could he be called a scholar?

I am an ignorant student. Though I have studied without yet apprehending the Way, I have nevertheless been unwilling to let my aspirations sink so low. Moreover, living in an age of sagely and enlightened rule, when the Learning of the Way shines so brightly, how could I dare willingly to abandon and cast myself away? Yet this is why I have come today bearing my examination papers, and this is what you have asked about. I therefore dare not refrain from answering on the basis of what I have recited and studied, though I have not yet ventured hastily to state my own humble aspirations. If you would receive and instruct me, allowing me fully to realize those aspirations, that is indeed what I desire. Should I someday have the opportunity to answer questions at the imperial court, I shall take Master Dong as my model and Gongsun Hong as my warning. Thus I may perhaps fulfill what a man of former times expressed as ‘above, not failing…’

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天子下不負所學也雖然其進其退其取其舍
是在於執事爾矣
第五問
王良策
同考試官知縣林批先王患教化不達於天下故
制為鄉飲酒禮凡儀文笙歌各有深義無非欲令觀聽者興其和順
之心焉耳然行之不以忠信則亦虛矣此篇說出我
聖祖制禮深意復欲有司以忠信行之是達禮樂之本者錄之
考試官左賛善吳批今天下鄉飲酒禮未嘗不行顧
有司視為文具漫不加意如子言恪遵
聖訓以忠信之心行之則王道真易易也宜錄出以為有司者告
考試官左中允李批考據精詳議論懇切有志於化
民成俗者觀於此而已矣
聖人之致治也興禮樂而已矣聖人之立
教也同風俗而已矣夫天下至大非度之
所能及生民至眾非數之所能領聖人以
一身而託於至大至眾之上將使至大至
眾者無一而不如吾之心吾之心欲其善

天子，下不負所學也。雖然，其進其退，其取其舍，是在於執事爾矣。

第五問
王良策

同考試官知縣林批：先王患教化不達於天下，故制為鄉飲酒禮。凡儀文笙歌，各有深義，無非欲令觀聽者興其和順之心焉耳。然行之不以忠信，則亦虛矣。此篇說出我聖祖制禮深意，復欲有司以忠信行之，是達禮樂之本者，錄之。

考試官左賛善吳批：今天下鄉飲酒禮未嘗不行，顧有司視為文具，漫不加意。如子言，恪遵聖訓，以忠信之心行之，則王道真易易也。宜錄出，以為有司者告。

考試官左中允李批：考據精詳，議論懇切，有志於化民成俗者，觀於此而已矣。

聖人之致治也，興禮樂而已矣；聖人之立教也，同風俗而已矣。夫天下至大，非度之所能及；生民至眾，非數之所能領。聖人以一身而託於至大至眾之上，將使至大至眾者無一而不如吾之心。吾之心欲其善
translation_en:
…the Son of Heaven, and below, not fail what I have learned. Nevertheless, whether I am advanced or turned back, selected or rejected, rests solely with you.

Fifth Question
Policy essay by Wang Liang

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, District Magistrate: The former kings were concerned that moral instruction did not reach all under Heaven, and therefore instituted the village drinking ceremony. Its ceremonial forms, mouth-organ music, and singing each have profound significance: all are intended to awaken harmonious and compliant sentiments in those who watch and listen. Yet if it is performed without loyalty and trustworthiness, it too becomes empty. This essay explains the profound intention of our sagely founder in instituting the ceremony, and further urges the responsible officials to perform it with loyalty and trustworthiness. Its author understands the foundations of rites and music. Select it for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Wu, Left Assistant Adviser: Today the village drinking ceremony is indeed performed throughout the realm. Yet the responsible officials regard it as a mere formality and carelessly give it no attention. If, as you say, they scrupulously followed the sacred instructions and performed it with hearts imbued with loyalty and trustworthiness, the kingly Way would truly be very easy to realize. This essay should be selected for publication to instruct those serving as responsible officials.

Comment by Examiner Li, Left Companion: The examination of evidence is precise and detailed, and the argument earnest and compelling. Those intent on transforming the people and establishing good customs need only look here.

To bring about good government, the sage simply promotes rites and music; to establish moral instruction, the sage simply unifies customs. Now, all under Heaven is so vast that measurement cannot encompass it; the people are so numerous that calculation cannot comprehend them. The sage, a single person entrusted with a position above this immense realm and this multitude, would ensure that within such vastness and among such numbers there is nothing that does not accord with his own heart. When my heart desires that they be good…

也，則不必爵賞而民勸；吾之心欲其無惡也，則不必刑罰而民不犯。此其道何繇哉？亦惟興禮樂以爲治，同風俗以爲教而已矣。夫禮有五，凡以制外也；樂有六，凡以脩内也。自造始之教而言，謂之風；自習而尚之而言，謂之俗。鄉飲乃禮之一節，而風俗係習之所成。執事舉安上治民、移風易俗之説，而獨揭鄉飲酒禮以爲問，無乃以禮始諸飲食，而爭每出於大欲，成周載在《儀禮》以爲政教之本，而孔子以爲王道之易易也哉？愚也嘗聞其槩矣，敢掇拾以對。

translation_en:
…then the people are encouraged without any need to confer ranks or rewards. If my heart desires that they commit no evil, then the people refrain from transgression without any need for punishments. By what means is this achieved? Simply by promoting rites and music as the means of government, and bringing customs into accord as the means of instruction. Rites have five categories, all intended to regulate outward conduct; music has six forms, all intended to cultivate the inner person. Viewed in terms of the instruction that first establishes them, customs are called feng; viewed in terms of what people practice and esteem, they are called su. The district drinking ceremony is but one component of ritual, while customs are formed through habitual practice. You, sir, invoke the teachings concerning securing those above and governing the people, and transforming prevailing ways and changing customs, yet single out the district drinking ceremony for your question. Is this perhaps because rites originated in eating and drinking, while contention so often arises from powerful desires; because the fully established Zhou dynasty recorded this ceremony in the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili) as a foundation of government and instruction; and because Confucius regarded it as making the Kingly Way exceedingly easy to realize? I, ignorant though I am, have heard something of its general principles and venture to gather what I know in reply.
In ancient times, the sages instituted rites to order the states and created music to bring spirits and human beings into harmony. Rites were practiced at court, yet among the people of distant regions there were those who never witnessed them in their entire lives. Music was performed in the ancestral temples, yet among the communities of distant regions there were those who never heard it in their entire lives. Even when people had seen and heard these things, the sages still feared that they would not follow their lead. Suppose people had never seen what are called rites, and one reproached them, saying, “Why do you not turn and move, bend and bow, in conformity with ritual?” Who among them would not look at one another in astonishment? If they had never heard what is called…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
謂樂者而責之曰何不雍雍和易而比於
樂乎其誰不掩口而笑是以羣之以會聚
而不免凌犯之患接之以飲食而不免爭
鬭之虞貴財而賤禮獄蕃而禍作聖人之
心蓋有不勝其憂者矣於是制為飲宴之
禮頒於鄉校之間辨以儀文浹以風雅自
邑而郡而天下俾其帥而行之名之曰鄉
飲酒禮是非徒以羣居焉也亦非專以飲
食焉也一鄉之中其必有賢能者乎飲以

…what is called music, yet rebuke them, saying, “Why do you not conduct yourselves harmoniously and amiably, in accord with music?” Who among them would not cover his mouth and laugh? Thus, when people are brought together in gatherings, the danger of encroachment and affront remains; when they are entertained with food and drink, the risk of contention and fighting remains. Wealth is prized and ritual held cheap; lawsuits multiply and calamities arise. The sages’ hearts surely could not bear such anxiety.

They therefore established rites for drinking and feasting and promulgated them among the local schools, distinguishing ranks through ceremonial forms and permeating the people with the influence of the Airs and Odes. From district to prefecture and throughout the realm, they caused people to follow and practice these rites, naming them the village wine-drinking ceremony. This was not merely a means of gathering people together, nor was it solely concerned with eating and drinking.

Within any village, must there not be men of worth and ability? Wine is served to honor them as guests and recommend them for office; otherwise, the ceremony is not held. Thus there is a village wine-drinking ceremony for the worthy and able. Within any village, must there not be elders? Wine is served to honor and sustain them; otherwise, the ceremony is not held. Thus there is a village wine-drinking ceremony for the elders. Within any village, must there not be those who toil diligently? Wine is served at the year-end agricultural sacrifice (zha); otherwise, the ceremony is not held. Thus there is a village wine-drinking ceremony for those who toil diligently. Within any village, must there not be those who practice archery? Wine is served so that their virtue may be observed; otherwise, the ceremony is not held. Thus there is a village wine-drinking ceremony for those who practice archery.

These are what earlier Confucian scholars called the four forms of this rite. They are recorded in the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili), where clear evidence for them can be found; they are further explained in “The Meaning of the Village Wine-Drinking Ceremony,” where they are set forth lucidly and intelligibly. 不順者乎是以繼之以樂工入而升堂歌
鹿鳴四牡皇皇者華每一篇而一終吹笙
者入於堂下奏南陔白華華黍亦一篇而
一終此非升歌笙入各三終者耶及笙與
歌皆畢矣則堂上歌魚麗堂下之笙則由
庚焉堂上歌南有嘉魚堂下之笙則崇丘
焉堂上歌南山有臺堂下之笙則由儀焉
punctuated:
聚，當行此禮，不特四者而已者，蓋飲不以禮，不免於亂，而非禮之飲，當曲為之防耳。聖人所以使人必飲以禮，而繼之以樂者，蓋其禮至辨而詳，其樂至和而平。人惟不知禮也，故有強暴者矣；人惟不知樂也，故有乖戾者矣。是以示之以禮，有獻祭之儀焉，有爼豆之數焉，有賓主僎介之位焉，有謀介速迎之序焉，有進退升降之等焉，有興坐酬酢之節焉。一揖似敬矣，而必至於三揖三讓；再拜似恭矣，而必至於三拜百拜。是禮也，日暮人倦而不已，孰有行之而不順者乎？
是以繼之以樂，工入而升堂，歌《鹿鳴》《四牡》《皇皇者華》，每一篇而一終。吹笙者入於堂下，奏《南陔》《白華》《華黍》，亦一篇而一終。此非升歌笙入各三終者耶？及笙與歌皆畢矣，則堂上歌《魚麗》，堂下之笙則《由庚》焉；堂上歌《南有嘉魚》，堂下之笙則《崇丘》焉；堂上歌《南山有臺》，堂下之笙則《由儀》焉。
translation_en:
…gathering, this rite should be performed, and not only on those four occasions. For drinking without ritual propriety inevitably leads to disorder, and safeguards against improper drinking must therefore cover every detail. The reason the sages required people to drink according to ritual and followed it with music was that these rites make distinctions with the utmost precision, while the music brings the utmost harmony and balance. It is because people do not understand ritual that some become violent; it is because people do not understand music that some become unruly. Thus people are instructed through ritual: there are prescribed forms for presenting wine and making offerings; prescribed numbers of offering stands and vessels; positions for the guest, host, assisting dignitary, and assistant guest; a sequence for selecting the assistant guest, inviting the guests, and welcoming them; gradations in advancing, withdrawing, ascending, and descending; and rules for rising, sitting, and exchanging cups. A single bow with clasped hands might seem respectful, yet three such bows and three acts of yielding are required. Bowing twice might seem reverent, yet one must proceed to three bows and a hundred bows. These rites continue even when evening falls and people grow weary. Who could perform them without becoming compliant?
They are therefore followed by music. The musicians enter and ascend the hall, singing “The Deer Call” (Lu ming), “The Four Stallions” (Si mu), and “Splendid Are the Flowers” (Huanghuang zhe hua), each piece once in full. The mouth-organ players enter below the hall and perform “The Southern Slope” (Nan gai), “White Flowers” (Bai hua), and “Millet in Flower” (Hua shu), likewise each piece once in full. Is this not what is meant by the singers ascending and the mouth-organ players entering, each performing three complete pieces? Once both the mouth-organ music and the singing have finished, “Fish in the Weir” (Yu li) is sung above in the hall, followed by “Following the Path” (You geng) on the mouth organs below; “In the South Are Fine Fish” (Nan you jia yu) is sung above, followed by “The Lofty Hill” (Chong qiu) on the mouth organs below; and “On the Southern Mountain Is Terrace Grass” (Nan shan you tai) is sung above, followed by “Following Proper Forms” (You yi) on the mouth organs below.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
及其間歌既畢矣工歌關雎則笙吹鵲巢
合之工歌葛覃則笙吹采蘩合之工歌卷
耳則笙吹采蘋合之此非間歌合樂各三
終者耶是樂也其聲足樂而不流孰有聽
之而不和者耶夫聖人之禮樂如此將見
天下之人見先於祭獻則知不忘本矣祀
以蘋蘩則知所貴者誠矣賢者爲主則知
懋德可尊矣老者爲賓則知高年可恭矣
揖讓拜起則知謙恭撙節之可學矣升降
===
進退則知折旋俯仰之可習矣聞鹿鳴四
牡之什則知慕於賓賢矣聽白華南陔之
聲則知孝於父母矣盈雅音正聲之奏則
知說於和樂矣月而習之歲而行之優而
柔之而使自趨之感而慕之而自化之不
覺其自納于禮樂之域而於變於可封之
俗也
朝廷雖設刑以罰惡而天下無惡之可刑矣
雖懸賞以旌善而天下不勝善之可賞矣

俗也

雖懸賞以旌善而天下不勝善之可賞矣
punctuated:
及其間歌既畢矣，工歌《關雎》，則笙吹《鵲巢》合之；工歌《葛覃》，則笙吹《采蘩》合之；工歌《卷耳》，則笙吹《采蘋》合之。此非間歌、合樂各三終者耶？是樂也，其聲足樂而不流，孰有聽之而不和者耶？夫聖人之禮樂如此，將見天下之人，見先於祭獻，則知不忘本矣；祀以蘋蘩，則知所貴者誠矣；賢者爲主，則知懋德可尊矣；老者爲賓，則知高年可恭矣；揖讓拜起，則知謙恭撙節之可學矣；升降進退，則知折旋俯仰之可習矣；聞《鹿鳴》《四牡》之什，則知慕於賓賢矣；聽《白華》《南陔》之聲，則知孝於父母矣；盈雅音正聲之奏，則知說於和樂矣。月而習之，歲而行之，優而柔之而使自趨之，感而慕之而自化之，不覺其自納于禮樂之域，而於變於可封之俗也。
朝廷雖設刑以罰惡，而天下無惡之可刑矣；雖懸賞以旌善，而天下不勝善之可賞矣。
translation_en:
When the alternating songs have ended, the musicians sing “The Ospreys” (Guanju), while the mouth organs play “The Magpie’s Nest” (Quechao) in accompaniment; the musicians sing “The Spreading Kudzu” (Getan), while the mouth organs play “Gathering Southernwood” (Caifan) in accompaniment; and the musicians sing “Gathering Cocklebur” (Juan’er), while the mouth organs play “Gathering Duckweed” (Caiping) in accompaniment. Is this not the alternating singing and the combined music, each performed through three pieces? Such music gives sufficient pleasure through its sounds without leading to excess. Who could hear it and fail to become harmonious?
Such are the sages’ rites and music. We shall see that when people throughout the realm observe priority being given to sacrificial offerings, they learn not to forget their origins. When duckweed and southernwood are used in sacrifice, they learn that sincerity is what is prized. When the worthy serve as hosts, they learn that abundant virtue deserves honor. When the aged serve as guests, they learn that advanced years deserve respect. Through bowing, yielding precedence, prostrating themselves, and rising, they learn that humility, reverence, and restraint can be acquired. Through ascending, descending, advancing, and withdrawing, they learn that turning, bending, and straightening the body can be practiced. Hearing the songs “The Deer Call” (Luming) and “The Four Stallions” (Simu), they learn to aspire to honoring the worthy as guests. Listening to the melodies of “White Blossoms” (Baihua) and “The Southern Terrace” (Nanhai), they learn filial devotion to their parents. Filled with the performance of elegant melodies and correct sounds [?], they learn to delight in harmony and joy. Practicing these every month and performing them every year, they are gently nurtured and led to pursue them of their own accord; moved to admiration, they transform themselves. Without realizing it, they enter the realm of rites and music, and their customs are transformed until all are worthy of receiving a fief.
Although the imperial court establishes punishments to penalize evil, there will be no evil throughout the realm to punish. Although it offers rewards to commend goodness, there will be more goodness throughout the realm than can possibly be rewarded.

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
由是觀之天下之言致治而立教者尚有
急於興禮樂以同風俗者乎是故聖人務
焉夫何秦承周衰漢承秦亂遂至禮廢樂
崩使聖人之教不行於後世而天下之民
日入於罪戾也可勝歎哉至後漢明帝時
始詔郡縣通行於學校其後又廢矣至西
晉泰始間乃復講論僅行於辟雍唐之貞
觀詔天下通行之或於貢士或於季冬宋
之淳化詔有司講求之而命撰樂章改宴
===
鄉飲是皆蔽於一曲而不見聖人之全因
陋就簡而不臻先王之盛亦何望其能興
禮樂而同風俗如成周也哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝以脩明禮樂表正風俗莫有要於
斯禮者乃備之官制著之
大誥又嚴之
大明律一則曰豐儉得宜敢有喧嘩失禮者
以禮責之一則曰叙長幼論賢良別奸頑
異罪人大哉

焉夫何秦承周衰漢承秦亂遂至禮廢樂
崩使聖人之教不行於後世而天下之民
日入於罪戾也可勝歎哉至後漢明帝時

晉泰始間乃復講論僅行於辟雍唐之貞
觀詔天下通行之或於貢士或於季冬宋
之淳化詔有司講求之而命撰樂章攷宴
===
鄉飲是皆蔽於一曲而不見聖人之全因
陋就簡而不臻先王之盛亦何望其能興
禮樂而同風俗如成周也哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝以脩明禮樂表正風俗莫有要於
斯禮者乃備之官制著之
大誥又嚴之
大明律一則曰豐儉得宜敢有喧嘩失禮者
以禮責之一則曰敘長幼論賢良別奸頑
異罪人大哉
punctuated:
由是觀之，天下之言致治而立教者，尚有急於興禮樂以同風俗者乎？是故聖人務焉。夫何秦承周衰，漢承秦亂，遂至禮廢樂崩，使聖人之教不行於後世，而天下之民日入於罪戾也，可勝歎哉！至後漢明帝時，始詔郡縣通行於學校，其後又廢矣。至西晉泰始間，乃復講論，僅行於辟雍。唐之貞觀，詔天下通行之，或於貢士，或於季冬。宋之淳化，詔有司講求之，而命撰樂章，改宴鄉飲。是皆蔽於一曲，而不見聖人之全，因陋就簡，而不臻先王之盛，亦何望其能興禮樂而同風俗，如成周也哉！

洪惟我太祖高皇帝，以脩明禮樂、表正風俗，莫有要於斯禮者，乃備之官制，著之《大誥》，又嚴之《大明律》。一則曰：「豐儉得宜，敢有喧嘩失禮者，以禮責之。」一則曰：「叙長幼，論賢良，別奸頑，異罪人。」大哉！
translation_en:
Viewed in this light, among those throughout the realm who speak of achieving good government and establishing moral instruction, is there any task more urgent than promoting rites and music to bring customs into harmony? This is why the sages devoted themselves to it. Yet how was it that Qin inherited Zhou’s decline, and Han inherited Qin’s disorder, until rites fell into disuse and music collapsed, preventing the sages’ teaching from being practiced in later ages, while the people of the realm sank daily into wrongdoing? How deeply lamentable!

Only in the time of Emperor Ming of the Later Han was an edict first issued requiring commanderies and counties to practice this rite universally in their schools; afterward it again fell into disuse. During the Taishi era of the Western Jin, it was once more discussed and studied, but practiced only at the Biyong, the imperial ritual academy. During the Zhenguan era of the Tang, an edict ordered its universal practice throughout the realm, either when presenting candidates for examination or in the last month of winter. During the Chunhua era of the Song, the responsible officials were ordered to investigate it, and commands were issued to compose musical texts and replace banquets with the community drinking ceremony [?]. All these efforts were confined to a single aspect and failed to perceive the entirety of the sages’ teaching. They made do with rudimentary and simplified arrangements, never attaining the flourishing institutions of the former kings. How, then, could one expect them to promote rites and music and bring customs into harmony as in the perfected Zhou order?

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao considered no rite more essential than this one for cultivating and clarifying rites and music and setting customs aright. He therefore provided fully for it in the official regulations, set it forth in the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao), and further enforced it through the Great Ming Code (Da Ming lü). One provision states: “Let lavishness and frugality be appropriately balanced. Should anyone dare to make a disturbance or violate ritual propriety, hold him accountable according to the rites.” Another states: “Order the old and young by seniority, assess the worthy and good, distinguish the wicked and recalcitrant, and set offenders apart.” Great indeed is…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皇言警俗之深意如天之大福雖堯舜禹湯文
武之心典謨訓誥之文無以加也今海內
孟春之望行之孟冬之朔又行之信可以
懸諸日月頒之天下者矣窮鄉下邑之所
至愚極賤之氓皆得拭目以觀扶杖而聽
宜古禮可復而風俗可同也而執事猶曰
戶尚罕可封之俗士未必崇偕讓之節是
豈禮樂之不足以化人哉愚以為禮樂者
化民之具也忠信者禮樂之本也化民有
===
道禮樂而已矣禮樂無他忠信而已矣苟
不知化理之大本而徒為粉飾之虛文則
訐愎者無柔和之期狠戾者違貞順之軌
無恠乎世道之日衰也昔舜庭奏樂而鳥
獸率舞燕谷吹律而草木遂萌雖天下之
至蠢而無情者尚能感而通之而況於人
乎為今之道欲變今之俗亦在有司者加
之意焉耳必敬脩先王之禮恪遵
聖祖之訓存忠信之心盡化導之術行之而不

化民之具也忠信者禮樂之本也化民有
===
道禮樂而已矣禮樂無他忠信而已矣茍
不知化理之大本而徒爲粉飾之虚文則

乎爲今之道欲變今之俗亦在有司者加
之意焉耳必敬脩先王之禮恪遵
聖祖之訓存忠信之心盡化導之術行之而不
punctuated: 皇言警俗之深意，如天之大福，雖堯舜禹湯文武之心、典謨訓誥之文，無以加也。今海內孟春之望行之，孟冬之朔又行之，信可以懸諸日月、頒之天下者矣。窮鄉下邑之所，至愚極賤之氓，皆得拭目以觀，扶杖而聽，宜古禮可復而風俗可同也。而執事猶曰：「戶尚罕可封之俗，士未必崇偕讓之節。」是豈禮樂之不足以化人哉？愚以為禮樂者，化民之具也；忠信者，禮樂之本也。化民有道，禮樂而已矣；禮樂無他，忠信而已矣。苟不知化理之大本，而徒為粉飾之虛文，則訐愎者無柔和之期，狠戾者違貞順之軌，無恠乎世道之日衰也。昔舜庭奏樂而鳥獸率舞，燕谷吹律而草木遂萌。雖天下之至蠢而無情者，尚能感而通之，而況於人乎？為今之道，欲變今之俗，亦在有司者加之意焉耳。必敬脩先王之禮，恪遵聖祖之訓，存忠信之心，盡化導之術，行之而不
translation_en:
…The profound intent of these imperial words to admonish prevailing customs is a blessing as vast as Heaven. Even the hearts of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and the writings in the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Announcements of the Book of Documents, could add nothing to it. Now throughout the realm this rite is performed on the fifteenth day of the first month of spring and again on the first day of the first month of winter. Truly, it may be hung alongside the sun and moon and promulgated throughout the world. Even in remote villages and humble towns, the most ignorant and lowly people can all wipe their eyes to watch and lean on their staffs to listen. Surely the ancient rites should thereby be restored and customs brought into harmony. Yet you, honored examiners, still say: “Households whose virtue merits enfeoffment remain rare, and scholars do not necessarily esteem the propriety of mutual deference.” Can this mean that rites and music are insufficient to transform people?

In my humble view, rites and music are the instruments for transforming the people; loyalty and trustworthiness are the foundation of rites and music. The way to transform the people is simply rites and music; rites and music are nothing other than loyalty and trustworthiness. If one fails to understand the great foundation of moral transformation and governance and merely produces empty forms for outward embellishment, the faultfinding and obstinate will never become gentle and harmonious, while the fierce and perverse will stray from the path of uprightness and obedience. No wonder the moral condition of the age declines daily. In former times, when music was performed in Shun’s court, birds and beasts all danced; when pitch pipes were sounded in the valley of Yan, plants and trees began to sprout. If even the dullest and unfeeling things in the world can respond and be moved, how much more so human beings!

The course to follow today, if we wish to change present customs, lies simply in the responsible officials giving this their attention. They must reverently cultivate the rites of the former kings, scrupulously follow the instructions of the sagely founding ancestor, preserve hearts of loyalty and trustworthiness, and fully employ the means of moral transformation and guidance, putting them into practice without…

title: 嘉靖二十五年順天府鄉試錄
text:
輟用之而能久必使觀者皆踴躍聽者皆
感泣如裴耀卿之爲宣州也如是而天下
之民有不回心而嚮道不反薄而歸厚吾
不信也將見比屋可封士崇偕讓不獨在
堯舜之時而復見於
今日矣又何成周之治不可及哉謹對
alt_text:

感泣如裴耀卿之爲宣州也如是而天下

不信也將見比屋可封士崇偕讓不獨在

今日矣又何成周之治不可及哉謹對
punctuated: 輟，用之而能久，必使觀者皆踴躍，聽者皆感泣，如裴耀卿之爲宣州也。如是而天下之民有不回心而嚮道、不反薄而歸厚，吾不信也。將見比屋可封，士崇偕讓，不獨在堯舜之時，而復見於今日矣。又何成周之治不可及哉？謹對。
translation_en: …ceasing, and sustain its application over time: surely all who witness it will leap with joy, and all who hear it will be moved to tears, as when Pei Yaoqing governed Xuanzhou. If this is done, I cannot believe that any among the people of the realm would fail to turn their hearts toward the Way and forsake meanness for generosity. We shall then see every household worthy of enfeoffment and scholars honoring mutual deference [?]. Such things will belong not only to the age of Yao and Shun but will appear again today. Why, then, should the good government of the Zhou at its height be beyond our reach? Respectfully submitted in reply.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the bingwu year of Jiajing [1546], the Provincial Examination was held in Shuntian Prefecture. His Majesty appointed your servant Ben, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, and your servant Shan, Left Admonisher to the Heir Apparent, as Examiners. From our taking leave of His Majesty and entering the examination compound through the completion of this record, your servant Ben has already recounted every matter in his preface. What remains for your servant Shan to say? I reverently reflect that our August Emperor has now occupied the throne for twenty-five years. The Way shines forth, his transforming influence works wondrously, and literary culture flourishes brightly. Thus scholars bearing their literary accomplishments have gathered like clouds in the capital to sit the examination. Their writings glittered brilliantly, dazzling our eyes; indeed, there were more worthy of selection than we could take. Ah, how flourishing an age!

I humbly observe that, since antiquity, talent has never flourished more abundantly than under Tang and Yu, or in the established Zhou dynasty. translation_en:
…“it was then that talent flourished most.” True indeed! Yet when Confucius enumerates them, he speaks of only five under Shun and nine under King Wu. Why is this? What the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents say concerns those evident in their own time; those whom Confucius discusses are all men whose achievements and virtue were especially renowned in later generations. Looking back from today, the five were Yu, Ji, Xie, Gao Yao, and Bo Yi; the nine were Dan, Duke of Zhou; Shi, Duke of Shao; Wang, the Grand Duke; the Duke of Bi; the Duke of Rong; Tai Dian; Hong Yao; San Yisheng; and Nangong Kuo. Their achievements and virtue are still praised today without abatement. Since the Zhou, although no age has lacked talented men, how many men like these could one find? Confucius also said, “Talent is hard to find.” Is this not so?
Our dynasty established examinations to select men for office, consulting antiquity to determine its regulations. An examination is held every three years; across the two capitals and all the provinces, each round yields more than a thousand men in total. From…

punctuated: 國初迄今，名臣碩輔，後先相望，由此其選，眞有以邁唐虞成周，不可以數計者。迨我皇上，亦凡九舉矣。卽畿內所舉，已千餘人，曾有若人者幾乎？夫必勳業樹於當時，然後休光垂於後世。今之與茲錄者，又百三十五人，夫孰不曰俊乂乎，濟濟乎？雖有司亦莫不云然也。斯時則然，他日校于南宫，對于大廷，又其後服有官政，則有不盡然者。求其光明俊偉，卓然表見于時者，且不知有幾，况後世乎？
translation_en: …from the dynasty’s founding down to the present, renowned ministers and eminent councillors have followed one another in succession, selected through this system. Truly, in this it has surpassed the ages of Tang and Yu and the flourishing Zhou; their numbers defy counting. Under our present Emperor, too, the examination has now been held nine times. Those selected within the metropolitan region alone already number more than a thousand. Yet how many have there been like those men? Meritorious achievements must first be established in one’s own time before their lustre can descend to later generations. Those included in this record now number another 135. Who would not call them outstanding talents, a splendid gathering? Even the responsible officials all say so. At this moment, that is indeed the case. Yet when they are later examined at the Ministry of Rites and give their replies in the imperial court, and subsequently undertake the duties of government office, some will not entirely live up to this judgment. Even among their contemporaries, who knows how many will distinguish themselves conspicuously through their integrity, brilliance, and exceptional ability—much less among later generations?

Yet I, your unworthy servant, believe that among them there must be men of this kind. Why? The capital is the foremost seat of moral excellence.
